UK: After the last Ice Age, hunter-gatherers moved into Britain while it was still joined to Europe by land. Rising seas cut it off as an island around 6000 BC. Farming, pottery and long barrow tombs arrived with newcomers from the continent from about 4000 BC, and people began clearing forests for fields.

Neolithic farmers built great ceremonial monuments, including the stone circles at Stonehenge (begun c. 3000 BC) and Avebury and the village of Skara Brae in Orkney. Around 2500 BC Beaker people arrived from the continent, bringing metalworking and new burial customs. They largely replaced the earlier population and began Britain's Bronze Age.

Bronze Age Britain was a land of farming communities, field systems and round barrow burials. Cornish tin was valuable for making bronze and drew trade from across Europe. Chiefs grew rich from metalwork, and later in the period people built more permanent farms and hillside enclosures as the climate cooled.

Iron working spread across Britain from about 800 BC, and hillforts multiplied as tribal chiefs competed for land and cattle. The population lived mostly in round houses on scattered farms. Celtic languages and art styles linked Britain to Gaul and the wider Celtic world across the Channel.

Iron Age tribes ruled Britain and Ireland from hillforts and farmsteads, with druids serving as priests, judges and keepers of tradition. Mediterranean traders knew the islands mainly as a source of tin. Daily life centered on mixed farming, cattle herding and frequent small wars between neighbouring chiefdoms.

Britain remained a patchwork of Celtic tribes living in round houses and defended hillforts such as Maiden Castle. Ireland and Scotland had their own warrior societies and crannogs, or lake dwellings. Contact with the continent continued through trade in metals, salt and luxury goods along the Atlantic coast.

Around 325 BC the Greek explorer Pytheas of Massalia sailed around Britain, giving the earliest written description of the islands. He found tin traders in Cornwall and farming peoples elsewhere. Celtic tribes, druid religion and hillfort chiefdoms still shaped politics and life across Britain and Ireland.

British tribes grew more organized, with larger territories and fortified centers. La Tène style Celtic art flourished on shields, torcs and mirrors. Trade with Gaul expanded, and southern Britain was increasingly tied to continental Celtic peoples, some of whom would later cross the Channel to settle.

Belgic peoples from northern Gaul settled in southeast Britain, bringing coinage and wheel-thrown pottery. Large tribal centers called oppida appeared, foreshadowing towns. Southern tribes traded with the Roman world through Gaul, importing wine and luxuries, while the north and west remained more traditional.

Julius Caesar raided Britain in 55 and 54 BC, defeated the chief Cassivellaunus and took tribute, but did not stay. Afterward southern kings such as Cunobelinus of the Catuvellauni grew powerful and traded heavily with Roman Gaul, adopting Roman goods and coin styles while staying independent.

Emperor Claudius invaded in AD 43, and Rome conquered most of southern Britain within decades. Boudica of the Iceni led a fierce revolt in 60 to 61, burning London and Colchester before being crushed. Roman towns, roads and villas began to spread, while Scotland and Ireland stayed outside Roman rule.

Roman Britain settled into prosperity under governors and legions based at York, Chester and Caerleon. Hadrian's Wall, begun in 122, marked the northern frontier against the Picts, and the Antonine Wall briefly pushed it further. Towns such as London grew, and local elites adopted Latin, baths and villas.

Britain was a wealthy Roman province, divided into two in the early 200s. Emperor Septimius Severus campaigned in Scotland and died at York in 211. During the empire's third-century crisis, Britain briefly formed part of breakaway regimes, and coastal forts were built against Saxon pirates.

Fourth-century Roman Britain saw rich villas and the spread of Christianity, but also growing raids by Picts, Scots from Ireland and Saxons. Constantine the Great was proclaimed emperor at York in 306. Generals repeatedly took British troops to the continent to bid for the throne, weakening defences.

Roman rule ended around 410 as Rome withdrew and told the Britons to defend themselves. Towns and the money economy collapsed. Angles, Saxons and Jutes from northern Germany and Denmark began settling the east and south, while British kingdoms held the west. In Ireland, Saint Patrick spread Christianity.

Anglo-Saxon kingdoms expanded across lowland England while Britons held Wales, Cornwall and the northwest, a time later mythologized in the legends of King Arthur. Irish monks such as Columba founded Iona in 563, and in 597 Augustine's mission from Rome began converting the English, starting with Kent.

England was divided among Anglo-Saxon kingdoms such as Northumbria, Mercia, East Anglia and Wessex, which fought for supremacy. Christianity spread, and the Synod of Whitby in 664 aligned the English church with Rome. The Sutton Hoo ship burial shows the wealth of early kings, while Scotland was split among Picts, Scots and Britons.

Mercia dominated England under King Offa, who built Offa's Dyke along the Welsh border. Northumbria produced great learning, including Bede's history and the Lindisfarne Gospels. In 793 Vikings raided the monastery of Lindisfarne, beginning centuries of Norse attacks on Britain and Ireland.

The Viking Great Army invaded in 865 and conquered most English kingdoms. Alfred the Great of Wessex resisted, defeated the Danes in 878 and fortified towns called burhs, while the Danes settled the Danelaw in the north and east. In Scotland, Kenneth MacAlpin united Picts and Scots c. 843.

Alfred's heirs reconquered the Danelaw, and Athelstan became the first king of all England in 927. England developed shires, coinage and royal law. Late in the century Viking raids resumed under King Æthelred. Scotland grew as the kingdom of Alba, while Ireland remained divided among rival kings.

Danish king Cnut ruled England from 1016 as part of a North Sea empire. In 1066 William of Normandy defeated Harold at Hastings, and the Norman Conquest replaced the English nobility with a French-speaking elite. Castles, the Domesday Book of 1086 and a strong feudal monarchy followed.

After a civil war called the Anarchy, Henry II founded the Angevin or Plantagenet dynasty in 1154, ruling England and much of France. He strengthened royal courts and common law, clashed with Archbishop Thomas Becket and began the English invasion of Ireland in 1169. Richard the Lionheart went on crusade.

King John lost Normandy and was forced to accept Magna Carta in 1215, limiting royal power. Parliament began taking shape later in the century. Edward I conquered Wales in 1282 to 1283 and tried to subdue Scotland, sparking wars in which William Wallace and Robert the Bruce resisted.

Scotland secured independence at Bannockburn in 1314. England began the Hundred Years' War with France in 1337, winning victories such as Crécy. The Black Death of 1348 killed perhaps a third or more of the population, raising wages and leading to the Peasants' Revolt of 1381. Chaucer wrote in English.

England lost its French lands except Calais by 1453, then fell into the Wars of the Roses between the houses of York and Lancaster. Henry VII won at Bosworth in 1485 and founded the Tudor dynasty. The printing press reached England in 1476, and a stronger central government emerged.

Henry VIII broke with Rome in 1534 to create the Church of England, and dissolved the monasteries. After religious swings under his children, Elizabeth I settled a Protestant church. England defeated the Spanish Armada in 1588, and the Elizabethan era saw Shakespeare, exploration and early colonial ventures.

James VI of Scotland became James I of England in 1603, uniting the crowns. Clashes between kings and Parliament led to the Civil War, the execution of Charles I in 1649 and Cromwell's republic. The monarchy returned in 1660, and the Glorious Revolution of 1688 set limits on royal power.

The Acts of Union in 1707 joined England and Scotland as Great Britain. The Hanoverian kings arrived in 1714, and real power shifted to Parliament and prime ministers such as Robert Walpole. Overseas trade and colonies grew, and Jacobite risings in support of the exiled Stuarts were crushed by 1746.

Britain won the Seven Years' War in 1763, gaining Canada and dominance in India, but lost the thirteen American colonies in 1783. The Industrial Revolution began with steam engines, canals and cotton mills. Britain then entered a long war with Revolutionary France in 1793.

The 1801 Act of Union created the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland. Britain led the coalitions against Napoleon, winning at Trafalgar in 1805 and Waterloo in 1815. It ended its slave trade in 1807. Industrial towns grew quickly, along with unrest such as the Luddites and Peterloo in 1819.

The Great Reform Act of 1832 widened the vote, and slavery was abolished in most of the empire in 1833. Queen Victoria came to the throne in 1837. Railways spread rapidly, and Chartists campaigned for democracy. The Irish Famine of 1845 to 1852 killed about a million people and drove mass emigration.

Victorian Britain was the world's leading industrial and naval power, showcased at the Great Exhibition of 1851. After the 1857 rebellion, the Crown took direct rule over India. The Crimean War was fought against Russia, and the 1867 Reform Act gave the vote to many urban working men.

Britain expanded its empire rapidly during the Scramble for Africa and declared Victoria Empress of India in 1876. Industrial rivals such as Germany and the United States began catching up. Trade unions grew, the Labour Party's roots formed, and Irish Home Rule became a dividing issue.

The costly Boer War ended in 1902, and Victoria's death in 1901 closed an era. Britain ended isolation through alliances with Japan, France and Russia. A Liberal government began welfare reforms such as old-age pensions, while suffragettes campaigned for women's votes and a naval race with Germany intensified.

Britain fought in the First World War from 1914, losing about 900,000 soldiers on the Western Front and elsewhere. The Easter Rising of 1916 in Dublin led to the Irish War of Independence. In 1918 most women over 30 and all men over 21 gained the vote.

The Irish Free State was created in 1922, while Northern Ireland stayed in the UK. The empire reached its greatest extent, about a quarter of the world, but faced growing independence movements. Labour formed its first government in 1924, and the General Strike of 1926 reflected industrial tensions.

The Great Depression hit industrial regions hard, causing mass unemployment and hunger marches. The Statute of Westminster in 1931 made the dominions self-governing. Edward VIII abdicated in 1936. Britain tried to appease Hitler, notably at Munich in 1938, but declared war when Germany invaded Poland in 1939.

Under Churchill, Britain fought on alone in 1940, winning the Battle of Britain and enduring the Blitz before helping defeat Germany in 1945. The Labour government built the welfare state, nationalized industries and founded the NHS in 1948. Indian independence in 1947 began the end of the empire.

Britain recovered slowly from the war; rationing ended in 1954 and Elizabeth II was crowned in 1953. The Suez Crisis of 1956 exposed Britain's decline as a great power. Ghana gained independence in 1957, starting African decolonization, and immigrants from the Caribbean and South Asia reshaped society.

Most remaining colonies in Africa and the Caribbean gained independence. Britain applied to join the European Economic Community but was vetoed by France. London became a center of youth culture, with the Beatles and 'Swinging London.' The Troubles erupted in Northern Ireland in 1969.

Britain joined the EEC in 1973 and confirmed membership in a 1975 referendum. Oil shocks, inflation and strikes troubled the economy, culminating in the 'Winter of Discontent' in 1978 to 1979. North Sea oil began flowing. Violence continued in Northern Ireland, and Margaret Thatcher became prime minister in 1979.

Thatcher's government privatized industries, cut union power and defeated the miners' strike of 1984 to 1985. Britain won the Falklands War in 1982. Finance boomed in London after the 1986 'Big Bang' deregulation, while manufacturing regions declined, deepening divides between north and south.

John Major's government signed the Maastricht Treaty, though Britain opted out of the euro. Tony Blair's New Labour won in 1997, creating devolved parliaments for Scotland and Wales and returning Hong Kong to China. The Good Friday Agreement of 1998 largely ended the Troubles in Northern Ireland.

Britain joined the US in the wars in Afghanistan and Iraq, which proved divisive. Immigration rose after the EU expanded east in 2004. London's financial sector boomed until the 2008 financial crisis forced bank bailouts. Gordon Brown succeeded Blair in 2007.

A Conservative-led coalition imposed austerity after the financial crisis. Scotland voted to stay in the UK in 2014. In 2016 Britain voted narrowly to leave the European Union, setting off years of political turmoil over how to carry out Brexit, while London hosted the 2012 Olympics.

The UK formally left the EU in 2020 as the COVID-19 pandemic struck. Queen Elizabeth II died in 2022 after 70 years on the throne, and Charles III succeeded her. Rapid changes of prime minister and a cost-of-living crisis followed, and Labour returned to power in 2024.
Scandinavia: As the ice sheets melted after c. 10,000 BC, hunter-gatherers moved north into Scandinavia, fishing, sealing and hunting reindeer. Coastal Ertebølle and Maglemosian cultures left shell middens and dugout canoes. Around 4000 BC farming arrived in southern Scandinavia with the Funnel Beaker culture, which built the first megalithic tombs.

Farmers in Denmark and southern Sweden built dolmens and passage graves, while hunter-fisher peoples continued older ways further north. Around 2800 BC the Corded Ware or Battle Axe culture spread in, likely bringing Indo-European languages. Flint daggers imitating metal weapons show growing contact with Bronze Age Europe.

The Nordic Bronze Age flourished from c. 1700 BC, even though bronze had to be imported in exchange for amber and furs. Chiefs were buried under large mounds with fine weapons, and rock carvings show ships, sun symbols and rituals. The Trundholm sun chariot from Denmark dates to this era.

Late Bronze Age Scandinavia produced elaborate bronze horns called lurs and rich metal hoards, though a cooling climate made farming harder. Around 500 BC iron working began to spread. Communities of farmers and herders lived in longhouses shared with livestock, while Sami ancestors hunted and herded in the far north.

The Pre-Roman Iron Age began in Scandinavia, with simpler graves and fewer luxury goods than in the Bronze Age. Farmers used local bog iron to make tools. Villages of longhouses surrounded by fenced fields were common in Denmark and southern Sweden, and Germanic languages were developing.

Scandinavian peoples lived in small farming communities, raising cattle and growing barley in a cool, wet climate. Offerings of weapons, goods and sometimes people were placed in bogs as sacrifices. Contact with the Celtic and Mediterranean worlds was limited, so society remained relatively equal and rural.

Iron Age farming communities spread across southern Scandinavia. The Hjortspring boat, a war canoe sunk in a Danish bog c. 350 BC with weapons for about 80 warriors, shows organized raiding and warfare. Chieftains were gaining power, and the far north remained home to hunting and fishing peoples.

Southern Scandinavia was home to Germanic tribes living in villages of longhouses. Bog offerings continued, and iron tools improved farming. Some groups, perhaps including the Cimbri and Teutones who later invaded the Roman world, may have come from Jutland in Denmark.

The Cimbri and Teutones, possibly from Jutland, migrated south and fought Rome from 113 BC until their defeat in 101 BC. The Gundestrup cauldron, found in a Danish bog, dates from around this time. At home, Scandinavians farmed, raised cattle and traded amber southward.

Scandinavian tribes lived beyond Rome's frontiers but began to feel its influence through trade. Bog bodies such as Tollund Man, from around this era, reflect ritual killings. Chiefs controlled farmsteads and warrior followings, and the region was known to Romans only by rumor.

The Roman Iron Age began, as Roman goods such as glassware, bronze vessels and coins reached Scandinavian chiefs through trade and gifts. Roman writers like Pliny and Tacitus described peoples such as the Suiones of Sweden. Society grew more stratified, with powerful families controlling trade.

Germanic chieftains in Denmark, Sweden and Norway grew rich through contact with the Roman Empire, some serving as mercenaries. Runic writing appeared in the 100s, adapted from Mediterranean alphabets. Large weapon sacrifices in Danish bogs, such as at Illerup, show armies of hundreds clashing in local wars.

Scandinavia's chiefdoms became more powerful, with central places such as Gudme on the Danish island of Funen hosting halls, workshops and trade. Runes were used for inscriptions on weapons and jewelry. Roman silver and gold flowed north as the empire's frontier grew unstable.

Chiefly elites in Scandinavia built large halls and controlled networks of farms and craftsmen. Weapon offerings in bogs continued, showing ongoing warfare among regional powers. The Nydam boat, a large rowing vessel, was sunk in a Danish bog around this time, pointing toward later Viking ships.

During the Migration Period, Scandinavian chiefs received large amounts of Roman gold as the Western Empire collapsed, making gold bracteates and ring forts. Angles and Jutes from Denmark crossed to Britain. Hillforts such as Eketorp on Öland reflect insecurity and competition among local rulers.

A climate crisis around 536, caused by volcanic eruptions, brought cold years, crop failure and population decline. Power concentrated in fewer hands, as seen in royal mounds at Old Uppsala in Sweden. Rich boat graves at Vendel show a warrior elite that would set the stage for the Viking Age.

The Vendel period saw Swedish and Danish kings and chieftains ruling from great halls, buried with helmets, swords and ships. Trade centers grew in the Baltic, linking Scandinavia to Frisia and Francia. Norse pagan religion centered on gods such as Odin, Thor and Freyr.

Improved sailing ships and growing populations set the stage for expansion. Trading towns such as Ribe and Birka developed, and the Danevirke earthwork defended Denmark's southern border. The Viking Age began with the raid on Lindisfarne in England in 793, launching attacks across western Europe.

Vikings raided and settled from Ireland to Russia. Danes conquered much of England, Norwegians colonized the Faroes and Iceland from c. 870, and Swedish Rus traders founded states along Russian rivers. At home, kings such as Harald Fairhair began uniting Norway.

Norse settlers founded Iceland's Althing assembly in 930 and settled Greenland c. 986 under Erik the Red. Harald Bluetooth unified Denmark and made it Christian around 965, and Christianization slowly spread through Norway. Vikings also served the Byzantine emperor as the Varangian Guard.

Leif Erikson reached North America c. 1000. Cnut the Great ruled England, Denmark and Norway from 1016 to 1035. The Viking Age ended around 1066 with the failed Norwegian invasion of England. Christian kingdoms of Denmark, Norway and Sweden took shape, with bishops and stone churches.

The three Scandinavian kingdoms became settled Christian monarchies, with archbishoprics at Lund and Nidaros. Civil wars over royal succession troubled Norway and Sweden. Danish kings such as Valdemar the Great fought the pagan Wends on the Baltic coast, and Sweden began expanding into Finland.

Denmark under Valdemar II conquered Estonia in 1219, and legend says the Danish flag fell from the sky in the battle. Norway reached its medieval peak under Haakon IV, gaining Iceland and Greenland in 1262 to 1264. Icelanders wrote down the sagas, and German Hanseatic merchants dominated trade.

The Black Death struck in 1349 to 1350, devastating Norway in particular and weakening its kingdom. The German Hanseatic League dominated Baltic trade from cities like Visby and Bergen. In 1397 Queen Margaret I formed the Kalmar Union, joining Denmark, Norway and Sweden under one crown.

The Kalmar Union was dominated by Denmark, and Swedish nobles and peasants repeatedly rebelled. The Norse settlements in Greenland died out during this century. Universities were founded at Uppsala in 1477 and Copenhagen in 1479, and the Danish king began collecting tolls on ships passing the Sound.

After the Stockholm Bloodbath of 1520, Sweden broke away under Gustav Vasa in 1523, ending the Kalmar Union. Denmark and Sweden both adopted Lutheranism, with the crown seizing church lands. Norway became a Danish province, and Denmark and Sweden fought repeatedly for control of the Baltic.

Sweden became a great power under Gustavus Adolphus, who intervened decisively in the Thirty Years' War. Sweden won Baltic territories and took southern provinces such as Skåne from Denmark in 1658. Denmark became an absolute monarchy in 1660, and Sweden followed under Charles XI.

In the Great Northern War from 1700 to 1721, Charles XII of Sweden won early victories but was crushed by Russia at Poltava in 1709, ending Sweden's empire. Sweden then entered an 'Age of Liberty' with parliamentary rule. Denmark-Norway remained an absolutist kingdom focused on trade.

Sweden flourished culturally under Gustav III, who restored royal power and was assassinated in 1792. Scientists such as Linnaeus made Sweden a center of natural history. Denmark-Norway grew rich from neutral shipping and colonies, and reformers abolished serfdom-like restrictions on Danish peasants in 1788.

Russia took Finland from Sweden in 1809, and Sweden chose the French marshal Bernadotte as heir. Denmark sided with Napoleon, suffering the British bombardment of Copenhagen in 1807, and in 1814 lost Norway to Sweden. Norway gained its own constitution in 1814 while in union with Sweden.

Scandinavia recovered from the Napoleonic wars and began slow modernization. Folk high schools inspired by N.F.S. Grundtvig spread in Denmark, and Scandinavianism promoted unity among the Nordic peoples. In 1849 Denmark ended absolute monarchy and adopted a constitution, while Finland was a Russian grand duchy.

Denmark lost Schleswig and Holstein to Prussia and Austria in 1864, a national trauma. Poverty and population growth drove mass emigration to the United States, especially from Sweden and Norway. Railways and industry began to spread, and Sweden reformed its parliament in 1866.

Scandinavia industrialized through timber, iron, paper and shipping. Emigration to America peaked in the 1880s. Writers and artists such as Henrik Ibsen, August Strindberg and Edvard Munch won fame. Labour movements and social democratic parties emerged, and Norwegian demands for independence grew.

Norway peacefully became independent from Sweden in 1905, choosing a Danish prince as King Haakon VII. Finland, under Russian rule, gave women the vote in 1906, among the first in the world. Industry and democratic reforms advanced, and the Nobel Prizes were first awarded in 1901.

Denmark, Norway and Sweden stayed neutral in the First World War, though trade disruptions caused shortages. Finland declared independence from Russia in 1917, followed by a brief civil war in 1918. Women gained the vote in Denmark in 1915 and in Sweden by 1919 to 1921.

The Nordic countries strengthened parliamentary democracy and expanded welfare programs. Iceland became a separate kingdom in union with Denmark from 1918. The League of Nations awarded the Åland Islands to Finland in 1921. Swedish industry, including firms like Volvo founded in 1927, grew rapidly.

Social Democrats came to power in Sweden, Denmark and Norway, building the foundations of the Nordic welfare model through deals between workers, farmers and employers. In 1939 the Soviet Union attacked Finland in the Winter War, which the Finns fiercely resisted.

Germany occupied Denmark and Norway in 1940, while Sweden stayed neutral and Finland fought the Soviet Union again. Danes rescued most of their Jews to Sweden in 1943. Iceland became an independent republic in 1944. After the war Denmark, Norway and Iceland joined NATO in 1949.

The Nordic countries rebuilt and expanded generous welfare states funded by high taxes. They created the Nordic Council in 1952 and a passport union. Sweden and Finland remained neutral in the Cold War, with Finland carefully balancing between the Soviet Union and the West.

Scandinavia enjoyed rising prosperity, full employment and broad social reforms in education, health and housing. Sweden's Olof Palme became a prominent voice on world affairs. Norway discovered oil in the North Sea in 1969, which would transform its economy.

Denmark joined the European Economic Community in 1973, while Norway voted against membership in 1972. Oil revenues made Norway wealthy. Nordic countries led in gender equality, environmental policy and foreign aid, and Swedish exports such as ABBA, IKEA and Volvo gained worldwide fame.

The Nordic welfare model faced economic strain and debates over taxes. Swedish Prime Minister Olof Palme was assassinated in 1986. Norway created a petroleum fund to manage oil wealth, and Nordic countries remained among the world's richest and most equal societies.

Sweden and Finland suffered banking crises early in the decade, then recovered. With the Cold War over, Sweden and Finland joined the European Union in 1995, while Norway again voted no. Finland's Nokia led the mobile phone boom, and Baltic neighbors regained independence.

Scandinavian economies thrived on technology, energy and exports. Finland adopted the euro, while Denmark and Sweden kept their own currencies. Iceland's banks collapsed in the 2008 financial crisis. A Danish newspaper's cartoons of Muhammad in 2005 sparked global protests.

Norway suffered the 2011 terrorist attacks in Oslo and on Utøya island. Sweden took in large numbers of refugees during the 2015 migration crisis, fueling debates over immigration. Nordic countries ranked highly in happiness and quality of life, and Greta Thunberg's school strike in 2018 launched a global climate movement.

After Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Finland joined NATO in 2023 and Sweden in 2024, ending long traditions of military non-alignment. The region coped with the COVID-19 pandemic, an energy crunch and debates over migration, while pushing ahead with green energy.
Spain & Portugal: Iberia has been home to humans for over a million years, with Neanderthals surviving there until c. 40,000 years ago. Modern hunters painted the great caves of Altamira and Côa. Farming spread along the coasts from c. 5500 BC, and from about 4000 BC people built megalithic tombs such as dolmens across the peninsula.

Copper Age communities flourished, building fortified settlements such as Los Millares in Spain and Zambujal in Portugal. Bell Beaker pottery, which spread across Europe, may have originated in Portugal's Tagus region. Large villages, metalworking and megalithic tombs show growing wealth and social ranking.

The El Argar culture of southeast Spain built hilltop towns and buried its elite with silver and bronze from c. 2200 BC, then collapsed around 1550 BC. Elsewhere, Bronze Age farmers and herders lived in smaller villages. Atlantic trade linked western Iberia to Britain and France.

Phoenicians founded Gadir (Cádiz) and other trading posts, drawn by silver and tin. The rich kingdom of Tartessos in the southwest grew wealthy through this trade. Greeks later set up colonies on the Mediterranean coast, while Celtic peoples settled the interior and north.

Tartessos faded around this time, and Iberian peoples in the east and south built fortified towns and adopted writing. Celts and Celtiberians dominated the central plateau and northwest. The Greek colony of Emporion traded with the Iberians, and Carthage became the leading power among the Phoenician settlements.

Iberian culture flourished in the east and south, with stone sculptures such as the Lady of Elche, coinage and a script of its own. Celtiberians in the interior lived in hillforts and were known as fierce warriors. Carthage controlled trade from bases like Gadir and Ibiza.

Iberian, Celtiberian and Lusitanian peoples governed themselves in tribal territories and small towns. Mercenaries from Iberia fought for Carthage and Greek cities in Sicily. Celtic hillfort settlements known as castros dominated the northwest, in what is now Galicia and northern Portugal.

After losing the First Punic War, Carthage built an empire in Spain from 237 BC, founding Carthago Nova (Cartagena). In 218 BC Hannibal marched from Spain over the Alps to invade Italy. Rome responded by invading Spain and took over Carthaginian territory by 206 BC.

Rome organized its Spanish provinces but faced long resistance from Celtiberians and Lusitanians. The Lusitanian leader Viriathus fought Rome until his murder in 139 BC, and Numantia fell after a famous siege in 133 BC. Roman silver mines and settlers began reshaping the south and east.

Roman civil wars were partly fought in Spain, including Caesar's campaigns against Pompey's supporters. Augustus finished the conquest with the Cantabrian Wars, completed in 19 BC. Spain was divided into new provinces, and cities such as Mérida were founded for veteran soldiers.

Hispania became one of Rome's most Romanized regions, producing olive oil, wine, fish sauce and metals for the empire. Latin replaced local languages in the south and east. Cities gained theaters and aqueducts, and Spaniards such as the philosopher Seneca rose to prominence in Rome.

Two emperors, Trajan and Hadrian, came from Spanish families in Italica near Seville. Hispania prospered as a peaceful, urbanized part of the empire, with monuments like the Segovia aqueduct and the Alcántara bridge. Olive oil from Baetica was shipped to Rome in huge quantities.

Hispania was affected by the third-century crisis, with Frankish raiders attacking c. 260 and some cities building walls. Christianity was spreading, and the Council of Elvira c. 305 is among the earliest known church councils. Rural villas became more important as towns declined.

Under Diocletian and Constantine, Hispania was reorganized as a diocese of several provinces. Wealthy landowners lived on large villas, and Christianity became dominant. Theodosius I, born in Spain, became emperor in 379 and made Christianity the official religion of the empire.

In 409 Vandals, Suebi and Alans crossed into Spain. The Vandals moved on to Africa in 429, and the Suebi set up a kingdom in the northwest. The Visigoths, first allied with Rome, established their own kingdom across most of the peninsula as Roman rule ended.

The Visigoths ruled Spain from Toledo after being pushed out of most of Gaul in 507. The Byzantines held part of the southern coast from 552. King Leovigild conquered the Suebic kingdom in 585, and in 589 King Reccared converted from Arian to Catholic Christianity, uniting rulers and subjects in faith.

The Visigothic kingdom, now Catholic, drove the Byzantines from Spain by c. 625. Isidore of Seville wrote encyclopedic works preserving classical learning. Church councils at Toledo held great influence, but disputes over royal succession and harsh laws against Jews weakened the kingdom.

Umayyad forces from North Africa crossed in 711 and swiftly conquered the Visigothic kingdom, creating Muslim al-Andalus. Christians held out in the mountainous north, winning at Covadonga c. 722, a moment later seen as the start of the Reconquista. In 756 Abd al-Rahman I founded an independent emirate at Córdoba.

The emirate of Córdoba governed most of Iberia, building the Great Mosque and fostering trade, irrigation and new crops such as citrus and rice. In the north, the kingdom of Asturias grew, and Santiago de Compostela became a pilgrimage site. Charlemagne's Franks created the Spanish March around Barcelona.

Abd al-Rahman III declared the Caliphate of Córdoba in 929. Córdoba became one of Europe's largest and richest cities, famous for learning, libraries and the palace city of Madinat al-Zahra. Christian kingdoms such as León, Navarre and Castile grew in the north, while the general al-Mansur raided them.

The Caliphate collapsed in 1031 into rival taifa kingdoms, which paid tribute to Christian rulers. Castile took Toledo in 1085, and the warrior El Cid seized Valencia. The Almoravids from Morocco then crossed into Spain and reunited al-Andalus, halting the Christian advance for a time.

The Reconquista advanced as Aragon took Zaragoza in 1118. Portugal became an independent kingdom under Afonso Henriques in 1139 and captured Lisbon in 1147 with crusader help. The Almohads replaced the Almoravids in al-Andalus, while thinkers such as Averroes and Maimonides flourished.

Christian kingdoms won a decisive victory at Las Navas de Tolosa in 1212. Castile took Córdoba and Seville, Aragon took Valencia and the Balearics, and Portugal completed its southern conquest. By 1250 only Granada remained Muslim. Alfonso X of Castile sponsored translations and law codes.

The Iberian kingdoms of Castile, Aragon, Portugal, Navarre and Granada competed and intermarried. Aragon built a Mediterranean empire including Sicily and Sardinia. The Black Death and civil wars struck hard, and in 1391 violent attacks on Jewish communities spread across Spain. Portugal secured its independence at Aljubarrota in 1385.

Portugal took Ceuta in 1415 and, led by Prince Henry the Navigator, explored Africa's coast; Vasco da Gama reached India in 1498. Ferdinand and Isabella's marriage in 1469 united Spain, which conquered Granada in 1492, expelled its Jews and sponsored Columbus. The Treaty of Tordesillas in 1494 split new lands with Portugal.

Spain conquered the Aztec and Inca empires, and American silver poured in. Under the Habsburgs Charles V and Philip II, Spain ruled a global empire and was Europe's leading Catholic power. Portugal built a trading empire in Asia, Africa and Brazil. From 1580 to 1640 Spain and Portugal shared one king.

Spain declined amid repeated bankruptcies, plague, the expulsion of the Moriscos and losses in the Thirty Years' War. The Dutch won independence, and Portugal regained its own king in 1640. Even so, writers and artists such as Cervantes, Lope de Vega and Velázquez made it a Golden Age of culture.

When the last Spanish Habsburg died, the War of the Spanish Succession from 1701 to 1714 brought the French Bourbon Philip V to the throne but cost Spain its European possessions. Britain took Gibraltar. Portugal grew rich from Brazilian gold and allied closely with Britain.

The 1755 Lisbon earthquake destroyed much of the city, and the Marquis of Pombal rebuilt it while modernizing Portugal. In Spain, Charles III carried out Enlightenment reforms and expelled the Jesuits. Both countries tried to tighten control over their American colonies as revolutionary ideas spread.

Napoleon invaded Iberia from 1807. The Portuguese court fled to Brazil, and Spain endured the brutal Peninsular War until 1814, coining the word guerrilla. Spain's liberal Constitution of 1812 was drafted at Cádiz. Meanwhile, Spain's American colonies broke away between 1810 and 1825, and Brazil declared independence in 1822.

Spain and Portugal were torn by civil wars between liberals and conservatives, including Spain's First Carlist War and Portugal's Liberal Wars. Church lands were sold off, and both countries adopted constitutional monarchies, though military coups and unstable governments were frequent.

Spain's Queen Isabella II was overthrown in 1868, leading to a short-lived First Republic from 1873 to 1874. Portugal enjoyed relative calm under constitutional monarchy, building railways. Both countries lagged behind industrializing northern Europe, and many people emigrated to the Americas.

The Bourbon monarchy was restored in Spain in 1874, with parties taking turns in rigged elections. Catalonia industrialized and anarchism grew among workers. Spain lost Cuba, Puerto Rico and the Philippines to the United States in 1898. Portugal clung to its African colonies against British pressure.

Portugal's king and heir were assassinated in 1908, and a republic was declared in 1910. Spain, shaken by the loss of its empire, debated national renewal. Tensions erupted during Barcelona's Tragic Week in 1909 over military conscription for Morocco.

Both countries faced instability; Spain stayed neutral in the First World War and profited from trade, while Portugal joined the Allies in 1916. The 1918 flu struck hard. Strikes and anarchist violence spread in Spain, and Portugal's republic was racked by coups.

Spain's defeat at Annual in Morocco in 1921 helped bring General Primo de Rivera's dictatorship in 1923. In Portugal a military coup in 1926 ended the republic, and António de Oliveira Salazar rose to lead the country's finances and later its government.

Spain became the Second Republic in 1931. Deep divisions led to the Civil War from 1936 to 1939, in which Franco's Nationalists, backed by Germany and Italy, defeated the Republicans. Franco's dictatorship followed. Salazar created the authoritarian Estado Novo in Portugal in 1933.

Franco's Spain stayed officially neutral in the Second World War but sent volunteers to fight the Soviets. Repression and hunger marked the postwar years, and Spain was isolated internationally. Portugal, also neutral, joined NATO as a founding member in 1949.

The Cold War ended Spain's isolation, as the US signed bases agreements in 1953 and Spain joined the UN in 1955. Spain lost most of its Moroccan protectorate in 1956. Both dictatorships remained poor and repressive, prompting large-scale emigration to northern Europe.

Spain's economy boomed through tourism, industry and foreign investment in an 'economic miracle.' Portugal fought costly colonial wars in Angola, Mozambique and Guinea-Bissau, while India seized Goa in 1961. Salazar was incapacitated in 1968 and replaced by Marcelo Caetano.

Portugal's Carnation Revolution of 1974 ended the dictatorship and quickly gave independence to its African colonies. Franco died in 1975, and King Juan Carlos led Spain's transition to democracy, with a new constitution in 1978. Regions such as Catalonia and the Basque Country gained autonomy.

Spain survived a coup attempt in 1981 and elected Felipe González's Socialists in 1982. Both countries joined the European Economic Community in 1986, bringing investment and rapid modernization. Basque separatist group ETA continued its violent campaign.

Spain showcased its new image with the 1992 Barcelona Olympics and Seville Expo. EU funds built highways and high-speed rail. Portugal hosted Expo '98 in Lisbon and handed Macau back to China in 1999. Both countries adopted the euro in 1999.

Both economies grew, fueled in Spain by a construction boom, until the 2008 financial crisis. Islamist terrorists bombed Madrid's trains in 2004, killing 193 people. Spain legalized same-sex marriage in 2005, and both countries became major destinations for immigrants.

The euro crisis brought deep recessions, high unemployment and bailouts for Portugal. Protest movements reshaped Spanish politics. ETA announced the end of its violence in 2011. Catalonia held an independence referendum in 2017 that Spain declared illegal, causing a constitutional crisis.

Spain and Portugal were hard hit by COVID-19 but recovered strongly, helped by tourism and renewable energy growth. Spain's politics remained fragmented and divided over Catalan amnesty. Portugal saw shifting governments and rising support for new parties, while both countries attracted migrants and remote workers.
France: France holds some of Europe's richest Ice Age sites, where Neanderthals and later modern humans lived. Hunters painted the caves of Chauvet and Lascaux tens of thousands of years ago. Farming arrived from c. 5500 BC, and by 4500 BC people in Brittany were raising the great standing stones of Carnac.

Neolithic and Copper Age farmers lived in villages across France, building megalithic tombs and stone alignments, especially in Brittany. Bell Beaker people spread new customs and metalworking from c. 2500 BC. Trade in flint, copper and polished stone axes linked communities across the region.

Bronze Age chiefs controlled trade in metals along France's rivers and Atlantic coast. Burial mounds in Brittany held rich goods, and later the Urnfield culture spread cremation burials. Farming villages grew, and society became more ranked, with warrior elites holding bronze swords.

Iron working spread in the Hallstatt period, and powerful Celtic chiefs emerged in eastern France. Around 600 BC Greeks from Phocaea founded Massalia (Marseille), which became the main trading gateway between the Mediterranean and the Celtic interior, exchanging wine for metals and slaves.

Celtic chiefs in eastern France grew rich from trade with Massalia. The princess buried at Vix c. 500 BC was laid to rest with a giant Greek bronze krater, the largest known from the ancient world. Hillfort centers such as Mont Lassois dominated the surrounding countryside.

The Hallstatt chiefdoms collapsed and the La Tène culture rose, with distinctive swirling art and warrior burials with chariots. Celtic Gauls lived in tribes ruled by nobles and druids. Many began migrating out of Gaul toward Italy and central Europe.

Gaulish warriors spread across Europe, sacking Rome c. 390 BC and later raiding into the Balkans and Greece. Back in Gaul, the tribes grew more organized, and Massalia's Greek colonies along the coast continued trading wine, pottery and coins with Celtic peoples.

Gaul was home to many Celtic tribes such as the Arverni, Aedui and Sequani, living in farming villages and hillforts. Hannibal crossed southern Gaul in 218 BC on his way to Italy. Coinage spread, and Gaulish society grew wealthier and more connected to the Mediterranean.

Rome conquered southern Gaul around 121 BC, creating the province of Gallia Narbonensis. The Cimbri and Teutones swept through Gaul before Marius defeated them in 102 to 101 BC. Elsewhere, Gauls built large fortified towns called oppida, such as Bibracte, which served as tribal capitals.

Julius Caesar conquered Gaul from 58 to 50 BC, defeating Vercingetorix at Alesia in 52 BC. Hundreds of thousands died or were enslaved. Augustus then organized Gaul into provinces, founded Lugdunum (Lyon) as a capital and began building roads and Roman towns.

Gaul was steadily Romanized, with towns like Nîmes, Arles and Lyon gaining temples, arenas and aqueducts such as the Pont du Gard. Gaulish nobles became Roman citizens and senators. Latin spread among elites, and trade in wine, pottery and grain flourished along Roman roads.

Roman Gaul enjoyed peace and prosperity during the Pax Romana. Workshops at La Graufesenque and Lezoux mass-produced fine red pottery for the empire. Christianity reached Gaul, and martyrs were executed at Lyon in 177. Gauls mostly lived on farms and villas, speaking Latin and Celtic.

The third-century crisis hit Gaul hard, with Frankish and Alemannic raids across the Rhine. From 260 to 274 a breakaway Gallic Empire ruled Gaul, Britain and Spain. Towns shrank behind new walls, and the countryside grew less secure as power shifted to large estates.

Roman rule was restored, and Trier became an imperial residence. Christianity spread, with Saint Martin of Tours founding monasteries and converting the countryside. Germanic troops increasingly guarded the Rhine frontier, and some Franks settled inside the empire as allies.

Vandals, Alans and Suebi crossed the frozen Rhine c. 406, and Burgundians, Visigoths and Franks carved out kingdoms in Gaul. Romans and Germanic allies halted Attila's Huns in 451. In 486 Clovis of the Franks defeated Syagrius, the last Roman ruler in northern Gaul.

Clovis defeated the Visigoths in 507, converted to Catholic Christianity and made Paris his capital, founding the Merovingian dynasty. His sons conquered Burgundy in 534. The Frankish kingdom was often divided among royal heirs, and Gallo-Roman bishops shaped society and learning.

Merovingian kings ruled divided Frankish kingdoms such as Neustria, Austrasia and Burgundy, briefly reunited under Dagobert I. Royal power weakened, and court officials called mayors of the palace grew dominant. Irish missionaries founded monasteries, and towns remained small and rural life prevailed.

Charles Martel, mayor of the palace, defeated an Umayyad army near Tours and Poitiers in 732. His son Pepin the Short became king in 751, founding the Carolingian dynasty with papal blessing. Charlemagne then expanded the Frankish realm across much of western Europe.

Charlemagne was crowned emperor in 800, and the Carolingian Renaissance revived learning. His empire was divided by the Treaty of Verdun in 843, with West Francia becoming the basis of France. Viking raids up rivers such as the Seine, including attacks on Paris, weakened royal power.

In 911 the Viking leader Rollo was granted Normandy. Royal authority dwindled as dukes and counts held real power from their castles. In 987 Hugh Capet was crowned king, founding the Capetian dynasty, though he directly ruled only a small area around Paris. Cluny Abbey led monastic reform.

Feudal lords dominated France, while the Capetian kings slowly gained respect. Norman knights from France conquered England in 1066 and southern Italy. Pope Urban II preached the First Crusade at Clermont in 1095, and French nobles led the expedition to Jerusalem.

Gothic architecture was born at Saint-Denis c. 1144, followed by great cathedrals like Notre-Dame de Paris. Towns, trade fairs in Champagne and the early University of Paris grew. Through marriage, Henry II of England's Angevin kings ruled much of western France from 1154.

Philip II Augustus took Normandy from England and won at Bouvines in 1214, greatly expanding royal power. The Albigensian Crusade of 1209 to 1229 crushed the Cathars and brought the south under the crown. Louis IX led crusades and was made a saint, and France was Europe's leading kingdom.

Philip IV clashed with the papacy, which moved to Avignon in 1309. When the Capetian line ended, the Hundred Years' War with England began in 1337, bringing defeats at Crécy and Poitiers. The Black Death of 1348 killed a large share of the population, and peasant revolts erupted.

England dominated after Agincourt in 1415, but Joan of Arc rallied French forces in 1429. France won the Hundred Years' War by 1453. Louis XI then strengthened the monarchy and absorbed Burgundy and other lands. In 1494 Charles VIII invaded Italy, beginning decades of Italian Wars.

Francis I brought the Renaissance to France, building châteaux and hosting Leonardo da Vinci. Protestantism spread, and the Wars of Religion from 1562 to 1598 included the St. Bartholomew's Day massacre of 1572. Henry IV ended the wars and granted Protestants tolerance with the Edict of Nantes.

Cardinals Richelieu and Mazarin strengthened royal power, and France gained from the Thirty Years' War. Louis XIV, ruling from 1643 to 1715, built Versailles, made the monarchy absolute and made France Europe's leading power. He fought costly wars and revoked the Edict of Nantes in 1685.

Louis XIV's last war, over the Spanish succession, placed his grandson on Spain's throne but drained France. Under Louis XV, Paris became the center of the Enlightenment with thinkers like Montesquieu and Voltaire. France competed with Britain for empire in North America and India.

France lost Canada and most of India to Britain in 1763, then helped the Americans win independence. Debt led to the French Revolution in 1789, which abolished feudal privileges. Louis XVI was executed in 1793, the Terror followed, and Napoleon Bonaparte seized power in 1799.

Napoleon crowned himself emperor in 1804, issued the Napoleonic Code and dominated much of Europe. His invasion of Russia in 1812 failed, and he was defeated at Waterloo in 1815. The Bourbon monarchy was restored under Louis XVIII, and France lost its conquests.

The July Revolution of 1830 replaced the Bourbons with the 'citizen king' Louis-Philippe. France began conquering Algeria the same year. Railways and industry developed slowly, and the 1848 Revolution created the Second Republic with universal male suffrage, electing Louis-Napoleon president.

Louis-Napoleon made himself Emperor Napoleon III in 1852. Paris was rebuilt with grand boulevards, and France expanded into Indochina and Mexico. Defeat by Prussia in 1870 to 1871 cost France Alsace-Lorraine, sparked the Paris Commune and led to the Third Republic.

The Third Republic built a secular state with free public schools. France created the second-largest colonial empire, spanning North and West Africa, Indochina and Madagascar. The Eiffel Tower opened in 1889, Impressionism flourished, and the Dreyfus Affair bitterly divided the nation.

France separated church and state in 1905 and formed the Entente Cordiale with Britain in 1904. The Belle Époque saw Paris lead the world in art, fashion and early aviation and cinema. Tensions with Germany grew over Morocco and lost Alsace-Lorraine.

France fought on the Western Front from 1914 to 1918, enduring battles such as the Marne, Verdun and the Somme. About 1.4 million French soldiers died and the northeast was devastated. Victory restored Alsace-Lorraine, and the 1919 Treaty of Versailles imposed harsh terms on Germany.

France rebuilt its war-damaged regions and occupied the Ruhr in 1923 to force German reparations. Paris was a magnet for artists and writers during the Roaring Twenties. Low birth rates and war losses left France anxious, and it began building the Maginot Line.

The Great Depression reached France later but lingered, fueling political extremes. The Popular Front government of 1936 introduced paid holidays and a 40-hour week. France followed Britain in appeasing Hitler but declared war on Germany in 1939.

Germany defeated France in 1940, occupying the north while Marshal Pétain's Vichy regime collaborated. De Gaulle led the Free French, and the Resistance fought on. France was liberated in 1944, gave women the vote, founded the Fourth Republic and fought to keep Indochina from 1946.

France lost Indochina at Dien Bien Phu in 1954, then fought the brutal Algerian War from 1954. France helped found the European Economic Community in 1957. The Algerian crisis brought de Gaulle back to power in 1958, creating the Fifth Republic with a strong presidency.

Algeria won independence in 1962, and most French African colonies became independent around 1960. De Gaulle pursued an independent foreign policy, building nuclear weapons and leaving NATO's command. Student and worker protests in May 1968 shook the country, and de Gaulle resigned in 1969.

France's postwar boom, known as the Trente Glorieuses, ended with the 1973 oil shock. Presidents Pompidou and Giscard d'Estaing modernized the economy, expanded nuclear power and built high-speed rail. Abortion was legalized in 1975, and France pushed European integration with West Germany.

Socialist François Mitterrand won the presidency in 1981, abolished the death penalty and nationalized industries before shifting toward the market. France cooperated closely with Germany to build the European single market. Immigration and unemployment became major political issues.

France backed the Maastricht Treaty, which created the European Union in 1993, and prepared for the euro. Jacques Chirac became president in 1995. The Channel Tunnel opened in 1994, and France won the 1998 World Cup with a diverse team celebrated as a symbol of unity.

France adopted euro notes and coins in 2002 and opposed the US-led invasion of Iraq in 2003. French voters rejected the EU constitution in 2005. Riots in the suburbs that year exposed tensions over discrimination and unemployment, and Nicolas Sarkozy became president in 2007.

France intervened militarily in Libya and Mali. Islamist terrorist attacks struck Paris in 2015, including at Charlie Hebdo and the Bataclan, and Nice in 2016. The Paris climate agreement was signed in 2015, and Emmanuel Macron won the presidency in 2017. The Yellow Vest protests began in 2018.

France faced the COVID-19 pandemic, protests over raising the retirement age, and a growing far-right National Rally. Notre-Dame cathedral, damaged by fire in 2019, reopened in 2024, the year Paris hosted the Olympics. A snap election in 2024 produced a deeply divided parliament.
Italy/Rome: Italy was home to Neanderthals and then modern hunter-gatherers during the Ice Age. Farming spread along the coasts from c. 6000 BC, bringing villages, pottery and herding. By the late fourth millennium BC, Copper Age peoples were working metal; Ötzi the Iceman, found in the Alps, lived c. 3300 BC.

Copper Age cultures such as Remedello in the north and Rinaldone in central Italy buried their dead with copper daggers and axes. Farming and herding villages spread across the peninsula. In Sardinia and Sicily, distinct island cultures built rock-cut tombs and early stone monuments.

Bronze Age communities flourished, including the terramare villages of the Po Valley and the Apennine herding culture. Sardinia's Nuragic people built thousands of stone towers. Mycenaean Greek traders reached southern Italy and Sicily, linking the region to the eastern Mediterranean.

The Etruscans built wealthy city-states in central Italy, while Greeks founded colonies across the south and Sicily, such as Syracuse and Naples. Phoenicians settled western Sicily and Sardinia. According to legend, Rome was founded in 753 BC as a small settlement of Latin farmers on the Tiber.

Etruscan kings ruled Rome until 509 BC, when the Romans expelled them and founded a republic led by elected consuls and a senate. Etruscan power peaked and then began to fade. Greek cities in southern Italy, known as Magna Graecia, prospered, and Pythagoras taught at Croton.

The young Roman Republic fought its neighbors and struggled internally as plebeians demanded rights from patrician aristocrats. Rome's first written law code, the Twelve Tables, appeared c. 450 BC. Syracuse defeated an Athenian invasion of Sicily in 413 BC, and Etruscan cities declined.

Gauls sacked Rome c. 390 BC, but the city recovered and built new walls. Rome dissolved the Latin League in 338 BC and fought the Samnite Wars, gaining control of central Italy. Roads such as the Via Appia, begun in 312 BC, connected its growing network of allies and colonies.

Rome defeated Pyrrhus and the Greek cities to control all of peninsular Italy by 264 BC. It then fought Carthage, taking Sicily in the First Punic War. In the Second, Hannibal crossed the Alps and won great victories such as Cannae, but Rome triumphed at Zama in 202 BC.

Rome conquered Greece and destroyed Carthage and Corinth in 146 BC, becoming master of the Mediterranean. Wealth and slaves flooded in, but small farmers suffered. The Gracchi brothers' reforms and murders from 133 BC began a century of political violence, slave revolts and civil wars.

Generals such as Pompey and Caesar dominated the failing Republic. Caesar crossed the Rubicon in 49 BC, became dictator and was assassinated in 44 BC. After more civil war, Octavian defeated Antony and Cleopatra and became Augustus, the first emperor, in 27 BC, beginning the Pax Romana.

The Roman Empire was at peace under the Julio-Claudian and Flavian emperors, though rulers like Caligula and Nero were notorious. Rome was a city of perhaps a million people. The Great Fire struck in 64, the Colosseum was built, and Vesuvius buried Pompeii and Herculaneum in 79.

Under Trajan the empire reached its greatest extent in 117. Hadrian, Antoninus Pius and Marcus Aurelius ruled during a golden age of peace and building, including the Pantheon. The Antonine Plague from 165 killed millions, and the death of Marcus Aurelius in 180 ended the Pax Romana.

The Severan dynasty ruled until 235, and in 212 citizenship was extended to nearly all free people of the empire. The Crisis of the Third Century followed, with dozens of short-lived emperors, invasions and inflation. Diocletian restored order and created the Tetrarchy in 293.

Constantine legalized Christianity in 313 and moved the capital to Constantinople in 330, reducing Rome's political importance. Christianity became the official religion under Theodosius. The empire was permanently divided in 395, and Italy now sat at the heart of the weaker western half.

The Western Empire collapsed. Visigoths sacked Rome in 410 and Vandals in 455, and in 476 Odoacer deposed the last western emperor. In 489 the Ostrogoth Theodoric the Great invaded, ruling Italy from Ravenna with Roman administrators and preserving much of Roman life.

Emperor Justinian's Byzantine armies defeated the Ostrogoths between 535 and 554, but the long war and plague devastated Italy. In 568 the Lombards invaded and took much of the peninsula, leaving the Byzantines with Ravenna, Rome, Naples and the south. Pope Gregory the Great became a leading figure.

Italy was divided between the Lombard kingdom, centered at Pavia, and Byzantine territories along the coasts. The popes in Rome gained influence as Byzantine power weakened, and the Lombards gradually converted to Catholicism. Towns were small and the economy largely rural.

The Lombards captured Ravenna in 751, ending Byzantine rule in the north. The pope turned to the Franks, and Pepin gave him lands that became the Papal States in 756. Charlemagne conquered the Lombard kingdom in 774. Venice was emerging as an independent lagoon city.

In 800 the pope crowned Charlemagne emperor in Rome, linking the papacy and the Frankish empire. After his empire split, northern Italy had weak kings and local lords. Arabs began conquering Sicily from 827 and raided Rome in 846, while Venice and Amalfi grew through trade.

Italy was fragmented among local rulers and a weak papacy dominated by Roman noble families. In 962 the German king Otto I was crowned emperor, beginning centuries of German claims to northern Italy. Muslim Sicily flourished, and Venice grew as a maritime power trading with Byzantium.

Normans conquered southern Italy and Sicily between 1061 and 1091. The Investiture Controversy pitted popes against emperors, and at Canossa in 1077 Pope Gregory VII humbled Emperor Henry IV. Italian towns grew and began governing themselves, and Pisa, Genoa and Venice profited from the crusades.

Self-governing city-states such as Venice, Genoa, Milan and Florence rose and prospered through trade and banking. The Lombard League defeated Emperor Frederick Barbarossa at Legnano in 1176. The Norman Kingdom of Sicily blended Latin, Greek and Arab cultures, and the University of Bologna grew.

Emperor Frederick II ruled Sicily and fought the popes until his death in 1250, after which the French Angevins took the south. The Sicilian Vespers revolt of 1282 brought Sicily under Aragon. Cities split into Guelph and Ghibelline factions, while Marco Polo traveled to China and banks spread.

Dante, Petrarch, Boccaccio and Giotto launched the early Renaissance. The papacy moved to Avignon from 1309 to 1377. The Black Death in 1348 killed perhaps half the people in some cities. Signori and families such as the Visconti of Milan increasingly took power from city councils.

Medici Florence led the Renaissance, with artists such as Brunelleschi, Donatello and Botticelli and humanist scholars reviving classical learning. The Peace of Lodi in 1454 balanced Venice, Milan, Florence, Naples and the Papal States. France's invasion in 1494 began the Italian Wars.

Leonardo, Michelangelo and Raphael defined the High Renaissance, even as Italy became a battleground for France and Spain. The Sack of Rome in 1527 marked Spanish dominance of Italy, confirmed in 1559. The Catholic Counter-Reformation, led from Rome, followed the Council of Trent.

Spain ruled Milan, Naples, Sicily and Sardinia, while Venice declined as trade shifted to the Atlantic. Plague struck hard in the 1630s and 1650s. Galileo's scientific discoveries led to his trial in 1633, and Baroque art and architecture flourished under Bernini in Rome.

After the War of the Spanish Succession, Austria replaced Spain as the dominant power in Italy, taking Milan and Naples. Savoy gained Sardinia in 1720 and became the Kingdom of Sardinia. A Spanish Bourbon branch took Naples and Sicily in 1734. Venice and Genoa were in decline.

Enlightened reforms were pursued in Habsburg Tuscany and Lombardy, and Cesare Beccaria argued against torture and the death penalty. Excavations at Pompeii fascinated Europe. In 1796 to 1797 Napoleon invaded, ending the Venetian Republic and creating French-style sister republics.

Napoleon created a Kingdom of Italy in the north from 1805 to 1814 and placed relatives on the throne of Naples, introducing modern laws and administration. After his fall, the Congress of Vienna restored old rulers, with Austria dominant. Secret societies such as the Carbonari plotted revolts.

Giuseppe Mazzini's Young Italy promoted a united, republican Italy. Revolutions broke out across Italy in 1848, and Rome briefly became a republic, but Austria and France restored the old order. Piedmont-Sardinia kept its new constitution and became the leading hope for unification.

Led by Cavour and Garibaldi, Piedmont-Sardinia unified most of Italy, and the Kingdom of Italy was proclaimed in 1861. Venice was added in 1866, and Rome was taken in 1870, completing unification. The new state faced deep north-south divides, poverty and banditry in the south.

The young kingdom built railways, an army and colonies, though Ethiopia defeated it at Adwa in 1896. Poverty drove millions of Italians to emigrate to the Americas. Socialism and anarchism grew, and King Umberto I was assassinated in 1900.

Under Prime Minister Giovanni Giolitti, Italy industrialized in the north and expanded voting rights. Emigration to the Americas reached its peak. An earthquake destroyed Messina in 1908, killing tens of thousands. Italy seized Libya from the Ottoman Empire in 1911 to 1912.

Italy joined the First World War on the Allied side in 1915, fighting Austria-Hungary in the Alps and suffering a defeat at Caporetto in 1917 before winning at Vittorio Veneto in 1918. About 600,000 Italians died. Postwar unrest, strikes and anger over limited territorial gains followed.

Benito Mussolini's March on Rome in 1922 made him prime minister, and he built a fascist dictatorship by 1925. Opposition was crushed, and the state promoted nationalism and public works. The Lateran Treaty of 1929 made Vatican City an independent state and settled relations with the church.

Fascist Italy conquered Ethiopia in 1935 to 1936, using poison gas. Mussolini aided Franco in Spain and allied with Hitler in the Rome-Berlin Axis. Racial laws against Jews were passed in 1938, and Italy invaded Albania in 1939.

Italy entered the Second World War in 1940 and suffered defeats in Greece and Africa. The Allies invaded in 1943, Mussolini was overthrown, and Germany occupied the north, where partisans fought back. Mussolini was killed in 1945, and in 1946 Italians voted to become a republic.

Italy rebuilt with Marshall Plan aid and was a founding member of NATO in 1949 and the European Economic Community in 1957, signed in Rome. The Christian Democrats dominated politics. The 'economic miracle' brought cars, appliances and mass migration from the south to northern factories.

The economic miracle peaked as Italy became an industrial power, known for brands such as Fiat and for its film and fashion. The Second Vatican Council modernized the Catholic Church. Student and worker protests erupted in 1968 and 1969, along with the start of political terrorism.

During the 'Years of Lead,' left- and right-wing terrorists carried out bombings and killings; the Red Brigades kidnapped and murdered former Prime Minister Aldo Moro in 1978. Divorce was confirmed by referendum in 1974. Italy also faced oil shocks, inflation and regional devolution.

Terrorism waned, and the economy grew strongly, with small family firms in the north and center leading exports in fashion, design and machinery. Bettino Craxi became the first Socialist prime minister. The state took on the Mafia in large 'maxi-trials,' though public debt mounted.

The 'Clean Hands' corruption investigations destroyed the old parties in the early 1990s, and the Mafia murdered judges Falcone and Borsellino in 1992. Media tycoon Silvio Berlusconi entered politics in 1994. Italy qualified for the euro, adopting it in 1999.

Berlusconi dominated politics for much of the decade. Italy's economy stagnated, burdened by high debt, low growth and an aging population. Migration from Africa across the Mediterranean grew, and the 2008 global financial crisis pushed Italy into recession.

The eurozone debt crisis forced Berlusconi out in 2011, and technocrat Mario Monti imposed austerity. Thousands of migrants arrived by sea each year, fueling populist parties. In 2018 the Five Star Movement and the League formed a populist government.

Italy was the first European country hit hard by COVID-19 in 2020. Mario Draghi led a unity government, and in 2022 Giorgia Meloni became Italy's first woman prime minister, heading a right-wing coalition. Italy remained a major EU economy with high public debt.
Germany: Early humans left traces here long before history: the Mauer jaw of Homo heidelbergensis is about 600,000 years old, and Neanderthals are named after a valley near Düsseldorf. Modern humans carved ivory figurines in the Swabian caves c. 40,000 years ago, and Linear Pottery farmers brought agriculture c. 5500 BC.

Farming villages covered the fertile loess lands, building timber longhouses and earthworks. From c. 2800 BC the Corded Ware culture spread, linked to newcomers from the steppe who brought new herding ways and probably Indo-European speech. Bell Beaker groups followed, and the first bronze working appeared in central Germany with the Únětice culture c. 2200 BC.

This was a Bronze Age world of chiefs, metal traders and warriors. The Nebra sky disc, the oldest known image of the cosmos, was buried c. 1600 BC, and a large battle was fought in the Tollense valley c. 1250 BC. From c. 1300 BC the Urnfield culture spread its custom of cremating the dead.

Iron working spread into southern Germany with the Hallstatt culture from c. 800 BC, creating a wealthier elite of chieftains. In the north the Nordic Bronze Age gave way to the Jastorf culture c. 600 BC, usually seen as the cradle of the early Germanic peoples. Most people lived in small farming hamlets.

Celtic-speaking Hallstatt princes ruled hillforts such as the Heuneburg on the upper Danube, which even had Greek-style mudbrick walls. They traded with the Greek colony of Massalia for wine and luxury goods, and the Hochdorf chieftain was buried c. 530 BC with gold and a giant bronze cauldron. Germanic farmers lived further north.

The Hallstatt princely centers collapsed, and a new Celtic style called La Tène emerged in the Rhine and Moselle region c. 450 BC. Celtic society became more warlike and mobile, with groups soon raiding southward. In the north Germanic-speaking communities of the Jastorf culture kept a simpler farming and cattle-raising life.

Celtic peoples using La Tène art and iron weapons dominated the south and west, while many of their warriors migrated toward Italy and the Balkans. In the north Germanic groups grew in number. The Greek explorer Pytheas sailed the North Sea c. 325 BC and gave some of the first written reports of these lands.

The south remained Celtic, with growing trade, coinage and craft production, while Germanic tribes occupied the northern plains and coasts. Some Germanic groups, such as the Bastarnae, began to migrate southeast toward the Black Sea c. 200 BC. No states existed yet; people were organized into tribes led by chiefs and warrior bands.

Celtic towns called oppida, such as Manching in Bavaria, became busy centers of trade and minting. Around 120 BC the Germanic Cimbri and Teutones left the north and wandered across Europe until Rome destroyed them in 102 to 101 BC. It was Rome's first big encounter with Germanic peoples.

Germanic tribes pushed south and west, and Celtic oppida declined. Julius Caesar defeated the Germanic leader Ariovistus in 58 BC, made the Rhine a frontier and twice bridged it. From 12 BC Augustus sent his stepson Drusus to conquer the lands up to the Elbe, and Roman forts appeared on the Rhine.

In AD 9 Arminius of the Cherusci destroyed three Roman legions in the Teutoburg Forest, and Rome gave up conquering the lands beyond the Rhine. The river became a fortified border lined with towns such as Cologne, Mainz and Trier. Tacitus wrote his Germania in AD 98 describing the free tribes beyond.

Roman Germania Superior and Germania Inferior prospered along the Rhine, protected by the Limes, a wall and fort line between Rhine and Danube. Roman roads, villas, wine growing and baths spread. Beyond the border Germanic tribes traded with Rome, and the Marcomannic Wars of 166 to 180 showed that pressure on the frontier was growing.

New tribal confederations formed: the Alamanni appear in 213 and the Franks soon after. During Rome's third-century crisis they broke through the Limes, and c. 260 Rome abandoned the lands between Rhine and Danube. Trier briefly served as capital of the breakaway Gallic Empire, and Roman life near the frontier became insecure.

Trier became an imperial residence, where Constantine built a great basilica, and Christianity spread in the Roman Rhineland. Emperor Julian crushed the Alamanni at Strasbourg in 357, while Franks settled inside the empire as allies. From c. 375 the arrival of the Huns in eastern Europe set many peoples moving.

On the last day of 406 Vandals and others crossed the frozen Rhine, and Roman rule in the region collapsed. Burgundians settled at Worms until destroyed in 436, the event behind the Nibelungen legend. The Franks expanded, and their king Clovis defeated the Alamanni and accepted Catholic Christianity c. 496.

The Merovingian Frankish kings became overlords of most of southern and western Germany, conquering Thuringia in 531 and placing Alamannia and the new Bavarian duchy under their dukes. The Saxons in the north stayed pagan and independent. Slavic peoples moved west into the lands up to the Elbe left empty by migrating Germans.

Frankish royal power weakened and real authority passed to regional dukes and the mayors of the palace. Irish and Frankish missionaries such as Columbanus and Kilian preached among Alamanni, Bavarians and Thuringians. East of the Elbe and Saale lived Slavic tribes, and the Saxons in the north remained pagan raiders.

The Carolingian family took the Frankish throne in 751 and worked with the church. The missionary Boniface organized bishoprics such as Mainz before his murder in 754. Charlemagne then fought the pagan Saxons from 772 to 804, forcing conversion, and deposed the duke of Bavaria in 788, uniting all the German tribes under Frankish rule.

Charlemagne was crowned emperor in 800, and his court promoted learning and monasteries such as Fulda. His grandsons split the empire at Verdun in 843, giving East Francia, the core of later Germany, to Louis the German. Late in the century Viking and Magyar raids hit hard and regional dukes gained power.

The Carolingian line in the east died out in 911, and the dukes chose Saxon kings, first Henry the Fowler and then his son Otto I. Otto crushed the Magyars at Lechfeld in 955 and was crowned emperor in 962, founding the Holy Roman Empire. Bishops became pillars of royal government.

The Salian dynasty ruled the Holy Roman Empire from 1024 and built the great cathedral at Speyer. Henry IV clashed with Pope Gregory VII over who could appoint bishops, and in 1077 he stood penitent at Canossa. Towns grew along the Rhine, though crusaders massacred Jewish communities there in 1096.

The Concordat of Worms settled the investiture quarrel in 1122. The Hohenstaufen emperor Frederick Barbarossa spent decades fighting in Italy and broke the power of his rival Henry the Lion in 1180. German settlers moved east into Slavic lands, and trading towns like Lübeck were founded on the Baltic.

Emperor Frederick II focused on Sicily and handed German princes broad powers. After his dynasty fell, the Great Interregnum of 1250 to 1273 left the empire without an accepted ruler until Rudolf of Habsburg was elected. The Teutonic Knights conquered Prussia, and the merchant towns of the Hanseatic League prospered.

The Black Death of 1348 to 1350 killed perhaps a third of the population and set off terrible attacks on Jews. Emperor Charles IV ruled from Prague and his Golden Bull of 1356 fixed seven electors to choose the king. The Hanseatic League reached its peak, and Heidelberg University opened in 1386.

The Council of Constance tried to heal the church and burned Jan Hus in 1415. From 1438 the Habsburgs held the imperial crown almost continuously. Around 1440 Johannes Gutenberg developed printing with movable type in Mainz, and banking families such as the Fuggers of Augsburg grew rich on trade and mining.

Martin Luther's 95 Theses of 1517 launched the Reformation and split the empire between Catholic and Protestant princes. Emperor Charles V failed to stop it, the Peasants' War of 1524 to 1525 was bloodily crushed, and the Peace of Augsburg in 1555 let each prince choose his territory's religion.

The Thirty Years' War of 1618 to 1648 turned Germany into a battlefield for Europe's powers, and war, hunger and plague killed perhaps a fifth to a third of Germans. The Peace of Westphalia left the empire a loose patchwork of hundreds of states. Brandenburg-Prussia rose under the Great Elector.

Prussia became a kingdom in 1701, and Frederick William I built a large, disciplined army. In 1740 Frederick the Great seized rich Silesia from Austria, starting a long rivalry. Saxony's ruler also became king of Poland, Hanover's elector became king of Britain in 1714, and J.S. Bach worked in Leipzig.

Prussia barely survived the Seven Years' War of 1756 to 1763 and kept Silesia, becoming a great power, and later gained Polish lands in the partitions. German culture flowered with Kant, Goethe and Schiller. From 1792 Revolutionary France fought the German states and took the left bank of the Rhine.

Napoleon reshaped Germany: small states were absorbed into larger ones, the Confederation of the Rhine was formed, and in 1806 he dissolved the Holy Roman Empire and crushed Prussia at Jena. Germans rose against him in 1813. The Congress of Vienna created a loose German Confederation in 1815 under Austrian leadership.

Metternich's censorship held back liberal and nationalist hopes, but Prussia's Zollverein of 1834 created a customs union for most German states. The first railway opened in 1835 and industry began to grow. In 1848 revolutions swept the states, but the Frankfurt Parliament's plan for a united Germany failed in 1849.

Prussian chancellor Otto von Bismarck unified Germany through three short wars against Denmark in 1864, Austria in 1866 and France in 1870 to 1871. The German Empire was proclaimed at Versailles in 1871 under the Prussian king, excluding Austria. Coal, steel and railways turned the Ruhr into an industrial heartland.

The German Empire boomed as an industrial and scientific power in chemicals, steel and electricity. Bismarck fought Catholics and Socialists but also created the first state social insurance in the 1880s, and gained African and Pacific colonies. Wilhelm II took the throne in 1888, dismissed Bismarck in 1890 and began a naval buildup.

Wilhelmine Germany was rich, populous and ambitious, but its naval race with Britain and clumsy diplomacy, such as the 1905 Moroccan crisis, pushed Britain, France and Russia together. In German South West Africa troops carried out the genocide of the Herero and Nama from 1904. The Social Democrats became Germany's largest party.

Germany entered World War I in 1914 and fought for four years against Britain, France and Russia, with millions killed and civilians starving under blockade. Defeat in 1918 brought revolution and the Kaiser's abdication. The Weimar Republic was founded in 1919, and the Treaty of Versailles imposed territorial losses and reparations.

The Weimar Republic struggled with political violence and hyperinflation that wiped out savings in 1923, the year of Hitler's failed Munich putsch. After 1924 American loans brought a brief recovery, and Berlin became a center of modern art, film and Bauhaus design. The 1929 Wall Street crash ended the good years.

Mass unemployment in the Depression fed support for the Nazis, and Hitler became chancellor in 1933 and quickly built a dictatorship. Jews were stripped of rights by the 1935 Nuremberg Laws and attacked in the 1938 Kristallnacht pogrom. Germany rearmed, annexed Austria in 1938 and invaded Poland in 1939, starting World War II.

Nazi Germany conquered most of Europe, and carried out the Holocaust, murdering about six million Jews and millions of others. Allied bombing and invasion brought total defeat in 1945, the country was occupied and millions of Germans were expelled from the east. In 1949 it split into West Germany and communist East Germany.

West Germany under Konrad Adenauer enjoyed an economic miracle, joined NATO in 1955 and helped found the European Economic Community in 1957. In East Germany Soviet tanks crushed the workers' uprising of June 1953. Millions of East Germans fled west through Berlin, draining the communist state of workers.

East Germany built the Berlin Wall in 1961 to stop the flight west, dividing families for decades. West Germany prospered and invited guest workers from Turkey and southern Europe. The Auschwitz trials made Germans confront Nazi crimes, student protests erupted in 1968, and Willy Brandt became chancellor in 1969.

Willy Brandt's Ostpolitik eased relations with the East, and both German states joined the United Nations in 1973. Palestinian terrorists killed Israeli athletes at the 1972 Munich Olympics, and the Red Army Faction's attacks peaked in 1977. Under Helmut Schmidt West Germany weathered the oil shocks as Europe's strongest economy.

Helmut Kohl became West German chancellor in 1982, the Greens entered parliament and a large peace movement protested new nuclear missiles. East Germany's economy stagnated under Erich Honecker. In 1989 East Germans fled through Hungary and protested in Leipzig, and on 9 November the Berlin Wall fell.

Germany reunified on 3 October 1990 and later moved its capital back to Berlin. Rebuilding the former East cost huge sums and brought unemployment and resentment there. Germany helped create the European Union in 1992 and the euro in 1999, and Gerhard Schröder's government joined the 1999 Kosovo air war, Germany's first combat mission since 1945.
