Germany adopted euro cash in 2002 and carried out tough labor market reforms that helped it recover from being called the sick man of Europe. Angela Merkel became the first female chancellor in 2005. The country hosted the 2006 World Cup and came through the 2008 to 2009 financial crisis relatively well.

As Europe's economic anchor, Germany under Merkel led the response to the eurozone debt crisis. After Fukushima in 2011 it decided to close its nuclear plants. In 2015 it admitted more than a million refugees, mostly from Syria, which fueled the rise of the right-wing Alternative for Germany.

Olaf Scholz succeeded Merkel in 2021. Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022 ended Germany's reliance on Russian gas, caused an energy price shock and led to a major increase in defense spending. Scholz's coalition collapsed in late 2024, and Friedrich Merz became chancellor in 2025 amid economic stagnation.
Central Europe: Ice Age mammoth hunters lived here: the Venus of Willendorf in Austria and the fired clay figurines of Dolní Věstonice in Moravia date to c. 30,000 to 25,000 years ago. Farming arrived from the Balkans through Hungary c. 6000 BC, and the Linear Pottery culture spread from there across Europe c. 5500 BC.

Copper Age farmers of the Baden culture lived in the Carpathian Basin and beyond, while Globular Amphora and then Corded Ware peoples, linked to migrants from the steppe, spread across Poland and Bohemia c. 2800 BC. Bell Beaker groups followed, and the Únětice culture of Bohemia began working bronze c. 2200 BC.

Bronze Age chiefdoms flourished. The Únětice culture traded metal, and on the Hungarian plain people lived in fortified tell villages. From c. 1600 BC the Tumulus culture buried leaders under mounds, and from c. 1300 BC the Urnfield and Lusatian cultures spread cremation burial and fortified settlements across the region.

The Lusatian culture built fortified wooden villages in Poland, such as Biskupin with its streets and over a hundred houses (c. 740s BC). Iron working spread, and the Hallstatt culture, named after a salt-mining village in Austria, gave its name to Europe's early Iron Age. Steppe horsemen influenced the Hungarian plain.

The salt mines of Hallstatt made Alpine Austria rich, and Hallstatt chieftains traded with Italy. Scythian-influenced horse peoples lived on the Great Hungarian Plain, and raids may have weakened the Lusatian settlements of Poland. In Pomerania the face-urn culture buried ashes in pots modeled with human faces.

Celtic culture in the new La Tène style spread east along the Danube, and Celtic groups began settling Bohemia, Moravia and parts of the Carpathian Basin. In Poland the Pomeranian culture and remaining Lusatian communities lived as farmers and herders. Trade along the Amber Road carried Baltic amber south to the Mediterranean.

Celtic tribes such as the Boii, who gave Bohemia its name, dominated much of the region, building farmsteads, sanctuaries and workshops. Celtic warriors spread into the Carpathian Basin and pushed toward the Balkans. In Poland local cultures mixed with newcomers, and Celtic craftsmen settled in Silesia and around Kraków.

Celtic peoples held Bohemia, Moravia, western Hungary and the Alps, where the kingdom of Noricum formed around rich iron and salt deposits. In Poland the Przeworsk culture emerged, later linked to Germanic Vandals, and the Oksywie culture lived along the Baltic coast. Coins and wheel-made pottery appeared in Celtic lands.

Celtic towns called oppida, such as Závist and Stradonice in Bohemia, became centers of craft and coinage. Noricum traded its famous iron with Rome and became a Roman ally. Germanic groups were growing stronger in Poland, while Dacians expanded from Transylvania into the eastern Carpathian Basin.

Celtic power declined: the Dacian king Burebista crushed the Boii c. 40s BC, and Germanic Marcomanni under Maroboduus took over Bohemia c. 9 to 6 BC. Rome absorbed Noricum in 15 BC and conquered Pannonia, western Hungary, by 9 BC, reaching the Danube.

The Danube became Rome's frontier, with legionary camps at Vindobona (Vienna) and Carnuntum and the provinces of Noricum and Pannonia behind it. North of the river Maroboduus's Marcomannic kingdom fell apart after AD 19. Germanic Goths and Vandals lived in Poland, trading amber along the Amber Road to Rome.

Roman Pannonia flourished with towns such as Aquincum (Budapest) and Carnuntum, roads, villas and baths. In 166 to 180 Marcomanni, Quadi and Sarmatians invaded across the Danube, and Marcus Aurelius spent years fighting them, dying in 180. Late in the century the Goths began moving from Poland toward the Black Sea.

Pannonia was a key military province that produced several soldier emperors, but invasions and civil wars during Rome's third-century crisis brought insecurity. Sarmatian Iazyges held the Great Hungarian Plain, while Vandals and Gepids moved into the Carpathian region. Poland's Germanic population thinned as tribes migrated south.

Roman Pannonia and Noricum still guarded the Danube, and in 308 rival emperors met at Carnuntum to settle a dispute. Emperor Valentinian I died there in 375 while campaigning against the Quadi. That same decade the Huns arrived from the east, driving the Goths into the empire and unsettling the whole region.

The Huns made the Great Hungarian Plain the center of their empire, and under Attila (434 to 453) they terrorized Rome. After his death the subject peoples revolted at Nedao in 454, leaving Gepids and Ostrogoths in control. Roman Noricum faded and its remaining population was evacuated to Italy in 488.

Lombards and Gepids fought over the Carpathian Basin until 567, when the Avars, nomads from the steppe, destroyed the Gepids and the Lombards left for Italy. The Avar Khaganate ruled from the Hungarian plain. Slavic peoples spread across Bohemia, Moravia, Slovakia and Poland, settling in farming villages.

The Avar Khaganate dominated the Carpathian Basin and dragged Slavs along on raids. Around 623 the Frankish merchant Samo led Slavs in revolt, ruling a short-lived realm and defeating the Franks in 631. Slavic tribes such as the Czechs, Vistulans and Polans settled in, while Slavs in Austria formed Carantania.

The Avars still ruled the Hungarian plain, while Slavic tribes built wooden hillforts in Bohemia, Moravia and Poland. Carantania in Austria came under Bavarian overlordship and accepted Christianity. In 791 to 796 Charlemagne's armies destroyed the Avar Khaganate and seized its treasure, opening the Danube to Frankish missions.

Great Moravia, a Slavic state founded c. 833, grew to include Bohemia and Slovakia. The Byzantine missionaries Cyril and Methodius arrived in 863 and created a Slavic church liturgy. Around 895 the Magyars, a Hungarian-speaking horse people, settled the Carpathian Basin and soon destroyed Great Moravia.

Magyar raids terrorized Europe until Otto I defeated them at Lechfeld in 955, after which they settled down and their rulers began accepting Christianity. Přemyslid dukes ruled Bohemia within the empire, Austria became a margraviate under the Babenbergs in 976, and Duke Mieszko I's baptism in 966 began the Polish state.

Stephen I was crowned first King of Hungary in 1000 and firmly Christianized the Magyars. Poland gained its own archbishopric at Gniezno the same year, and Bolesław I was crowned king in 1025. Both kingdoms faced pagan revolts and civil wars, while Bohemia remained a duchy within the Holy Roman Empire.

Poland split into duchies among the sons of Bolesław III after 1138, weakening it for nearly two centuries. Hungary took the crown of Croatia in 1102 and became a regional power. Austria was raised to a duchy in 1156, and Bohemia became a hereditary kingdom in 1198. German settlers and towns spread eastward.

In 1241 the Mongols devastated Poland and Hungary, winning at Legnica and Mohi, then withdrew. Rebuilding brought stone castles and more German settlers. Polish Masovia invited the Teutonic Knights in 1226, Hungary's nobles won the Golden Bull of 1222, and Rudolf of Habsburg defeated Bohemia's Ottokar II in 1278, taking Austria.

Poland was reunited in 1320 and strengthened under Casimir the Great. Charles IV made Prague an imperial capital and founded Charles University in 1348, and Hungary prospered under Angevin kings. In 1386 Poland's queen Jadwiga married Grand Duke Jogaila of Lithuania, uniting the two states.

Poland-Lithuania crushed the Teutonic Knights at Grunwald in 1410. In Bohemia the burning of Jan Hus sparked the Hussite Wars of 1419 to 1434. The Habsburgs took the imperial crown in 1438, and Hungary's Matthias Corvinus built a Renaissance court and even took Vienna in 1485.

The Ottomans crushed Hungary at Mohács in 1526, and the Habsburgs inherited Bohemia and the rest of Hungary, which was split three ways. The Ottoman siege of Vienna in 1529 failed. The Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth was formed in 1569 as a vast elective monarchy run by its nobles, and Copernicus published his sun-centered theory in 1543.

The Defenestration of Prague in 1618 triggered the Thirty Years' War; the Habsburgs crushed the Czech Protestants in 1620 and enforced Catholicism. The Commonwealth was devastated by the Deluge of 1648 to 1667. Polish king John Sobieski helped beat the Ottomans at Vienna in 1683, and Austria regained Hungary by 1699.

The Habsburgs ruled Austria, Bohemia and Hungary, crushing Rákóczi's Hungarian revolt in 1711. The Pragmatic Sanction of 1713 let Maria Theresa inherit, but in 1740 Prussia seized Silesia. Poland, ruled by Saxon kings and ravaged in the Great Northern War, fell increasingly under Russian influence.

Maria Theresa and her son Joseph II modernized the Habsburg lands with schools, a stronger state and religious toleration, and Vienna became a capital of music with Haydn and Mozart. Poland adopted a reforming constitution in 1791, but Russia, Prussia and Austria partitioned it in 1772, 1793 and 1795 until it vanished from the map.

Napoleon defeated Austria and Russia at Austerlitz in Moravia in 1805 and created a Duchy of Warsaw for the Poles. Francis II declared the Austrian Empire in 1804. After Napoleon's fall, Metternich hosted the Congress of Vienna in 1815, which gave most of Poland to the Russian tsar and restored conservative order.

The Poles rose against Russia in 1830 to 1831 and were crushed, sending thousands into exile, including Chopin. In 1848 revolutions broke out in Vienna, Prague and Budapest, and serfdom was abolished in the Austrian lands. Hungary's revolution under Kossuth was crushed in 1849 with Russian help.

After defeats by France and Prussia, the Habsburgs struck a compromise with Hungary in 1867, creating Austria-Hungary with two governments under one emperor, Franz Joseph. The Polish January Uprising of 1863 failed against Russia. Vienna built its grand Ringstrasse, and Budapest was formed in 1873.

Austria-Hungary industrialized, especially in Bohemia, and Vienna and Budapest grew into great cities. Yet Czechs, Poles, Slovaks and others pressed for national rights, and disputes over language grew bitter. Poles faced Germanization in Prussia and Russification under the tsar, and millions of poor peasants emigrated to America.

Vienna was a cultural powerhouse, home to Freud, Klimt and Mahler, and Austria granted all men the vote in 1907. Yet ethnic tensions deepened, Hungary pushed Magyarization, and Austria-Hungary's annexation of Bosnia in 1908 angered Serbia and Russia. Russian Poland rose up in the revolution of 1905.

Austria-Hungary went to war in 1914 and suffered huge losses. In 1918 it dissolved: Poland, Czechoslovakia and Hungary became independent, and Austria became a small republic. Poland's leader Józef Piłsudski fought to set its borders, and Hungary briefly had a communist regime in 1919.

Poland defeated the Red Army near Warsaw in 1920, and Piłsudski took power in a coup in 1926. The Treaty of Trianon stripped Hungary of two-thirds of its territory, leaving a lasting grievance under Admiral Horthy. Czechoslovakia was the region's most stable democracy and industrial economy, while Austria struggled.

The Depression strengthened authoritarians, and Austria became a one-party state in 1934 before Germany annexed it in 1938. The Munich Agreement gave Hitler the Sudetenland, and he occupied the rest of the Czech lands in March 1939. In September 1939 Germany and the Soviet Union invaded and divided Poland.

Under Nazi occupation Poland lost about one in six of its people, including three million Polish Jews murdered at Auschwitz and other death camps. Warsaw rose up in 1943 and 1944 and was destroyed. The Red Army drove out the Germans, Poland's borders shifted west, and Soviet-backed communists took power by 1948.

Communist regimes copied the Soviet model, collectivizing farms and building heavy industry, with secret police silencing opponents. In 1956 Polish protests brought milder rule under Gomułka, but the Hungarian uprising was crushed by Soviet tanks and some 200,000 Hungarians fled. Austria regained independence in 1955 as a neutral state.

Hungary under János Kádár settled into a milder goulash communism with some consumer goods and market reforms. In Czechoslovakia Alexander Dubček's Prague Spring of 1968 promised socialism with a human face until Warsaw Pact troops crushed it. Poland saw student protests and an antisemitic purge in 1968.

Poland borrowed heavily from the West to raise living standards, but price rises sparked strikes in 1970 and 1976. In Czechoslovakia hard-line normalization led dissidents, including Václav Havel, to issue Charter 77. In 1978 a Polish cardinal became Pope John Paul II, and his 1979 visit home inspired millions.

The Solidarity trade union, born in Gdańsk's shipyards in 1980, grew to ten million members before martial law in 1981 drove it underground. Economic decline forced talks, and in 1989 Poland held semi-free elections, Hungary opened its border, and Czechoslovakia's Velvet Revolution peacefully ended communism.

The region rapidly turned to democracy and market economies, with painful shock therapy, privatization and unemployment. Czechoslovakia split peacefully into Czechia and Slovakia in 1993, and Austria joined the European Union in 1995. In 1999 Poland, Czechia and Hungary joined NATO.

Poland, Czechia, Slovakia and Hungary joined the European Union in 2004, opening borders and bringing investment and subsidies. Hundreds of thousands of young workers moved west, especially from Poland to Britain and Ireland. The region joined the Schengen zone in 2007, and Poland avoided recession in the 2008 crisis.

Viktor Orbán's Fidesz government in Hungary from 2010 promoted what it called illiberal democracy, and Poland's Law and Justice party from 2015 also clashed with the EU over courts and media. The 2015 migrant crisis divided the region from Western Europe. Poland's economy kept growing quickly.

After Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine, Poland took in millions of Ukrainian refugees and became a major military power and arms buyer. Poland changed government in 2023, while Orbán's Hungary kept close ties to Moscow and quarreled with the EU. The region also coped with high inflation and energy price shocks.
Russia: Denisovans and Neanderthals lived in Siberia's Altai caves, and modern humans reached Kostenki on the Don over 40,000 years ago. Ice Age hunters built mammoth-bone huts and buried their dead at Sungir with thousands of beads. Later the Trypillia farmers of Ukraine built huge towns c. 4000 BC, and steppe herders began riding horses.

The Yamnaya herders of the Pontic-Caspian steppe roamed with ox-drawn wagons and buried leaders in kurgan mounds; their descendants spread Indo-European languages across Europe and Asia. In the northern forests Finno-Ugric hunters and fishers lived on. By c. 2100 BC the Sintashta culture of the southern Urals was building fortified towns and early chariots.

Bronze Age herding cultures, such as the Srubnaya in the west and the Andronovo across Kazakhstan and Siberia, spread across the steppe, raising horses, cattle and sheep and mining copper. Indo-Iranian speakers moved south toward Iran and India. Forest peoples in the north still lived mainly by hunting, fishing and some farming.

Mounted nomads took over the steppe: first the Cimmerians, then from the east the Scythians, whose rich kurgan burials began c. 800 BC in Tuva. Greek colonists from Miletus founded trading towns on the northern Black Sea coast from c. 650 BC. Forest peoples lived in small fortified settlements.

Scythian horsemen ruled the Pontic steppe as skilled archers and herders, and c. 513 BC they lured the Persian king Darius I deep into the steppe until he retreated. Greek towns such as Olbia and Panticapaeum traded grain, fish and slaves with Greece. Pastoral peoples in the Altai buried chiefs in frozen tombs.

The Greek historian Herodotus visited Olbia and described the Scythians, their gold work and their royal burials. Greek cities around the Kerch Strait formed the Bosporan Kingdom, ruled from 438 BC by the Spartocid dynasty and a major supplier of grain to Athens. East of the Don lived the Sauromatians, ancestors of the Sarmatians.

Scythian kings were buried in great kurgans such as Chertomlyk and Solokha, filled with gold made by Greek craftsmen. The old Scythian king Ateas fell fighting Philip II of Macedon in 339 BC. The Bosporan Kingdom grew rich on grain exports, while Sarmatian tribes began pushing west from beyond the Don.

The Sarmatians, Iranian-speaking nomads famous for armored cavalry and women warriors, overran the Pontic steppe. The Scythians retreated to Crimea and the lower Dnieper, where they built a new capital at Scythian Neapolis. Greek towns on the coast kept trading but faced growing pressure from the nomads.

Sarmatian tribes such as the Roxolani and Iazyges dominated the steppe. Around 110 BC the Bosporan Kingdom and Chersonesus turned for protection to Mithridates VI of Pontus, who made the northern Black Sea part of his realm. The forest zone was home to Baltic and Finnic peoples and probably early Slavs.

Mithridates VI fought three wars against Rome and died at Panticapaeum in 63 BC, after which the Bosporan Kingdom became a Roman client state. The Sarmatians controlled the steppe, with the Alans rising among them. In the forests to the north lived farming and hunting peoples who left no written records.

The Bosporan Kingdom in Crimea was a Roman client, minting coins and exporting grain, and Rome guarded Chersonesus. The Alans became the leading nomad power north of the Caucasus. In the forest-steppe of Ukraine and Belarus, cultures such as the Zarubintsy may have included ancestors of the Slavs.

Gothic peoples migrated from the Vistula southeast toward the Black Sea late in the century, entering the steppe borderlands. The Alans and Sarmatians still roamed the steppe, and the Bosporan Kingdom continued under Roman protection. Finno-Ugric peoples lived across the northern forests and the Volga region.

The Goths settled north of the Black Sea, where the Chernyakhiv culture mixed Goths, Sarmatians and local peoples. From the 250s Gothic fleets raided Roman Asia Minor and the Balkans from the Crimean and Black Sea ports. The Greek city of Tanais was sacked and the Bosporan Kingdom weakened.

A Gothic realm under the legendary king Ermanaric stretched across Ukraine. Around 370 the Huns burst out of the east, crushed the Alans and the Goths and drove many of them into the Roman Empire, setting off the age of migrations. Early Slavs lived in the forest-steppe around Kyiv.

The Huns ruled the steppe until Attila's empire collapsed after his death in 453. Turkic-speaking groups such as the Onogurs and Bulgars then moved in from the east. Slavic peoples, known to the Byzantines as the Antes, expanded in Ukraine, and Byzantium held on to Chersonesus in Crimea.

The Avars swept through the steppe c. 558 on their way to Central Europe, and the Turkic Khaganate extended its power to the Volga. The Slavs spread widely, with the Antes and Sclaveni raiding the Byzantine Empire. Farming Slavs began moving north and east into the forests among Baltic and Finnic peoples.

Khan Kubrat founded Old Great Bulgaria on the steppe c. 632, but after his death the Khazars broke it up c. 660s. Some Bulgars moved to the Danube and founded Bulgaria in 681, others to the middle Volga. East Slavic tribes such as the Polians, Drevlians and Krivichs spread through the forests.

The Khazar Khaganate dominated the Volga and Don, collecting tribute from Slavic tribes and growing rich on trade; its elite later adopted Judaism. Khazars fought the Arab Caliphate in the Caucasus until c. 737. Scandinavian traders founded Staraya Ladoga c. 750 and began exploring river routes toward the Caspian.

Scandinavian Varangians, called Rus, controlled river trade routes carrying furs and slaves for Arab silver. According to the chronicle, Rurik ruled Novgorod from 862, and his kinsman Oleg seized Kyiv in 882, founding Kievan Rus. The Rus raided Constantinople in 860, while Khazaria and Volga Bulgaria dominated the east.

Kievan Rus grew powerful: Princess Olga was baptized in Constantinople, and her son Sviatoslav destroyed the Khazar Khaganate c. 965. Vladimir I adopted Orthodox Christianity from Byzantium in 988, linking Rus to Greek culture and the Cyrillic alphabet. Volga Bulgaria had already converted to Islam in 922.

Kievan Rus reached its height under Yaroslav the Wise (1019 to 1054), who built Kyiv's St. Sophia Cathedral and issued the first law code. After his death his sons and grandsons divided and fought over the lands. The 1054 schism tied Rus to Orthodoxy, and the nomadic Cumans began raiding from the steppe.

Kievan Rus broke into rival principalities ruled by branches of Rurik's family. Moscow is first mentioned in 1147, and Vladimir-Suzdal in the northeast grew strong enough for Prince Andrei Bogolyubsky to sack Kyiv in 1169. Novgorod became a merchant republic with an elected leadership and links to the Hanse.

The Mongols defeated the Rus at the Kalka in 1223 and from 1237 to 1240 conquered nearly all the principalities, sacking Kyiv. The Golden Horde ruled from Sarai, demanding tribute and confirming princes. Alexander Nevsky of Novgorod beat Swedes and Teutonic Knights, while Lithuania expanded into western Rus lands.

Moscow rose as the Mongols' favored tax collector under Ivan I, and the head of the Russian church moved there. Lithuania took Kyiv and much of today's Ukraine and Belarus. In 1380 Dmitry Donskoy won the first major victory over the Mongols at Kulikovo, though the Horde burned Moscow in 1382.

The Golden Horde broke apart into rival khanates. Ivan III (1462 to 1505) gathered the Russian lands, annexed Novgorod in 1478 and ended Mongol overlordship in 1480. He married a Byzantine princess, rebuilt the Moscow Kremlin with Italian architects and presented Moscow as heir to fallen Constantinople.

Ivan IV was crowned the first tsar in 1547 and conquered Kazan in 1552 and Astrakhan in 1556, gaining the whole Volga. His later reign turned to terror with the oprichnina and a long, failed Livonian War. Cossacks led by Yermak began the conquest of Siberia, while peasants were increasingly tied to the land.

The Time of Troubles brought famine, pretenders and Polish occupation of Moscow until the Romanovs took the throne in 1613. Russians reached the Pacific in 1639, serfdom became law in 1649, and Ukrainian Cossacks under Khmelnytsky joined the tsar in 1654. A church schism created the Old Believers.

Peter the Great modernized the army and state on Western lines, defeated Sweden at Poltava in 1709 and founded St. Petersburg in 1703 as his window on Europe. In 1721 he proclaimed the Russian Empire. After his death in 1725 a series of palace coups put empresses such as Anna and Elizabeth on the throne.

Catherine the Great (1762 to 1796) expanded the empire to the Black Sea, annexing Crimea in 1783, and took huge lands in the partitions of Poland. She admired the Enlightenment but strengthened noble power over serfs, and Pugachev's great peasant revolt of 1773 to 1775 was crushed. Russian traders settled in Alaska.

Alexander I fought Napoleon, who invaded in 1812 and took Moscow before cold and hunger destroyed his army. Russian troops entered Paris in 1814, and Russia gained Finland, Bessarabia and most of Poland. Russia emerged as Europe's mightiest land power and a guardian of conservative order.

The Decembrist revolt of liberal officers in 1825 was crushed, and Nicholas I ruled as a strict autocrat with a secret police. Russia crushed the Polish uprising of 1830 to 1831 and Hungary's revolution in 1849. Pushkin and Gogol founded modern Russian literature, and war dragged on in the Caucasus.

Defeat in the Crimean War exposed Russia's backwardness, prompting Alexander II's Great Reforms: the serfs were freed in 1861 and local government, courts and the army were reorganized. Russia sold Alaska to the United States in 1867 but expanded into Central Asia and the Far East. Tolstoy and Dostoevsky wrote their great novels.

Russia fought the Ottomans in 1877 to 1878 to support Balkan Slavs. Revolutionaries assassinated Alexander II in 1881, and Alexander III answered with repression, Russification and anti-Jewish pogroms. Industrialization took off with the Trans-Siberian Railway begun in 1891, and Nicholas II became tsar in 1894.

Russia's defeat by Japan in 1904 to 1905 and the Bloody Sunday massacre in St. Petersburg sparked the 1905 Revolution. Nicholas II conceded an elected parliament, the Duma, but kept most power. Prime Minister Stolypin pushed land reforms while hanging revolutionaries, and industry and cities grew quickly.

World War I brought massive defeats and shortages, and in February 1917 the tsar was overthrown; in October Lenin's Bolsheviks took power. They made peace with Germany in 1918 and killed the royal family. The Civil War of 1918 to 1922 between Reds and Whites, with terror and famine, killed millions.

Lenin's New Economic Policy allowed some private trade after the Civil War, and the USSR was formed in 1922. After Lenin died in 1924 Stalin outmaneuvered his rivals. In 1928 he launched the first Five-Year Plan, and in 1929 forced collectivization of farms began, uprooting the peasantry.

Stalin's crash industrialization built steel cities and dams, but collectivization caused the famine of 1932 to 1933 that killed millions, including in the Holodomor in Ukraine. The Great Purge of 1936 to 1938 executed some 700,000 people and filled the Gulag camps. In 1939 Stalin signed a pact with Hitler and invaded Poland.

Germany invaded in 1941, besieging Leningrad and reaching Moscow, but the Red Army won at Stalingrad and drove to Berlin by 1945 at the cost of about 27 million Soviet dead. The USSR then imposed communist regimes across Eastern Europe, starting the Cold War, and tested its first atomic bomb in 1949.

Stalin died in 1953, and Nikita Khrushchev denounced his crimes in 1956, freeing many Gulag prisoners in a thaw. The Soviets crushed the Hungarian uprising the same year. In 1957 they launched Sputnik, the first artificial satellite, while new apartment blocks and farm schemes aimed to raise living standards.

Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space in 1961. The Cuban Missile Crisis of 1962 brought the world close to nuclear war, and in 1964 Khrushchev was ousted and replaced by Leonid Brezhnev. The USSR split with communist China and crushed the Prague Spring in 1968.

Under Brezhnev the Soviet Union reached nuclear parity with the US and pursued detente, signing arms control treaties in 1972. Oil exports propped up an economy that was slowly stagnating, and dissidents like Solzhenitsyn and Sakharov were exiled. In 1979 the Soviets invaded Afghanistan, starting a costly war.

After a series of elderly leaders died, Mikhail Gorbachev took power in 1985 and launched glasnost (openness) and perestroika (restructuring). The Chernobyl nuclear disaster of 1986 exposed official secrecy. Gorbachev signed arms treaties with the US, pulled out of Afghanistan, and let Eastern Europe go in 1989.

A failed hardliner coup in August 1991 led to the USSR's dissolution into 15 states in December. Boris Yeltsin's Russia went through shock therapy, hyperinflation, rising oligarchs and the 1998 default, while war raged in Chechnya. In 1999 Yeltsin made Vladimir Putin prime minister, then resigned in his favor.

Vladimir Putin, president from 2000, centralized power and tamed the oligarchs and independent media, while an oil boom raised incomes. He fought a second war in Chechnya and handed the presidency to Dmitry Medvedev in 2008 while staying prime minister. That year Russia fought a short war with Georgia.

Putin returned to the presidency in 2012 after mass protests. In 2014, after Ukraine's pro-Western revolution, Russia annexed Crimea and backed a war in eastern Ukraine, leading to Western sanctions. Russia intervened militarily in Syria in 2015 to save the Assad regime.

Constitutional changes in 2020 let Putin potentially rule until 2036. In February 2022 Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine, bringing heavy losses, sweeping sanctions and a wave of emigration. Repression deepened, opposition leader Alexei Navalny died in prison in 2024, and the war dragged on.
Balkans: Early humans lived in Greek caves such as Petralona for hundreds of thousands of years. Farming arrived from Anatolia c. 6500 BC, reaching Europe first in Greece and the Balkans, and fishing villages flourished at Lepenski Vir on the Danube. Copper Age cultures such as Vinča grew, and Varna's graves hold the world's oldest worked gold, c. 4500 BC.

Bronze Age societies took shape around the Aegean. The Cycladic islanders carved elegant marble figurines, mainland Greeks built fortified centers such as Lerna, and Crete's Minoans laid the foundations of palace life. Further north, herders with steppe ancestry spread into the lower Danube region, mixing with local farming peoples.

Minoan Crete built great palaces such as Knossos (c. 2000 to 1450 BC), traded across the sea and wrote in Linear A, and the volcano of Thera erupted c. 1600 BC. Mycenaean Greek warrior kings then dominated (c. 1600 to 1100 BC), possibly fighting the legendary Trojan War, before collapsing in the wider Bronze Age crisis c. 1200 BC.

After the Dark Ages, Greece revived: the Olympic Games began in 776 BC, Greeks adopted the Phoenician alphabet and Homer's epics took shape. Independent city-states (poleis) grew, sending colonists across the Mediterranean and Black Sea. To the north lived Thracian, Illyrian and Dacian tribes in an Iron Age world of chiefs.

Greek city-states developed new forms of government: Solon reformed Athens' laws c. 594 BC, tyrants such as Peisistratus ruled, and Cleisthenes created Athenian democracy in 508 BC. Sparta led a powerful alliance in the Peloponnese. Persia's Darius I conquered Thrace and made Macedon a vassal c. 513 BC.

The Greeks defeated Persia at Marathon in 490 BC and at Salamis in 480 BC, after the heroic stand at Thermopylae. Athens then enjoyed a Golden Age under Pericles, building the Parthenon and nurturing drama and philosophy. The Peloponnesian War of 431 to 404 BC ended in Sparta's victory over Athens.

Sparta, then Thebes, led Greece while Plato and Aristotle taught in Athens. Philip II of Macedon built a powerful army and conquered Greece at Chaeronea in 338 BC. His son Alexander the Great (336 to 323 BC) conquered Persia, spreading Greek culture to Egypt and India, and his generals then divided his empire.

Antigonid kings ruled Macedon, and Greek city-states banded into the Achaean and Aetolian Leagues. Celtic invaders swept through in 279 BC, attacking Delphi and founding a kingdom in Thrace. Rome entered the region through wars against Illyrian pirates in 229 BC and fought its first war with Macedon from 214 BC.

Rome defeated Macedon at Cynoscephalae in 197 BC and Pydna in 168 BC, abolishing its monarchy. In 146 BC Rome annexed Greece and Macedonia, destroying Corinth, and built the Via Egnatia across the peninsula. Greek culture strongly influenced Roman elites, while Dacians and Thracians held the lands to the north.

Greece suffered as a battleground: Sulla sacked Athens in 86 BC, and Rome's civil wars were decided at Pharsalus, Philippi and Actium in 31 BC. North of the Danube, the Dacian king Burebista briefly built a large kingdom. Augustus's generals then conquered the lands up to the Danube.

Under the Pax Romana, the Balkans were divided into provinces, and Rome crushed the great Illyrian revolt of AD 6 to 9 and annexed Thrace in 46. The apostle Paul preached in Thessaloniki and Corinth, founding some of Europe's first Christian communities. North of the Danube, Dacia under Decebalus challenged Rome.

Emperor Trajan conquered Dacia in 101 to 106, settling colonists whose Latin became the root of Romanian. Hadrian lavished buildings on Athens, which remained a center of learning, and writers such as Plutarch flourished. Roman roads, towns and legions along the Danube brought prosperity to the region.

Rome's third-century crisis hit the Balkans hard: Goths killed Emperor Decius in 251 and raiders sacked Athens in 267. Rome abandoned Dacia c. 271. Yet Balkan soldiers rose to become emperors, including Aurelian and Diocletian, who built a vast palace at Split in Dalmatia.

Constantine reunified the empire in 324 and founded Constantinople, his new Christian capital, in 330. Christianity spread through the Balkans. Late in the century the Goths, fleeing the Huns, crossed the Danube and destroyed a Roman army at Adrianople in 378, and the empire was divided permanently in 395.

The Eastern Roman, or Byzantine, Empire survived as the West fell. Constantinople was protected by the huge Theodosian Walls built from 413. Attila's Huns ravaged the Balkans in the 440s, and the Ostrogoths roamed the region before leaving for Italy in 488.

Emperor Justinian (527 to 565) reconquered much of the West, codified Roman law and built the Hagia Sophia, completed in 537. But plague struck in 541, and Slavs, with the Avars, began raiding and then settling across the Balkans, transforming the population of the peninsula.

Slavs settled most of the Balkans, and Croats and Serbs arrived in the west, while Avars and Slavs besieged Constantinople in 626. Byzantium shifted to Greek as its official language and repelled an Arab siege in 674 to 678. In 681 Bulgars under Asparukh founded the First Bulgarian Empire south of the Danube.

The Byzantines repelled another Arab siege of Constantinople in 717 to 718 with Bulgar help. Iconoclast emperors banned religious images, causing bitter disputes until 787. Byzantium began reconquering Slavic-settled Greece, while the Bulgarian khans expanded north of the Danube.

Bulgaria's Khan Krum killed Byzantine Emperor Nikephoros I in battle in 811. Boris I converted Bulgaria to Christianity in 864, and disciples of Cyril and Methodius developed the Cyrillic alphabet there. The Serbs also converted, and Byzantium revived under the Macedonian dynasty from 867.

Bulgaria's Simeon I (893 to 927) created a golden age and fought Byzantium for supremacy. In 925 Croatia became a kingdom under Tomislav. Late in the century Byzantium attacked Bulgaria, which also suffered an invasion by the Rus prince Sviatoslav, and Tsar Samuel fought on from Macedonia.

Byzantine Emperor Basil II crushed Bulgaria and annexed it in 1018, making Byzantium master of the Balkans. The 1054 schism split Christianity, leaving Croatia Catholic and Serbia and Bulgaria Orthodox. Late in the century Byzantium faced Normans, Pecheneg raiders and crusaders.

Croatia entered a union with Hungary in 1102. The Komnenian emperors restored Byzantine strength but gave Venice wide trading privileges. In 1185 Bulgarians revolted and founded the Second Bulgarian Empire, and Stefan Nemanja founded the Serbian state, while Bosnia emerged under its own rulers.

The Fourth Crusade sacked Constantinople in 1204, creating a Latin Empire and giving Venice many islands and ports. Bulgaria thrived under Ivan Asen II, and Serbia became a kingdom with its own church in 1217 to 1219. The Byzantines retook Constantinople in 1261 but never fully recovered.

Serbia reached its peak when Stefan Dušan was crowned emperor in 1346. The Ottomans crossed into Europe in 1354 and won at Maritsa in 1371 and Kosovo in 1389. Bulgaria fell by 1396, and the principalities of Wallachia and Moldavia were founded north of the Danube.

The Ottomans conquered Constantinople in 1453, ending the Byzantine Empire, and absorbed Serbia, Bosnia and Albania despite Skanderbeg's resistance. Vlad III of Wallachia and Stephen the Great of Moldavia fought back. Venice kept coastal Dalmatia and Greek islands, and Dubrovnik thrived as a trading republic.

Under Suleiman the Magnificent the Ottomans took Belgrade in 1521 and Hungary in 1526, ruling the Balkans at their height. Christians kept their churches under a system of religious communities, but boys were taken for the janissary corps. The Holy League defeated the Ottoman fleet at Lepanto in 1571.

The Ottomans took Crete from Venice in 1669 after a long siege. After their defeat at Vienna in 1683 Habsburg armies pushed into the Balkans, and many Serbs fled north in the Great Migration of 1690. The Treaty of Karlowitz in 1699 gave Austria Hungary and Croatia, and Venice the Peloponnese.

The Ottomans retook the Peloponnese from Venice in 1715, but the Habsburgs won Belgrade in 1718, only to lose it again in 1739. Ottoman sultans began appointing Greek Phanariot governors to rule Wallachia and Moldavia. In Montenegro prince-bishops kept a mountain realm virtually independent.

Russia's wars with the Ottomans made it protector of Orthodox Christians in 1774, and a Russian-backed Greek revolt in 1770 failed. Strongmen such as Ali Pasha of Ioannina ruled almost independently. Greek merchants grew rich, the poet Rigas Feraios called for liberation, and Venice's Dalmatia went to Austria in 1797.

National revolts began against Ottoman rule. The Serbs rose in 1804 under Karađorđe and again in 1815, gaining autonomy. Napoleon ruled the Dalmatian coast as his Illyrian Provinces until 1813, Russia annexed Bessarabia in 1812, and in 1821 the Greek War of Independence began.

European powers destroyed the Ottoman-Egyptian fleet at Navarino in 1827, and Greece became independent by 1830 under a Bavarian king, Otto. Serbia gained recognized autonomy, and Wallachia and Moldavia came under Russian protection. Revolutions in 1848 stirred Romanians and Croats.

Wallachia and Moldavia united in 1859, forming Romania under a Hohenzollern prince from 1866. Britain gave the Ionian Islands to Greece in 1864, and the last Ottoman garrisons left Serbia in 1867. A separate Bulgarian church was set up in 1870, a step toward national independence.

Revolts in Bosnia and Bulgaria led to the Russo-Turkish War of 1877 to 1878. The Congress of Berlin made Serbia, Montenegro and Romania independent and Bulgaria autonomous, and let Austria-Hungary occupy Bosnia. Bulgaria united with Eastern Rumelia in 1885, and Athens hosted the first modern Olympics in 1896.

Rival nationalisms competed over Ottoman Macedonia, where the Ilinden Uprising of 1903 was crushed. In Serbia a 1903 coup brought in a pro-Russian dynasty. In 1908 Austria-Hungary annexed Bosnia and Bulgaria declared full independence, while Romania's peasant revolt of 1907 was put down bloodily.

The Balkan Wars of 1912 to 1913 drove the Ottomans almost out of Europe, and Albania became independent. In 1914 a Bosnian Serb assassinated Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo, triggering World War I. Serbia suffered terribly, and in 1918 the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, later Yugoslavia, was formed.

Greece's invasion of Anatolia ended in disaster in 1922, followed by the 1923 exchange of over a million Greeks and Turks. Romania doubled in size after the war. Yugoslavia was torn by Serb and Croat rivalry, and after the Croat leader Radić was shot in parliament, King Alexander imposed a dictatorship in 1929.

The Depression hit farmers hard, and most of the region slid into royal or military dictatorships, including Metaxas in Greece and Carol II in Romania. Yugoslav King Alexander was assassinated in 1934. Fascist Italy, already dominant in Albania, invaded it outright in 1939.

Greece resisted Italy in 1940, but the Axis occupied Yugoslavia and Greece in 1941. Croatia's fascist Ustaše committed genocide, and Tito's communist Partisans led resistance. After 1944 communists took over Yugoslavia, Albania, Bulgaria and Romania, while Greece fought a civil war in which royalists beat communists by 1949.

Tito's Yugoslavia broke with Stalin in 1948 and developed its own form of socialism with workers' self-management, accepting Western aid. Greece joined NATO in 1952 and slowly rebuilt. Bulgaria, Romania and Albania remained strict Soviet-style dictatorships with collectivized farms.

Yugoslavia co-founded the Non-Aligned Movement in Belgrade in 1961 and let citizens work abroad. Nicolae Ceaușescu took power in Romania in 1965, and Albania broke with Moscow to ally with China. In Greece a military junta seized power in 1967.

Greece's junta collapsed in 1974 after a failed coup in Cyprus, and a referendum abolished the monarchy. In Yugoslavia Tito suppressed the Croatian Spring of 1971, but a 1974 constitution gave republics more power. Ceaușescu's cult of personality grew, and Albania isolated itself further.

Tito's death in 1980 left Yugoslavia without its unifying leader, burdened by debt and nationalist tension, and Slobodan Milošević rose in Serbia from 1987. Greece joined the European Community in 1981. In 1989 communist rule ended in Bulgaria, and Romania's revolution toppled and executed Ceaușescu.

Yugoslavia broke apart in brutal wars: Slovenia and Croatia declared independence in 1991, and the Bosnian war of 1992 to 1995 included the siege of Sarajevo and the Srebrenica genocide. NATO bombing ended the Kosovo war in 1999. Albania, Bulgaria and Romania struggled through hard transitions.

Milošević fell in 2000 and was put on trial in The Hague. Athens hosted the 2004 Olympics, Slovenia joined the EU in 2004, and Bulgaria and Romania in 2007. Montenegro became independent in 2006, Kosovo declared independence in 2008, and Greece's debt crisis began in 2009.

Greece endured bailouts, austerity and deep recession, losing about a quarter of its economy. Croatia joined the EU in 2013, and in 2015 hundreds of thousands of refugees crossed the region on the Balkan route. North Macedonia settled its name dispute with Greece in 2018, opening the way to NATO.

Croatia adopted the euro and joined Schengen in 2023, and Bulgaria and Romania joined Schengen fully in 2025. The Western Balkan states pressed on with slow EU membership talks. In Serbia a deadly station canopy collapse in Novi Sad in late 2024 sparked mass protests against corruption.
Anatolia: Hunter-gatherers raised the carved stone enclosures of Göbekli Tepe around 9500 BC, long before farming was fully established. Later Neolithic villagers grew wheat, herded animals and traded obsidian, and Çatalhöyük became one of the world's earliest large towns by c. 7400 BC. Copper working spread in the Chalcolithic age.

Early Bronze Age Anatolia was a land of fortified towns ruled by local chiefs, such as Troy on the Dardanelles and Alaca Höyük with its rich royal tombs. The Hattians lived in the central plateau, while Indo-European speakers, ancestors of the Hittites and Luwians, were settling in. Metalwork and long-distance trade grew steadily.

Assyrian merchants ran trading colonies at Kanesh around 1900 BC, bringing writing to Anatolia. From c. 1650 BC the Hittites built an empire from their capital Hattusa, rivaling Egypt and Mitanni. Around 1200 BC the Late Bronze Age collapse swept the empire away and Troy was destroyed, leaving smaller Neo-Hittite states.

After the Hittites fell, new kingdoms rose. Phrygia, ruled from Gordion by kings like Midas, dominated the center until Cimmerian raiders struck c. 700 BC, while Lydia grew rich at Sardis and minted the first coins c. 630 BC. Greeks settled the Aegean coast, and Urartu held the eastern highlands.

Lydia under Croesus reached its peak until Cyrus the Great conquered it in 547 BC, bringing Anatolia into the Persian Achaemenid Empire. Persian satraps ruled from Sardis, the start of the Royal Road to Susa. The Greek cities of Ionia, home of early philosophers like Thales of Miletus, now paid tribute to Persia.

The Ionian Greek cities rebelled against Persia in 499–493 BC, sparking the Greco-Persian Wars. After Persia's defeats in Greece, many coastal cities joined Athens' Delian League, while the interior stayed under Persian satraps. Herodotus, the first great historian, was born in Halicarnassus in this century.

Persia regained the Ionian coast in 387 BC, and local dynasts like Mausolus of Caria built grand monuments such as the Mausoleum. In 334 BC Alexander the Great crossed into Anatolia, won at the Granicus and swept east. After his death his generals fought over the region, notably at Ipsus in 301 BC.

Anatolia split among Hellenistic powers. The Seleucids held much of it, while the Attalid kings made Pergamon a brilliant center of art and learning. Celtic Galatians invaded in 278 BC and settled the central plateau, and native kingdoms such as Bithynia, Pontus and Cappadocia grew in strength.

Rome defeated the Seleucid king Antiochus III at Magnesia in 190 BC and handed much of Anatolia to its ally Pergamon. When Attalus III died in 133 BC he bequeathed Pergamon to Rome, which formed the province of Asia. Roman tax collectors arrived, and the kingdom of Pontus began to rise.

Mithridates VI of Pontus challenged Rome in the Mithridatic Wars of 88–63 BC, at first massacring Romans across Asia. Sulla, Lucullus and finally Pompey defeated him and reorganized Anatolia into Roman provinces and client kingdoms. Caesar won quickly at Zela in 47 BC, and Augustus added Galatia in 25 BC.

Under the Roman peace, Anatolian cities like Ephesus, Smyrna and Pergamon flourished with theaters, baths and trade. The apostle Paul, from Tarsus, spread Christianity through the region, and early churches took root in many towns. Rome annexed Cappadocia in AD 17, tightening its hold on the interior.

The 100s were a golden age for Roman Anatolia. Emperors like Hadrian funded grand buildings, the Library of Celsus rose at Ephesus, and Greek orators and the physician Galen of Pergamon won fame. Christianity kept spreading, though the Antonine Plague of the 160s struck the population hard.

Rome's third-century crisis reached Anatolia as Gothic raiders plundered the coasts and burned the Temple of Artemis at Ephesus. Persian armies under Shapur I raided the east, and Zenobia of Palmyra briefly seized parts of the region. Diocletian restored order from 284, ruling from Nicomedia.

Constantine founded Constantinople in 330 on the Bosporus, making Anatolia the heartland of a new Christian Roman state. The Council of Nicaea in 325 defined Christian doctrine, and Cappadocian bishops like Basil shaped theology. By the 380s Christianity was the official religion and pagan temples declined.

While the western Roman Empire collapsed, the eastern or Byzantine Empire held firm, with Anatolia as its secure core of farms, cities and soldiers. Church councils at Ephesus in 431 and Chalcedon in 451 debated the nature of Christ. Isaurian highlanders gained power, and one, Zeno, became emperor.

Under Justinian the Byzantine Empire built Hagia Sophia and tried to reconquer the West. Anatolia supplied taxes and troops but suffered the Plague of Justinian from 541, which killed a large share of the population. Wars with Sasanian Persia flared repeatedly along the eastern frontier.

Persian armies overran Anatolia during the war of 602–628, reaching the Bosporus. Soon after, Arab Muslim armies began yearly raids and besieged Constantinople in 674–678. The Byzantines reorganized Anatolia into military districts called themes, and many cities shrank into fortified hilltop towns.

Leo III defeated the great Arab siege of Constantinople in 717–718, and Byzantine troops won at Akroinon in 740, securing Anatolia. Emperors began Iconoclasm, banning religious images, which divided the church until the Council of Nicaea in 787 restored them. Arab border raids continued each summer.

Abbasid armies sacked the Anatolian city of Amorion in 838, but Byzantium steadily recovered. Icon veneration was permanently restored in 843, and the heretical Paulician state in the east was crushed in 872. The Macedonian dynasty, from 867, began pushing the frontier back eastward.

The Byzantine Empire went on the offensive, retaking Melitene and in 969 Antioch under soldier-emperors like Nikephoros Phokas and John Tzimiskes. Great Anatolian landowning families grew powerful and sometimes rebelled. Basil II, crowned in 976, would lead the empire to a new peak.

Byzantium annexed Armenian lands early in the century, but Seljuk Turks raided deeper and won a crushing victory at Manzikert in 1071. Turkish groups settled much of the plateau, founding the Sultanate of Rum. The First Crusade crossed Anatolia in 1097, helping the Komnenos emperors regain the western coast.

The Seljuk Sultanate of Rum, ruling from Konya, controlled central Anatolia and competed with the Danishmendid Turks and the Byzantines on the coasts. Byzantium lost a major battle at Myriokephalon in 1176. Armenians built a kingdom in Cilicia, and Crusaders kept marching through, with Frederick Barbarossa drowning there in 1190.

Rum prospered early in the century, building caravanserais along trade roads, and the poet Rumi taught in Konya. The Fourth Crusade sacked Constantinople in 1204, leaving Greek successor states at Nicaea and Trebizond. After the Mongols made Rum a vassal in 1243, small Turkish emirates emerged, including Osman's c. 1299.

The Ottomans grew from a frontier emirate into a major power, taking Bursa in 1326, Nicaea in 1331 and crossing into Europe at Gallipoli in 1354. They moved their capital to Edirne and won in the Balkans at Kosovo in 1389. Bayezid I then absorbed rival Turkish emirates across Anatolia.

Timur crushed Bayezid I at Ankara in 1402, triggering an Ottoman civil war until 1413. The state recovered, and in 1453 Mehmed II conquered Constantinople, ending the Byzantine Empire and making Istanbul his capital. Trebizond and the emirate of Karaman were absorbed, uniting Anatolia under Ottoman rule.

Selim I defeated Safavid Iran at Chaldiran in 1514 and conquered the Mamluks in 1516–17, making the Ottomans masters of the Arab heartlands. Under Suleiman the Magnificent, 1520–66, the empire peaked, and the architect Sinan built great mosques. Late in the century the Celali revolts shook rural Anatolia.

Rural unrest, inflation and palace intrigue weakened the Ottoman state early in the century. The Köprülü family of grand viziers restored order from 1656, but the failed siege of Vienna in 1683 began a long retreat. The Treaty of Karlowitz in 1699 brought the first major territorial losses in Europe.

Istanbul's elite enjoyed the Tulip Era of 1718–30, with gardens, palaces and the first Ottoman Muslim printing press, until the Patrona Halil revolt ended it. Wars with Russia and Austria continued, though the Ottomans regained Belgrade in 1739. Provincial notables increasingly controlled Anatolian towns.

Defeat by Russia in 1768–74 ended with the Treaty of Küçük Kaynarca, and Russia annexed Crimea in 1783. Local notables called ayans held real power across Anatolia. Selim III, sultan from 1789, launched the New Order reforms to build a modern army, angering the Janissaries.

Selim III was overthrown in 1807 by conservative Janissaries, and Mahmud II took the throne in 1808, slowly rebuilding central authority. The empire faced national revolts in the Balkans, first in Serbia from 1804 and then the Greek War of Independence from 1821.

Mahmud II destroyed the Janissary corps in 1826 and built a modern army. Greece won independence in 1830, and the Egyptian forces of Muhammad Ali invaded Anatolia, reaching Konya in 1832. In 1839 the Tanzimat reforms began, promising equal rights and modern administration for all subjects.

Britain and France helped the Ottomans defeat Russia in the Crimean War of 1853–56, yet the empire was increasingly called the 'sick man of Europe'. The 1856 reform edict expanded equality for non-Muslims. Hundreds of thousands of Circassian refugees from Russia settled in Anatolia, and foreign debt mounted.

The Ottoman state went bankrupt in 1875, and in 1876 it adopted its first constitution. Abdulhamid II suspended parliament after losing the 1877–78 war with Russia and ruled as an autocrat, building railways and schools. European creditors took over parts of the finances, and massacres of Armenians in 1894–96 killed tens of thousands or more.

The Young Turk Revolution of 1908 restored the constitution, and Abdulhamid II was deposed in 1909. The Committee of Union and Progress rose to power. In 1908 Austria annexed Bosnia and Bulgaria declared full independence, and the 1909 Adana massacre killed thousands of Armenians, showing rising ethnic tension.

The Ottomans lost most of their Balkan lands in 1912–13 and entered World War I on Germany's side. They won at Gallipoli in 1915, but the government carried out the Armenian genocide, also killing many Assyrians and Greeks. After defeat in 1918, Mustafa Kemal led the Turkish War of Independence.

Turkish forces defeated Greece in 1922, and the Treaty of Lausanne in 1923 recognized the new Republic of Turkey under Atatürk, with Ankara as capital. Greece and Turkey exchanged populations. The caliphate was abolished in 1924, and sweeping secular reforms introduced Western law and the Latin alphabet.

Atatürk's one-party republic pushed modernization further: women gained the vote in 1934, citizens took surnames, and the state built factories. A Kurdish uprising in Dersim was harshly suppressed in 1937–38. Atatürk died in 1938, succeeded by İsmet İnönü, and Turkey gained Hatay from French Syria in 1939.

Turkey stayed neutral through most of World War II, joining the Allies only in 1945. A 1942 wealth tax fell heavily on non-Muslim citizens. After the war, Soviet pressure pushed Turkey toward the United States, which sent aid from 1947, and multiparty politics began in 1946.

The Democrat Party under Adnan Menderes won the 1950 election, ending one-party rule. Turkey sent troops to Korea and joined NATO in 1952. Farms mechanized and villagers flooded into cities, but debt and repression grew, and the 1955 Istanbul riots targeted the Greek community.

The army overthrew Menderes in 1960 and executed him in 1961, then introduced a more liberal constitution. Hundreds of thousands of Turkish workers began moving to West Germany and other European countries. Politics became polarized between left and right, and crises in Cyprus strained relations with Greece.

The military forced out the government in 1971, and Turkey invaded Cyprus in 1974 after a Greek-backed coup there, dividing the island. Economic crisis and street violence between leftists and nationalists killed thousands. The Kurdish militant group PKK was founded in 1978.

The army seized power in 1980 and imposed a new constitution in 1982. Turgut Özal then opened the economy to markets and exports. The PKK began an armed insurgency in the Kurdish southeast in 1984, a conflict that would last decades, and Turkey applied to join the European Community in 1987.

The war with the PKK peaked, displacing many Kurdish villagers, until leader Abdullah Öcalan was captured in 1999. The Islamist Welfare Party briefly led the government before military pressure forced it out in 1997. The İzmit earthquake of 1999 killed about 17,000, and Turkey became an EU candidate.

After a severe financial crisis in 2001, the AKP led by Recep Tayyip Erdoğan won power in 2002. Turkey enjoyed rapid growth, passed reforms and opened EU membership talks in 2005. Tensions grew between the governing party and the secular establishment, including the army.

Mass Gezi Park protests in 2013 challenged Erdoğan's rule, and Turkey took in several million Syrian refugees. Peace talks with the PKK collapsed in 2015. After a failed coup in 2016, the government purged tens of thousands, and a 2017 referendum created a powerful executive presidency.

Turkey faced high inflation and a currency slide. Earthquakes in February 2023 killed over 50,000 people in the southeast. Erdoğan won reelection in 2023, the 2025 arrest of Istanbul's opposition mayor sparked large protests, and the PKK announced in 2025 that it would disband.
Israel: Natufian hunter-gatherers built some of the first permanent villages here, and by c. 9000 BC Jericho had become one of the world's oldest towns, later ringed by a stone wall and tower. Farming and herding spread through the Neolithic, and later Chalcolithic villagers made fine copperwork.

Early Bronze Age Canaanites built walled towns such as Megiddo and Arad, growing olives, grapes and grain and trading with Egypt. Around 2300 BC many towns were abandoned, and for a few centuries people lived mainly in villages and as pastoral herders.

Canaanite city-states revived and grew rich, then came under Egyptian control in the New Kingdom, as the Amarna letters show. After the Bronze Age collapse c. 1200 BC, Philistines settled the coast and Israelites emerged in the hill country, first named on an Egyptian stele c. 1208 BC.

Tradition credits David and Solomon with a united kingdom c. 1000 BC, though historians debate its size. The northern Kingdom of Israel, capital Samaria, was destroyed by Assyria in 722 BC, while Judah, centered on Jerusalem, survived as a vassal. Prophets and royal reforms shaped Israelite religion.

Babylon destroyed Jerusalem and its Temple in 586 BC and deported much of Judah's elite. After Cyrus of Persia took Babylon, he allowed Jews to return in 538 BC, and the Second Temple was completed in 516 BC. Judah became the small Persian province of Yehud.

Yehud remained a modest Persian province centered on the rebuilt Temple. Leaders like Nehemiah restored Jerusalem's walls around 445 BC, and Ezra promoted Torah observance. Scribes were shaping the Hebrew scriptures, while Samaritans to the north developed their own tradition.

Alexander the Great took the region in 332 BC after besieging Tyre and Gaza. After his death it passed to the Ptolemies of Egypt from 301 BC. Greek-style cities, coins and culture began to spread, slowly influencing local Jewish life.

The Ptolemies ruled from Alexandria, taxing the land through local agents, while Jewish scholars in Egypt began translating the Torah into Greek. Ptolemaic and Seleucid kings fought repeated wars over the region, and in 200 BC the Seleucid Antiochus III won it at Panium.

The Seleucid king Antiochus IV banned Jewish practices and desecrated the Temple, sparking the Maccabean revolt of 167–160 BC. The Temple's rededication is remembered at Hanukkah. The Hasmonean family then built an independent Jewish kingdom that expanded its borders.

Hasmonean rivals called in Rome, and Pompey took Judea in 63 BC. Rome made Herod the Great king in 37 BC, and he rebuilt the Temple on a grand scale and founded Caesarea. Jesus of Nazareth was born c. 4 BC, near the end of Herod's reign.

Roman governors ruled Judea, and Jesus was crucified c. 30–33, after which his followers spread Christianity. Tensions with Rome exploded in the Jewish revolt of 66–73, and the Romans destroyed the Second Temple in 70. Rabbinic Judaism began to take shape without the Temple.

The Bar Kokhba revolt of 132–136 ended in massive destruction, and Hadrian rebuilt Jerusalem as a pagan colony, barring Jews from the city. Rome renamed the province Syria Palaestina. Jewish life shifted to Galilee, where rabbis compiled the Mishnah around 200.

Jewish scholars in Galilee built on the Mishnah, and synagogues were common in the region. Caesarea became a center of Christian learning under the scholar Origen. The region shared in the Roman Empire's third-century turmoil but stayed relatively stable.

After Constantine's conversion the land became the Christian Holy Land, with the Church of the Holy Sepulchre built in Jerusalem in the 330s. Pilgrims arrived from across the empire. Emperor Julian's plan to rebuild the Jewish Temple in 363 failed, and the Jerusalem Talmud was completed around 400.

Under Byzantine rule, the region was split into three provinces of Palaestina and grew prosperous and populous. Monasteries filled the Judean desert, and Jerusalem became a patriarchate in 451. Jewish and Samaritan communities continued, though under increasing legal restrictions.

Samaritan revolts against Byzantine rule were crushed in 529 and 556. Justinian built the great Nea Church in Jerusalem, and churches with fine mosaics, like the one recorded on the Madaba Map, dotted the land. The plague of 541 brought heavy losses.

Sasanian Persia captured Jerusalem in 614, Byzantium returned briefly, and Arab Muslim armies took the city in 637 under Caliph Umar. Under Umayyad rule the Dome of the Rock was finished in 691. Christians and Jews remained, while Arabic and Islam slowly spread.

The Umayyads built the al-Aqsa Mosque and founded Ramla as the capital of the province of Filastin. A major earthquake in 749 devastated towns like Beit She'an. In 750 the Abbasids took over, shifting power to distant Iraq, and the region became a quieter province.

Under the Abbasids and then, from 878, the Tulunids of Egypt, the region was a provincial backwater, but Jerusalem remained a pilgrimage site for Muslims, Christians and Jews. Arabic became the common language, and more of the population gradually converted to Islam.

Egyptian dynasties, first the Ikhshidids and then from the 970s the Shia Fatimids, contested control with Bedouin and Qarmatian raiders. In Tiberias, Jewish scholars called the Masoretes perfected the Hebrew Bible's text, producing manuscripts like the Aleppo Codex.

The Fatimid caliph al-Hakim destroyed the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in 1009, and Seljuk Turks took Jerusalem in 1073. Crusaders captured the city in 1099, massacring many inhabitants, and founded the Latin Kingdom of Jerusalem, ruled by European knights.

The Crusader kingdom built castles and relied on military orders like the Templars and Hospitallers. Saladin destroyed its army at Hattin in 1187 and retook Jerusalem. The Third Crusade under Richard the Lionheart regained the coast, leaving a smaller kingdom based at Acre.

Frederick II briefly regained Jerusalem by treaty in 1229, but it was lost for good in 1244. The Mamluk sultans of Egypt, led by Baybars, took Crusader castles one by one, and the fall of Acre in 1291 ended the Crusader states. Mamluks then ruled the region.

The Mamluks governed the land as provinces under Damascus and Cairo, endowing religious schools and hostels in Jerusalem. The Black Death of 1348 cut the population. Franciscan friars became custodians of Christian holy sites, and Jewish communities persisted in towns like Jerusalem.

Under late Mamluk rule the region was poor and thinly populated, troubled by plague, heavy taxes and Bedouin raids. After the expulsion of Jews from Spain in 1492, some Sephardic Jews began to settle here, especially in Safed and Jerusalem.

The Ottomans conquered the land in 1516, beginning four centuries of rule. Suleiman the Magnificent built Jerusalem's still-standing walls in 1537–41. Safed became a thriving center of Jewish mysticism and law, home to scholars like Isaac Luria and Joseph Karo.

Ottoman governors under Damascus ruled loosely, and the Druze emir Fakhr al-Din II controlled Galilee early in the century. In 1665 the self-proclaimed messiah Sabbatai Zevi was declared in Gaza, stirring Jewish communities worldwide. Local economies and towns declined.

Local strongmen gained power under loose Ottoman rule. Zahir al-Umar, an Arab chief, began building an autonomous domain in Galilee from the 1730s, based first at Tiberias and growing rich on cotton exports. Small groups of Jewish pilgrims settled in Jerusalem.

Zahir al-Umar ruled Galilee from Acre until he was killed in 1775, and the ruthless governor Jazzar Pasha took over. In 1799 Napoleon invaded from Egypt but failed to capture Acre. Hasidic Jews from Eastern Europe settled in Galilee from 1777.

After Jazzar's death in 1804, governors at Acre continued to dominate the region under nominal Ottoman rule. Disciples of the Vilna Gaon settled in Safed and Jerusalem. Most inhabitants were Arab Muslim and Christian villagers, with small Jewish communities in the holy cities.

Egypt's Ibrahim Pasha ruled the region from 1831 to 1840, introducing conscription and reforms and crushing a peasant revolt in 1834. An earthquake devastated Safed in 1837. European powers opened consulates, and Ottoman rule returned in 1840 with European help.

Ottoman Tanzimat reforms reshaped land ownership and administration. Disputes over Christian holy places helped trigger the Crimean War. Jerusalem began expanding beyond its walls in the 1860s, and missionaries, pilgrims and German Templer colonists added to a growing European presence.

Most of the population were Arab Muslims and Christians, while Jaffa and Jerusalem grew. In 1882 the First Aliyah brought Jewish immigrants from Russia and Romania, founding farm colonies supported by Baron Rothschild. In 1897 Theodor Herzl launched political Zionism at the First Zionist Congress.

The Second Aliyah from 1904 brought socialist Zionist pioneers who founded the first kibbutz at Degania in 1909, the same year Tel Aviv was founded. Arab newspapers and leaders began voicing concern about land sales and immigration. The 1908 Young Turk Revolution briefly raised hopes for reform.

World War I brought hunger, locusts and Ottoman repression. In 1917 Britain issued the Balfour Declaration, supporting a Jewish national home while promising to protect the rights of non-Jewish communities, and British forces took Jerusalem in December. Both Arab and Jewish national movements grew.

Britain governed Palestine under a League of Nations mandate. Jewish immigration and institutions expanded, including the Hebrew University in 1925. Arab Palestinians opposed the mandate's Zionist commitments, and violence erupted in 1920, 1921 and 1929, when the Jewish community of Hebron was attacked.

Nazi persecution drove a large wave of Jewish immigration. Palestinian Arabs launched a revolt in 1936–39, which Britain suppressed. The Peel Commission proposed partition in 1937, and the 1939 White Paper sharply limited Jewish immigration.

After World War II and the Holocaust, Jewish groups fought British rule. The UN proposed partition in 1947, civil war followed, and Israel declared independence in 1948. Arab states invaded, and about 700,000 Palestinians fled or were expelled (the Nakba). Jordan held the West Bank and Egypt Gaza.

Israel's population roughly doubled as Holocaust survivors and Jews from Arab countries arrived. Palestinian refugees lived in camps in neighboring lands and Gaza. Israel joined Britain and France in the 1956 Suez War, and Palestinian activists founded Fatah in 1959.

Israel tried Nazi official Adolf Eichmann in 1961, and Arab states created the PLO in 1964. In the Six-Day War of 1967 Israel captured the West Bank, Gaza, Sinai, Golan Heights and East Jerusalem. Military occupation and the first settlements followed.

Egypt and Syria attacked in the 1973 Yom Kippur War, and Israel prevailed at heavy cost. The right-wing Likud won power in 1977, and Egypt's Sadat visited Jerusalem, leading to the 1979 peace treaty. Settlements in the occupied territories expanded.

Israel returned Sinai to Egypt by 1982 and invaded Lebanon to expel the PLO. Ethiopian Jews were airlifted to Israel. In 1987 the First Intifada, a mass Palestinian uprising, erupted in the occupied territories, and Hamas was founded the same year.

Around a million immigrants arrived from the former Soviet Union. The 1993 Oslo Accords created the Palestinian Authority and a path to negotiations, and Israel made peace with Jordan in 1994. A Jewish extremist assassinated Prime Minister Rabin in 1995, and attacks and settlement growth eroded the process.

Peace talks failed in 2000, and the Second Intifada brought suicide bombings and Israeli military operations, killing thousands. Israel built a separation barrier and withdrew from Gaza in 2005. Hamas won Palestinian elections and seized Gaza in 2007, followed by a blockade and wars.

Israel's tech economy boomed and offshore gas was found, while Benjamin Netanyahu led long governments. Wars with Hamas in Gaza in 2012 and 2014 killed many civilians, mostly Palestinians. The US moved its embassy to Jerusalem in 2018, and peace talks stayed frozen.

Israel normalized ties with the UAE and others in 2020, and a judicial overhaul sparked mass protests in 2023. Hamas's October 7, 2023 attack killed about 1,200 people and took 250 hostages, and Israel's war in Gaza killed tens of thousands and caused a humanitarian catastrophe before a ceasefire in October 2025.
Levant: The Levant was one of the birthplaces of farming. Natufian foragers settled in villages, and by c. 9000 BC people at sites like Abu Hureyra and Tell Aswad were cultivating cereals. Later Neolithic towns such as Ain Ghazal made plaster statues, and Byblos began its long life as a settlement.

Early Bronze Age cities grew wealthy on trade. Ebla in Syria kept vast clay archives around 2400 BC, and Mari on the Euphrates was a major center. Byblos shipped cedar to Egypt, and Akkadian kings from Mesopotamia raided the region. Amorite peoples became prominent near the end.

Amorite kingdoms like Yamhad at Aleppo flourished, and Ugarit became a great trading port that used an early alphabet. Egypt, Mitanni and the Hittites competed for control, fighting at Kadesh in 1274 BC before signing a peace treaty. Around 1200 BC the Bronze Age collapse destroyed Ugarit, and Arameans spread.

Aramean kingdoms, especially Damascus, ruled inland Syria, while Phoenician cities like Tyre and Sidon spread trade and their alphabet across the Mediterranean, founding Carthage in 814 BC. Ammon, Moab and Edom held Jordan. Assyria conquered the region in the 700s BC, later followed by Babylon.

Babylon's Nebuchadnezzar besieged Tyre for 13 years and dominated the region until Persia took over after 539 BC. Under the Achaemenids, the Levant became the satrapy of 'Beyond the River'. Phoenician cities kept their kings and supplied Persia's navy.

Persian rule was mostly stable. Phoenician kings in Sidon, Tyre and Byblos governed their cities, minted coins and sent fleets against Greece. Aramaic served as the common administrative language, and Arab peoples controlled the desert trade routes to the south and east.

Persia crushed a revolt at Sidon in 351 BC. Alexander defeated Darius III at Issus in 333 BC and took Tyre after a long siege. After his death, Seleucus founded his empire in 312 BC and built new Greek cities like Antioch and Apamea, while the Nabataeans grew rich at Petra.

The Seleucids of Antioch and the Ptolemies of Egypt fought repeated Syrian Wars over the region, with the south under Ptolemaic rule. Greek-style cities, temples and theaters spread. In 200 BC Antiochus III won the whole Levant for the Seleucids at Panium.

After Rome defeated Antiochus III in 190 BC, the Seleucid kingdom weakened through civil wars among rival kings. Local powers took advantage: the Hasmoneans in Judea, Nabataean Arabs in the south and Iturean chiefs in Lebanon all expanded, while Parthia pressed from the east.

Armenia's Tigranes the Great briefly ruled Syria until Pompey made it a Roman province in 64 BC, with Antioch as its capital. Parthians invaded in 40 BC but were driven out. The Nabataean kingdom of Petra was at its height, controlling incense caravan routes.

Roman Syria prospered, and caravan cities like Palmyra grew wealthy on trade with the East. Christianity spread early, and followers were first called Christians at Antioch. Huge temples rose at Baalbek, and Greek cities of the Decapolis such as Gerasa flourished.

Trajan annexed the Nabataean kingdom in 106 as the province of Arabia and built a new road from Bosra to the Red Sea. Palmyra reached its peak as a trading hub. Cities across Syria built colonnaded streets and temples during this prosperous Roman century.

Syrians reached the top of Roman power: Julia Domna of Emesa became empress, and Philip the Arab was emperor in 244–249. Persia's Shapur I sacked Antioch, and Queen Zenobia of Palmyra briefly ruled the Roman East in 267–272 before Aurelian crushed her and destroyed Palmyra.

Christianity became the dominant faith as the empire converted, and Antioch was one of its great centers, home to preachers like John Chrysostom. Syriac-speaking writers such as Ephrem enriched Christian literature. The eastern frontier saw repeated wars with Sasanian Persia.

Under Byzantine rule the countryside thrived with olive-growing villages, now the 'Dead Cities' of northern Syria. Simeon Stylites drew pilgrims to his pillar near Aleppo. After the Council of Chalcedon in 451, many Syriac Christians split from the imperial church.

The Ghassanid Arabs guarded Byzantium's desert frontier. Disasters struck: earthquakes ruined Antioch in 526 and Beirut in 551, Persia's Khosrow I sacked Antioch in 540, and plague arrived in 541. Jacob Baradaeus organized the Syriac Orthodox Church.

Persia occupied the Levant in 611–628, and soon after, Arab Muslim armies won at Yarmouk in 636. Muawiya governed Syria and became the first Umayyad caliph in 661, making Damascus the capital of an empire from Spain to Central Asia. Christians remained the majority for some time.

The Umayyads built the Great Mosque of Damascus and desert palaces in Syria and Jordan. In 750 the Abbasids overthrew them and moved the capital to Iraq, and Syria lost its central role. Arabic spread as the language of government.

Syria was a province of the Abbasid caliphate, often restless under distant rule. In 878 the Tulunids of Egypt took control. Arabic was steadily replacing Aramaic and Greek in daily life, and the share of Muslims in the population grew.

The Hamdanid prince Sayf al-Dawla ruled Aleppo as a brilliant court, home to the poet al-Mutanabbi. Byzantium retook Antioch in 969, and the Fatimids of Egypt seized Damascus in the 970s. The Levant became a contested frontier between empires.

Fatimids, Byzantines and local Arab dynasties competed for Syria, and the Druze faith emerged in the mountains. Seljuk Turks took Damascus in 1076. The First Crusade captured Antioch in 1098 and founded Crusader states including the County of Tripoli.

Muslim leaders united against the Crusaders. Zengi took Edessa in 1144, Nur al-Din unified Syria, and Saladin, founder of the Ayyubid dynasty, retook most of the Levant after Hattin in 1187. Crusaders held coastal cities and castles like Krak des Chevaliers.

Ayyubid princes ruled Syrian cities. The Mongols took Aleppo and Damascus in 1260, but the Mamluks of Egypt defeated them at Ain Jalut that year. Sultan Baybars then captured Antioch and other Crusader strongholds, and Acre's fall in 1291 ended the Crusades.

The Mamluks ruled Syria from Cairo, repelling Mongol invasions in 1299–1303. Damascus and Aleppo flourished with mosques, schools and markets, and scholars like Ibn Taymiyya taught there. The Black Death in 1348 killed many people. Timur's armies approached at the century's end.

Timur sacked Aleppo and Damascus in 1400–01, carrying off artisans to Samarkand. The Mamluks slowly restored their rule, and Syrian cities rebuilt. Trade with Venice and other Italian cities through Beirut and Aleppo kept the economy going.

The Ottomans defeated the Mamluks at Marj Dabiq in 1516 and ruled Syria from Istanbul. Damascus organized the great hajj caravan to Mecca, and Aleppo became a major hub of silk and spice trade with European merchants. Druze emirs governed Mount Lebanon.

The Druze emir Fakhr al-Din II built a semi-independent state in Lebanon and northern Palestine until the Ottomans executed him in 1635. English and French merchants traded in Aleppo, and Ottoman governors struggled with local factions and Janissary garrisons.

The Shihab family led Mount Lebanon from 1697, and the al-Azm family governed Damascus, building the Azm Palace. In 1724 a split in the Antiochian Orthodox church created the Melkite Greek Catholic Church. Ottoman authority was increasingly delegated to local families.

Local strongmen like Zahir al-Umar and later Jazzar Pasha in Acre dominated parts of the Levant. A strong earthquake struck in 1759. Bashir II Shihab rose to power in Mount Lebanon in 1789, and Napoleon's 1799 invasion was halted at Acre.

Bashir II Shihab ruled Mount Lebanon with growing power, while Ottoman governors in Damascus and Aleppo faced Wahhabi raids from Arabia. Aleppo suffered a devastating earthquake in 1822. Central Ottoman control remained weak, and local families and governors ran most daily affairs.

Egypt's Ibrahim Pasha conquered Syria in 1831–32 and ruled until 1840, introducing conscription and modern administration but provoking revolts. European powers forced Egypt out and restored the Ottomans. Bashir II was exiled, and Druze-Maronite tensions rose in Mount Lebanon.

Civil war between Druze and Maronites in Mount Lebanon in 1860 and a massacre of Christians in Damascus brought French intervention. Mount Lebanon became an autonomous district under a Christian governor in 1861. Beirut grew into a port, and missionaries founded schools like the Syrian Protestant College in 1866.

Beirut became a center of the Arab cultural revival called the Nahda, with presses, newspapers and schools. The Beirut-Damascus railway opened in 1895. Large numbers of Syrians and Lebanese, especially Christians, began emigrating to the Americas.

The Hejaz Railway linked Damascus to Medina by 1908, partly to carry pilgrims. The Young Turk Revolution of 1908 brought elections and new freedoms, but growing Turkish centralization pushed Arab intellectuals to form nationalist societies.

World War I brought famine that killed a large share of Mount Lebanon's people, and Ottoman governor Jamal Pasha hanged Arab nationalists in 1916. Britain and France secretly divided the region in the Sykes-Picot Agreement. The Arab Revolt and British forces drove out the Ottomans in 1918.

Faisal proclaimed an Arab Kingdom of Syria in 1920, but France crushed it at Maysalun and took mandates over Syria and Greater Lebanon. Britain set up the Emirate of Transjordan under Abdullah in 1921. A Great Syrian Revolt against French rule in 1925–27 was suppressed.

Syrian and Lebanese nationalists pressed France for independence, winning a 1936 treaty that France never ratified. Turkey annexed the Syrian province of Alexandretta, now Hatay, in 1939. Transjordan developed under British guidance, and Lebanon's Christian and Muslim elites negotiated a shared vision of independence.

Allied forces took Syria and Lebanon from Vichy France in 1941. Lebanon became independent in 1943 under a power-sharing National Pact, Syria in 1946, and Jordan in 1946. The 1948 war brought Palestinian refugees to all three, and Syria suffered its first military coup in 1949.
