Jordan's King Abdullah was assassinated in 1951, and Hussein became king in 1953. Syria saw repeated coups and the rise of the Ba'ath Party, then merged with Egypt in the United Arab Republic in 1958. That year a crisis in Lebanon drew in US Marines.

Syria left the union with Egypt in 1961, and the Ba'ath Party seized power in 1963. In 1967 Israel took the Golan Heights from Syria and the West Bank from Jordan. Beirut boomed as a banking and cultural capital, and Palestinian militant groups grew.

Jordan expelled Palestinian guerrillas in Black September in 1970, and many moved to Lebanon. Hafez al-Assad seized power in Syria that year. After the 1973 war, Lebanon's tensions exploded into civil war in 1975, and Syrian troops entered in 1976.

Assad's forces crushed an uprising at Hama in 1982, killing thousands. Israel invaded Lebanon that year, and the Shia militia Hezbollah emerged with Iranian support. Bombings struck Western forces in Beirut in 1983, and the Taif Agreement of 1989 set terms to end Lebanon's war.

Lebanon's civil war ended in 1990, and Rafik Hariri led reconstruction under Syrian dominance. Jordan signed peace with Israel in 1994. King Hussein died in 1999 and was succeeded by Abdullah II, while Hafez al-Assad ruled Syria until 2000.

Bashar al-Assad succeeded his father in 2000, and Israel withdrew from southern Lebanon. The 2005 assassination of Rafik Hariri sparked protests that forced Syrian troops out of Lebanon. Israel and Hezbollah fought a war in 2006, and Iraqi refugees poured into Syria and Jordan.

Peaceful protests in Syria in 2011 turned into a brutal civil war, killing hundreds of thousands and displacing millions to Lebanon, Jordan and beyond. ISIS declared a 'caliphate' in 2014 before its defeat by 2019, and Russia and Iran helped Assad survive. Lebanon's economy collapsed in 2019.

A huge explosion devastated Beirut's port in 2020 amid Lebanon's financial crisis. Israel and Hezbollah fought an escalating war in 2024. In December 2024 rebels led by Hayat Tahrir al-Sham toppled the Assad regime, and Syria's new government faced the challenge of rebuilding a divided country.
Arabia: During wetter 'Green Arabia' phases, lakes and grasslands drew early human hunters across the peninsula. In the Neolithic, cattle and goat herders left rock art and built large stone monuments called mustatils. By c. 5000 BC fishing communities on the Gulf coast traded with Mesopotamia's Ubaid culture.

Dilmun, centered on Bahrain, became a trading hub linking Mesopotamia with the Indus Valley, while Magan in Oman mined copper. Oasis farmers grew date palms, and the Umm an-Nar culture built round stone tombs. Most of the interior remained home to mobile herders.

Dilmun continued to thrive on Gulf trade, and in Oman the Wadi Suq culture lived in oasis villages. Late in this period the camel was domesticated, opening the deserts to long-distance travel. Early frankincense and myrrh trading from the south began to take shape.

Camel caravans carried frankincense and myrrh from southern Arabia to the Mediterranean. The Kingdom of Saba (Sheba) in Yemen grew rich on this trade and built the great Marib dam. Oasis towns like Dedan and Tayma flourished, and Assyrian records mention Arab queens and tribes.

The Babylonian king Nabonidus lived for about ten years at the oasis of Tayma in northwest Arabia, c. 552–543 BC. In the south, kingdoms such as Saba, Qataban, Hadramawt and Ma'in prospered from incense. The Lihyanite kingdom rose at Dedan along the caravan road.

Greek writers like Herodotus marveled at Arabian spices. Minaean merchants from Yemen ran caravans north, and Gerrha on the Gulf coast grew rich in trade. Most Arabians lived as Bedouin herders or oasis farmers, organized by tribe.

Alexander the Great was planning an Arabian campaign when he died in 323 BC. The Gulf trading city of Gerrha prospered, Nabataean Arabs grew powerful in the northwest, and the South Arabian kingdoms continued to profit from the incense routes.

The South Arabian kingdoms of Saba, Qataban, Hadramawt and Ma'in shared the incense trade, building temples and irrigation works. In 205 BC the Seleucid king Antiochus III sailed to Gerrha and accepted tribute in silver and spices. Nabataean caravans dominated the northern routes.

Himyar emerged in the highlands of Yemen around 110 BC. Greek sailors began using the monsoon winds to sail to India, slowly shifting trade from camel caravans to sea routes. Nabataeans expanded their control of oases in the northwest.

Rome sent Aelius Gallus to conquer southern Arabia in 26–25 BC, but the expedition failed in the desert. The Nabataeans built monumental tombs at Hegra, and Himyar grew in power in Yemen. Incense remained Arabia's most famous export.

Red Sea and Indian Ocean shipping boomed, as described in the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, reducing the importance of overland caravans. Nabataean Hegra carved its finest tombs. In Yemen, Himyar and Saba vied for power as Qataban faded.

Rome annexed the Nabataean kingdom in 106, stationing troops as far as Hegra. In Yemen, Himyar, Saba and Hadramawt fought for supremacy, and Aksum from Ethiopia intervened across the Red Sea. Central Arabian tribes like Kinda began to rise.

Himyar conquered Saba around 275 and moved toward uniting all of Yemen. Arab client states formed on the empires' edges: the Lakhmids for Persia in Iraq. The Arabic language was developing, and caravan trade continued through oasis towns.

Himyar ruled all of Yemen and extended influence into central Arabia. Its kings abandoned traditional gods for monotheism around 380, with many of the elite favoring Judaism, while Christianity spread in Najran. Early Arabic inscriptions appear on the northern fringes.

Himyar dominated central Arabia through the Kinda tribal confederation. Arab client kingdoms, the Lakhmids for Persia and the Ghassanids for Byzantium, guarded the desert edges. Tradition says the Quraysh tribe settled Mecca, home of the Kaaba shrine, and Arabic poetry flourished.

Himyar's Jewish king Dhu Nuwas massacred Christians at Najran c. 523, prompting an Aksumite invasion. The Aksumite general Abraha ruled Yemen, the Marib dam finally failed, and Persia took over Yemen around 570. Muhammad was born in Mecca c. 570, a trading town of the Quraysh.

Muhammad began preaching in Mecca after his first revelation in 610 and moved to Medina in 622. He took Mecca in 630, and by his death in 632 Arabia was united under Islam. Arab armies conquered vast lands, and the capital moved to Damascus in 661.

With the caliphs ruling from Damascus and later Baghdad, Arabia became a province, but Mecca and Medina drew ever more pilgrims and scholars, like Malik ibn Anas. Kharijite groups resisted the caliphs, and Oman developed its own Ibadi imamate around 750.

Abbasid control weakened. Queen Zubayda funded a famous pilgrim road from Iraq to Mecca, the Zaydi imamate was founded in Yemen in 897, and the radical Qarmatians took power in eastern Arabia around 899. Bedouin tribes remained largely independent.

The Qarmatians shocked the Muslim world by sacking Mecca in 930 and carrying off the Black Stone, returning it in 951. Local dynasties ruled Yemen, and around the 960s the Sharifs, descendants of Muhammad, began ruling Mecca, an office they would hold for nearly a thousand years.

The Sulayhid dynasty ruled Yemen, where Queen Arwa held power for decades. The Qarmatian state in eastern Arabia fell in 1077. Pilgrims and merchants continued to travel to Mecca, governed by its Sharifs under the nominal authority of the Fatimids or Abbasids.

Saladin's Ayyubid dynasty conquered Yemen in 1174. The Crusader Reynald of Châtillon raided the Red Sea coast in 1182–83, threatening the holy cities. Pilgrims like Ibn Jubayr left vivid accounts of Mecca, and sea trade through Aden thrived.

The Rasulid dynasty took over Yemen in 1229 and grew wealthy from Indian Ocean trade through Aden. The Mamluks of Egypt became protectors of Mecca and Medina. On the Gulf, the kingdom of Hormuz controlled shipping routes.

Rasulid Yemen was a center of trade, farming and learning. Ibn Battuta visited Arabia, and Mansa Musa of Mali made a famous hajj in 1324. The Mamluks controlled the Hejaz, while Bedouin tribes dominated the interior.

The Tahirids replaced the Rasulids in Yemen in 1454. Chinese fleets under Zheng He visited Aden and Hormuz. Arab navigators like Ahmad ibn Majid wrote guides to the Indian Ocean, and at the century's end Portuguese ships arrived in these waters.

The Portuguese seized Muscat in 1507 and Hormuz in 1515 to control trade. The Ottomans took over the Hejaz in 1517 and Yemen later, while coffee from Yemen's port of Mocha spread across the Muslim world. Zaydi imams resisted the Ottomans in the highlands.

Zaydi imams expelled the Ottomans from Yemen in 1635, and Mocha's coffee exports boomed. In Oman, the Ya'ariba dynasty drove the Portuguese out of Muscat in 1650 and built a maritime empire reaching East Africa. Ottoman Sharifs ruled Mecca.

Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab preached a strict return to early Islam, and in 1744 he allied with Muhammad ibn Saud of Diriyah, founding the First Saudi State. In Oman, the Al Bu Said dynasty took power, and Yemen's coffee monopoly faded as plantations rose elsewhere.

The Saudi state expanded across Najd, taking Riyadh in 1773. On the Gulf coast, the Al Sabah family settled in Kuwait and the Al Khalifa took Bahrain in 1783. Britain's East India Company signed an agreement with Oman in 1798.

Saudi forces sacked Karbala in 1802 and took Mecca and Medina, challenging the Ottomans. Egypt's Muhammad Ali sent armies that destroyed the First Saudi State and its capital Diriyah in 1818. Britain attacked Gulf sea raiders and imposed a maritime treaty in 1820.

The Al Saud rebuilt a Second Saudi State from Riyadh, led by Faisal bin Turki. Britain seized Aden in 1839, and Egyptian troops withdrew from Arabia in 1840. Oman's sultan moved his court to Zanzibar, center of his East African trade.

Gulf sheikhdoms signed a perpetual maritime truce with Britain in 1853, becoming the Trucial States. Oman and Zanzibar split in 1861. The Ottomans reoccupied al-Hasa and Yemen in the early 1870s, and the Suez Canal of 1869 made Aden a key port.

The Rashidi dynasty of Ha'il defeated the Saudis in 1891, sending the Al Saud into exile in Kuwait. Britain signed exclusive treaties with Bahrain, the Trucial States and Kuwait, making them protectorates in all but name. Ottomans held the Hejaz and Yemen.

Abdulaziz ibn Saud recaptured Riyadh in 1902 and began rebuilding his family's realm. The Hejaz Railway reached Medina in 1908, and Hussein became Sharif of Mecca that year. In Yemen, Imam Yahya fought Ottoman rule.

Ibn Saud took al-Hasa from the Ottomans in 1913, backed by the Ikhwan religious militia. Sharif Hussein launched the Arab Revolt in 1916 with British support, helping drive the Ottomans out. Yemen under Imam Yahya became independent in 1918.

Ibn Saud conquered Ha'il in 1921 and the Hejaz, with Mecca and Medina, in 1924–25, ending Hashemite rule there. When the Ikhwan rebelled against his limits on raiding, he crushed them by 1930. Pearl diving remained the Gulf's main industry.

Ibn Saud proclaimed the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia in 1932, the same year oil was found in Bahrain. Saudi Arabia fought a short war with Yemen in 1934. American geologists struck oil at Dammam in 1938, and Kuwait found oil that year too.

Oil exports from Saudi Arabia and Kuwait grew rapidly after World War II, run by the American firm Aramco and British companies. President Roosevelt met Ibn Saud in 1945, beginning a lasting partnership. Imam Yahya of Yemen was assassinated in 1948.

Oil money transformed Saudi Arabia and Kuwait, funding new cities, roads and schools. Saudi Arabia won a 50-50 profit share from Aramco in 1950. Ibn Saud died in 1953, and disputes over oases and borders flared across the Gulf.

OPEC was founded in 1960, and Kuwait became independent in 1961. A 1962 revolution in North Yemen began a civil war in which Egypt and Saudi Arabia backed opposing sides. King Faisal took the Saudi throne in 1964, and South Yemen won independence from Britain in 1967.

Sultan Qaboos took power in Oman in 1970, and the UAE, Qatar and Bahrain became independent in 1971. The 1973 Arab oil embargo quadrupled prices and brought huge wealth. King Faisal was assassinated in 1975, and militants seized Mecca's Grand Mosque in 1979.

Gulf monarchies formed the Gulf Cooperation Council in 1981. They backed Iraq in the Iran-Iraq War, and tankers were attacked in the Gulf. Oil prices crashed in 1986, and Saudi Arabia helped fund Afghan fighters against the Soviets.

North and South Yemen united in 1990. Iraq invaded Kuwait that year, and a US-led coalition expelled it in 1991, leaving American troops in Saudi Arabia, which Osama bin Laden opposed. Qatar launched Al Jazeera in 1996, and Dubai grew into a global hub.

Fifteen of the 19 hijackers of September 11, 2001 were Saudi citizens, and al-Qaeda attacked inside Saudi Arabia in 2003–04. High oil prices funded rapid growth, especially in Dubai and Qatar. Yemen's government fought Houthi rebels in the north.

Arab Spring protests in Bahrain were crushed in 2011, and Yemen's president Saleh was pushed out. Houthi rebels took Sanaa in 2014, and a Saudi-led coalition intervened in 2015, causing a humanitarian disaster. Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman launched sweeping social and economic changes.

The UAE and Bahrain normalized ties with Israel in 2020, and Qatar hosted the 2022 World Cup. Saudi Arabia and Iran restored relations in 2023. Fighting in Yemen eased under a 2022 truce, but the Houthis attacked Red Sea shipping after the Gaza war began, drawing US and allied strikes.
Mesopotamia: Early farmers in northern Mesopotamia developed the Hassuna, Samarra and Halaf cultures. In the south, Ubaid villagers drained marshes and dug irrigation canals, building temples at Eridu. Uruk grew into one of the first true cities c. 4000–3100 BC, and cuneiform writing was invented c. 3200 BC.

Sumerian city-states such as Ur, Lagash and Uruk competed for land and water, each ruled by kings and devoted to patron gods. Sargon of Akkad built the first empire c. 2334 BC. Later, the Third Dynasty of Ur revived Sumer, and Ur-Nammu issued one of the earliest law codes c. 2100 BC.

Amorite kingdoms rose, and Hammurabi of Babylon united the south, issuing his famous code c. 1754 BC. The Hittites sacked Babylon in 1595 BC, after which the Kassites ruled it for centuries. In the north, Mitanni and then Assyria became great powers.

The Neo-Assyrian Empire, ruling from cities like Nimrud and Nineveh, dominated the Near East from 911 BC with a ruthless army and deportations. Ashurbanipal gathered a great library at Nineveh. Babylonians and Medes destroyed Nineveh in 612 BC, ending Assyria.

Nebuchadnezzar II made Babylon the world's greatest city, building the Ishtar Gate and deporting Judeans there. His successor Nabonidus lost the city to Cyrus of Persia in 539 BC. Under the Achaemenids, Babylon remained a rich royal capital and center of learning.

Babylonia was one of the Persian Empire's wealthiest satrapies. Revolts in 484 BC were crushed by Xerxes. Business families like the Murashu of Nippur managed land and taxes, and in 401 BC Greek mercenaries fought for a Persian prince at Cunaxa near Babylon.

Alexander the Great defeated Darius III at Gaugamela in 331 BC and entered Babylon, planning to make it his capital, but he died there in 323 BC. His general Seleucus took the region and founded Seleucia on the Tigris c. 305 BC, which drew people away from Babylon.

Under the Seleucids, Seleucia on the Tigris became one of the largest Hellenistic cities. Babylon's temples still functioned, and scholars kept recording astronomy in cuneiform. The Babylonian priest Berossus wrote a history of his land in Greek.

The Parthians of Iran took Mesopotamia from the Seleucids in 141 BC. They built Ctesiphon across the Tigris from Seleucia, which became a royal residence. Small kingdoms like Characene near the Gulf grew rich on trade.

Parthian Mesopotamia was the frontier with Rome, and the Parthians crushed the Roman general Crassus at Carrhae in 53 BC. Silk Road trade passed through, and local kingdoms such as Hatra, Adiabene and Osroene thrived under Parthian overlordship.

Under Parthian rule, Mesopotamia hosted a mix of Aramaic-speaking peoples, Greeks, Arabs and Jews. The royal family of Adiabene converted to Judaism. The last known cuneiform tablets were written around AD 75, ending a 3,000-year tradition.

Rome's Trajan captured Ctesiphon in 116, but Hadrian gave up the conquest. Roman armies sacked Seleucia in 165 and Ctesiphon in 198. The caravan city of Hatra withstood Roman sieges, and Jewish communities grew strong.

The Sasanians overthrew the Parthians in 224, ruling from Ctesiphon. The prophet Mani founded Manichaeism here, and Hatra was destroyed c. 240. Jewish academies at Sura and Pumbedita began the discussions later collected in the Babylonian Talmud.

Shapur II ruled Sasanian Persia for seventy years, fighting Rome along Mesopotamia's northern frontier. Roman emperor Julian invaded in 363 and died in retreat. Christians, increasingly seen as Roman sympathizers, faced periods of persecution. Rome ceded the fortress city of Nisibis to Persia after Julian's defeat.

The Church of the East organized itself at a council in Ctesiphon in 410 and spread eastward. Jewish scholars compiled the Babylonian Talmud. Late in the century the Mazdakite movement preached radical equality and briefly won royal support.

Khosrow I strengthened the Sasanian state, reforming taxes and building the great arched palace at Ctesiphon. The Lakhmid Arab kings at al-Hira guarded the desert frontier for Persia. Irrigated farmland in the south was among the most productive in the world.

Arab Muslim armies won at al-Qadisiyyah in 636 and took Ctesiphon, founding new garrison cities at Basra and Kufa. Iraq became a center of early Islamic politics, and the killing of Husayn at Karbala in 680 became a defining moment for Shia Islam.

Umayyad governors ruled Iraq firmly. The Abbasid revolution in 750 shifted the caliphate's center here, and in 762 Caliph al-Mansur founded Baghdad, which soon became one of the world's largest cities. Harun al-Rashid became caliph in 786.

Baghdad was a world center of trade and learning, where scholars translated Greek, Persian and Indian works. The caliphs moved to Samarra for a time and relied on Turkish soldiers. The Zanj rebellion of enslaved workers in the south lasted from 869 to 883.

The caliphate weakened from debts, revolts and military coups. In 945 the Buyids, a Shia dynasty from Iran, took Baghdad, and the caliph became a figurehead. Baghdad remained a lively intellectual center despite political decline.

The Seljuk Turks entered Baghdad in 1055 and ruled as sultans in the caliph's name. Their vizier Nizam al-Mulk founded the Nizamiyya college in 1067, where al-Ghazali taught. Arab dynasties held Mosul and the countryside.

As Seljuk power broke up, the Zengids ruled Mosul and the caliphs regained real control of central Iraq. Caliph al-Nasir, from 1180, revived Abbasid authority and prestige. Baghdad was smaller than at its height but still important.

Abbasid Baghdad built the Mustansiriya college in 1233, but in 1258 the Mongols under Hulagu sacked the city, killing the caliph and many inhabitants. Iraq became a province of the Mongol Ilkhanate, ruled from Iran, and irrigation systems declined.

After the Ilkhanate collapsed in 1335, the Jalayirids ruled Baghdad. The Black Death struck. Timur sacked Baghdad in 1393 and again in 1401, and the population shrank as canals and farmland fell into ruin. Nomadic tribes gained ground in the countryside.

Turkmen confederations, first the Kara Koyunlu and then the Ak Koyunlu, ruled Iraq after Timur's devastation. Baghdad was a modest provincial city, and Bedouin and Kurdish tribes held much of the land. In 1508 the new Safavid dynasty of Iran took Baghdad.

The Safavids held Baghdad until Suleiman the Magnificent conquered it for the Ottomans in 1534, and Basra followed in 1546. Iraq became a frontier between Sunni Ottomans and Shia Safavids. Shrine cities like Najaf and Karbala drew pilgrims.

The Safavids under Shah Abbas retook Baghdad in 1623, but the Ottomans regained it in 1638. The 1639 Treaty of Zuhab set a frontier that roughly survives today as the Iran-Iraq border. Local families controlled Basra and many tribes were self-governing.

Hasan Pasha and his son Ahmad Pasha governed Baghdad, founding a line of semi-independent rulers drawn from their household of Georgian mamluks. Nader Shah of Iran besieged Baghdad in 1733 and Mosul in 1743 but failed to conquer them.

Georgian mamluk pashas governed Baghdad with little interference from Istanbul. Persia occupied Basra in 1776–79. Under Büyük Sulayman Pasha from 1780, order improved, and the British East India Company set up a residency at Basra.

Wahhabi raiders from Arabia sacked Karbala in 1802. The mamluk governor Dawud Pasha, from 1817, built an army and schools and expanded trade. Kurdish emirates such as Baban held power in the north, and British trade at Basra kept growing.

In 1831 plague and floods devastated Baghdad, and the Ottomans used the moment to end mamluk rule and govern directly. They suppressed the Kurdish emirates in the following years. The 1847 Treaty of Erzurum tried to settle the border with Iran.

Governor Midhat Pasha, 1869–72, introduced land registration, schools, a printing press and a tramway, pushing tribes to settle and farm. British steamers on the Tigris and the opening of the Suez Canal tied Iraq more closely to world trade.

Iraq was divided into the Ottoman provinces of Mosul, Baghdad and Basra. Many southern tribes, settling as farmers, adopted Shia Islam. British commercial influence grew, and Germany began seeking a railway concession to Baghdad. Ottoman schools trained a new generation of Iraqi officers and officials.

Germany won the Baghdad Railway concession in 1903. The 1908 Young Turk Revolution brought elections but also stronger Turkish centralization, and some Iraqi officers and intellectuals joined Arab nationalist groups. Foreign companies began competing for rights to the region's suspected oil.

Britain invaded in 1914 to protect its oil interests, suffered a major defeat at Kut in 1916, then took Baghdad in 1917 and Mosul in 1918. The war brought hunger and disease to Iraqis, and Britain set up direct military administration, angering many who had hoped for self-rule.

A large revolt against British rule in 1920 was suppressed, and Britain created the Kingdom of Iraq under Faisal I in 1921 within a League of Nations mandate. Mosul was confirmed as part of Iraq in 1926, and oil was struck near Kirkuk in 1927.

Iraq became independent in 1932, though Britain kept bases and oil interests. The army massacred Assyrians at Simele in 1933, King Faisal died that year, and in 1936 Iraq saw the Arab world's first military coup.

A pro-Axis coup in 1941 led to a British invasion and the Farhud, a deadly attack on Baghdad's Jews. Protests in 1948 overturned a new treaty with Britain, and Iraq fought in the 1948 Arab-Israeli war.

Most of Iraq's ancient Jewish community left in 1950–51. Oil income funded development projects, and Iraq joined the pro-Western Baghdad Pact in 1955. In 1958 army officers overthrew and killed the royal family, and Abd al-Karim Qasim took power.

The Ba'ath Party killed Qasim in a 1963 coup, but was soon pushed out, and returned in 1968, with Saddam Hussein rising behind President al-Bakr. Kurdish forces under Mustafa Barzani fought the government in the north.

Iraq nationalized its oil in 1972 and used rising revenues for roads, schools and hospitals. A Kurdish revolt collapsed in 1975 after Iran ended its support. In 1979 Saddam Hussein became president and purged rivals.

Saddam invaded Iran in 1980, starting an eight-year war that killed hundreds of thousands. In the Anfal campaign against the Kurds, his forces used chemical weapons, killing about 5,000 at Halabja in 1988. Iraq ended the war deeply in debt.

Iraq invaded Kuwait in 1990 and was expelled by a US-led coalition in 1991. Uprisings by Shia and Kurds were crushed, but the Kurds gained self-rule under a no-fly zone. Harsh UN sanctions impoverished ordinary Iraqis.

A US-led invasion toppled Saddam Hussein in 2003. An insurgency and sectarian civil war killed tens of thousands of civilians, peaking in 2006–07. Iraqis voted on a new constitution in 2005, and Saddam was executed in 2006.

US troops left in 2011, and sectarian tensions grew. ISIS seized Mosul in 2014 and committed genocide against the Yazidis before Iraqi and Kurdish forces, with international help, defeated it by 2017. Mass protests against corruption erupted in 2019.

A US strike killed Iranian general Qasem Soleimani in Baghdad in 2020. Iraq experienced relative stability under governments balancing ties with Iran and the US, funded by oil. Corruption, unemployment, and severe drought and water shortages remained major challenges.
Persia: In the Zagros Mountains, people at sites like Ganj Dareh were among the first to herd goats, c. 8000 BC. Farming villages spread across the Iranian plateau, making painted pottery at sites like Tepe Sialk. Susa was founded c. 4200 BC, and Proto-Elamite writing appeared near the end of the period.

Elam, centered on Susa and Anshan in southwest Iran, was a major civilization that alternately traded and fought with Mesopotamia. Eastern Iran had its own urban cultures, such as Shahr-i Sokhta and the Jiroft culture. Elamites helped bring down the Sumerian city of Ur c. 2004 BC.

Elamite kings ruled from Susa, and Untash-Napirisha built the great ziggurat of Chogha Zanbil c. 1250 BC. Shutruk-Nakhunte raided Babylon c. 1158 BC, carrying off Hammurabi's law stele. Indo-Iranian speaking peoples moved onto the plateau, and Zoroaster may have lived in this era, though his dates are debated.

Iranian peoples, the Medes and Persians, settled western Iran and spread Zoroastrian belief. Assyria campaigned in the Zagros and sacked Susa c. 646 BC, weakening Elam. The Medes grew strong and, with Babylon, destroyed Nineveh in 612 BC.

Cyrus the Great founded the Achaemenid Empire in 550 BC, conquering Media, Lydia and Babylon. His son Cambyses took Egypt in 525 BC. Darius I, from 522 BC, organized the empire into satrapies, built the Royal Road and began Persepolis, creating the largest empire yet seen.

Xerxes invaded Greece in 480 BC but was defeated at Salamis and Plataea. The Persian Empire nevertheless remained vast and wealthy, using Aramaic in administration and tolerating local religions. Persepolis was completed as a ceremonial capital.

Persia remained powerful, reconquering Egypt in 343 BC, but palace murders weakened the throne. Alexander the Great conquered the empire in 334–330 BC, defeated Darius III and burned Persepolis. After his death the Seleucids ruled Iran from 312 BC.

Seleucid control over Iran slipped. Bactria in the northeast broke away c. 250 BC, and in 247 BC the Parni nomads founded the Parthian or Arsacid kingdom. Antiochus III marched east in 209 BC to reassert power, but the Parthians endured.

The Parthian king Mithridates I conquered the Iranian plateau and took Mesopotamia in 141 BC. Parthia traded with Han China along the Silk Road but faced dangerous nomad invasions from the east. Mithridates II restored Parthian strength late in the century.

Parthian horse archers crushed the Roman general Crassus at Carrhae in 53 BC, establishing Parthia as Rome's great eastern rival. They raided Syria in 40 BC and defeated Mark Antony's invasion in 36 BC. Parthian kings ruled through powerful noble families.

Parthian kings like Vologases I balanced Rome by sharing influence over Armenia after the Treaty of Rhandeia in 63. Silk Road trade enriched the empire, though rival claimants often fought for the throne. Zoroastrian traditions were preserved and promoted.

Trajan invaded and took Ctesiphon in 116, and later Roman armies sacked Mesopotamian cities in the 160s and 190s. Weakened by these wars and internal revolts, the Parthian state declined. The Kushan Empire dominated lands to the east.

Ardashir I overthrew the Parthians and founded the Sasanian Empire in 224, centralizing power and promoting Zoroastrianism. His son Shapur I defeated Rome and captured Emperor Valerian in 260, celebrated in rock reliefs. The prophet Mani preached his new religion at court.

Shapur II ruled for about seventy years, fighting Rome and repelling Julian's invasion in 363. Armenia was divided between Rome and Persia c. 387. Christians in the empire were sometimes persecuted as potential allies of Christian Rome.

Sasanian kings like Bahram V faced the Hephthalites, nomads from Central Asia who killed King Peroz in 484 and demanded tribute. Kavad I briefly backed the Mazdakite movement, which preached sharing property, causing social upheaval.

Khosrow I, 531–579, the high point of Sasanian Persia, reformed taxes and the army, crushed the Mazdakites and built palaces. Scholars translated Greek and Indian works, and chess arrived from India. Persia fought Justinian's Byzantium and extended its reach to Yemen.

Khosrow II's war against Byzantium in 602–628 exhausted both empires. Arab Muslim armies then won at al-Qadisiyyah and Nahavand, and the death of Yazdegerd III in 651 ended the Sasanian Empire. Iran came under the caliphate, and Islam spread slowly.

Iran was ruled by Umayyad governors, and many Zoroastrians gradually converted to Islam, while some migrated to India as the Parsis. The Abbasid revolution began in Khorasan in 747, and Persians, such as the Barmakid family, gained great influence at the Abbasid court.

As Abbasid control weakened, Iranian dynasties rose: the Tahirids, Saffarids and Samanids. New Persian emerged as a literary language written in Arabic script, and the poet Rudaki wrote at the Samanid court. Scholars like the physician al-Razi made Iran a center of learning.

The Samanids of Bukhara patronized Persian culture, and Ferdowsi began the Shahnameh. The Buyids, a Shia dynasty from northern Iran, ruled the west and took Baghdad in 945. The Ghaznavids rose in the east, and Ibn Sina was born in 980.

Ferdowsi completed the Shahnameh c. 1010, and Ibn Sina wrote his medical and philosophical works. Seljuk Turks conquered Persia in the 1040s, ruling with Persian administrators like vizier Nizam al-Mulk. Omar Khayyam reformed the calendar, and the Assassins seized Alamut in 1090.

Seljuk power declined after Sultan Sanjar, and the Khwarazmshahs took over much of Iran. The Ismaili Assassins held mountain fortresses. Persian poetry flourished with Nizami and Attar. Fertile cities like Nishapur and Merv were rich trading centers, unaware of the Mongol storm to come.

The Mongols devastated Persia in 1219–21, destroying cities and killing vast numbers. Hulagu destroyed the Assassins and founded the Ilkhanate in 1256. Nasir al-Din Tusi built an observatory at Maragheh, poets like Saadi wrote in Shiraz, and the Ilkhan Ghazan converted to Islam in 1295.

Ghazan's reforms and Rashid al-Din's world history marked the Ilkhanate's height, but it collapsed in 1335. Local dynasties like the Muzaffarids ruled, and Hafez wrote poetry in Shiraz. In the 1380s Timur conquered Persia with great brutality.

Timur's son Shah Rukh ruled eastern Iran from Herat, sponsoring art and architecture. Turkmen confederations, the Kara Koyunlu and then Ak Koyunlu, ruled western Iran. The Safavid Sufi order of Ardabil built a militant following.

Shah Ismail founded the Safavid dynasty in 1501 and made Shia Islam the state religion, converting most of Iran over time. The Ottomans defeated him at Chaldiran in 1514. Shah Tahmasp held off Ottomans and Uzbeks, and Abbas I took the throne in 1588.

Shah Abbas I, 1588–1629, rebuilt the army, retook lands from the Ottomans and seized Hormuz from Portugal. He made Isfahan a magnificent capital with grand mosques and squares. Silk trade with Europe prospered, but later shahs were weaker.

Afghan invaders took Isfahan in 1722, ending effective Safavid rule. Nader Shah drove them out, crowned himself in 1736 and sacked Delhi in 1739, carrying off the Peacock Throne. After his assassination in 1747, Iran fell into civil war.

Karim Khan Zand ruled most of Iran from Shiraz, 1751–79, bringing peace. After his death the Qajar chief Agha Mohammad Khan fought his way to power, made Tehran his capital in 1786, sacked Tbilisi in 1795 and was crowned in 1796.

Fath Ali Shah ruled Qajar Iran, presiding over an elaborate court. Iran lost Georgia and other Caucasus lands to Russia in the war of 1804–13. Britain and France competed for influence in Tehran, and a second war with Russia broke out in 1826.

Russia defeated Iran again, and the 1828 Treaty of Turkmenchay took more Caucasus land and imposed trade privileges. Iranian sieges of Herat in 1837–38 failed. In 1844 the Báb started a new religious movement, and Naser al-Din Shah took the throne in 1848.

Chief minister Amir Kabir founded the Dar ul-Funun college before his execution in 1852, and Bábis were persecuted, giving rise to the Bahá'í Faith. Britain defeated Iran in 1856–57 over Herat. A severe famine in 1870–72 killed many people.

Britain and Russia competed for influence as Naser al-Din Shah sold concessions to foreigners. The Tobacco Protest of 1891–92, backed by Shia clerics, forced him to cancel a British tobacco monopoly. He was assassinated in 1896.

Iranians launched the Constitutional Revolution in 1905, winning a parliament in 1906. Britain and Russia divided Iran into spheres of influence in 1907. The shah bombarded parliament in 1908, the year oil was discovered in the southwest.

Russian pressure ended the Constitutional Revolution in 1911. The Anglo-Persian Oil Company began exporting oil. Though neutral in World War I, Iran was occupied by foreign armies and struck by a terrible famine in 1917–19.

Reza Khan took power in a 1921 coup and founded the Pahlavi dynasty in 1925. He built a modern army, centralized the state, created secular courts and schools, and began the Trans-Iranian Railway in 1927. Nomadic tribes were forcibly settled, and the clergy lost influence.

Reza Shah officially asked foreign governments to call the country Iran in 1935. He banned the veil in 1936 and harshly suppressed opposition, while the Trans-Iranian Railway was finished in 1938. Iran developed trade ties with Germany.

Britain and the Soviet Union invaded in 1941 and forced Reza Shah to abdicate in favor of his son Mohammad Reza. The Allied leaders met at the Tehran Conference in 1943. After the war, Soviet-backed separatists in Azerbaijan were removed in 1946.

Prime Minister Mosaddegh nationalized Iran's oil in 1951, but a US and British-backed coup ousted him in 1953. The shah then ruled with growing power, supported by the United States and the SAVAK secret police, created in 1957.

The shah's White Revolution of 1963 brought land reform and votes for women. Ayatollah Khomeini denounced the shah and was exiled in 1964. Oil revenues grew, and the economy modernized rapidly as cities grew. Political parties were tightly controlled, and resentment of the shah's rule spread quietly.

The oil boom of 1973 brought rapid wealth along with inflation and inequality. Mass protests in 1978 forced the shah to leave, and in 1979 the Islamic Revolution created an Islamic Republic led by Khomeini. Students seized the US embassy, holding hostages for 444 days.

The Iran-Iraq War of 1980–88 killed hundreds of thousands. The new government suppressed opposition, executing thousands of prisoners in 1988. Khomeini died in 1989, and Ali Khamenei became Supreme Leader. The Islamic Republic's institutions, including the Revolutionary Guards, grew in power.

President Rafsanjani focused on rebuilding the economy after the war. Reformist Mohammad Khatami won the 1997 election, promising greater openness, but hardliners resisted, closing newspapers, and student protests in 1999 were crushed. A young population pushed for social change.

Iran's nuclear program came to international attention in 2002, leading to sanctions. Hardliner Mahmoud Ahmadinejad became president in 2005. His disputed 2009 reelection sparked the mass Green Movement protests, which were suppressed. The economy suffered from sanctions and mismanagement.

Sanctions hurt the economy. President Rouhani agreed to the JCPOA nuclear deal in 2015, but the US withdrew in 2018. Iran expanded its influence in Syria, Iraq and beyond, and protests over economic hardship erupted in 2017–18 and 2019.

The death of Mahsa Amini in custody sparked the 'Woman, Life, Freedom' protests in 2022, met with a harsh crackdown. Iran and Israel exchanged direct strikes in 2024, and in June 2025 a 12-day war with Israel ended with US strikes on nuclear sites.
Egypt: Farming villages spread along the Nile from c. 5000 BC as the Sahara dried and people crowded toward the river. Predynastic cultures such as the Badarian and Naqada built chiefdoms, traded widely, and buried elites with rich goods. Around 3100 BC Upper and Lower Egypt were unified under one king, and hieroglyphic writing appeared.

Kings of the Early Dynastic period and the Old Kingdom (c. 2686 to 2181 BC) ruled a centralized state from Memphis, treating the pharaoh as a god-king. They built the Step Pyramid of Djoser and the Giza pyramids. Royal power then fragmented in the First Intermediate Period until Mentuhotep II reunited Egypt c. 2055 BC, founding the Middle Kingdom.

The Middle Kingdom produced classic literature and built forts in Nubia, but foreign Hyksos rulers later seized the Nile Delta. Theban kings expelled them c. 1550 BC and founded the New Kingdom, an empire reaching into the Levant and Nubia. Hatshepsut, Akhenaten, Tutankhamun and Ramesses II reigned before power faded after c. 1070 BC.

In the Third Intermediate Period Egypt was divided among Libyan-descended dynasties and powerful priests of Amun at Thebes. Kushite kings from Nubia ruled as pharaohs from c. 744 BC until Assyria invaded in 671 BC and drove them out. Psamtik I then reunited the country in 664 BC, founding the Saite dynasty with Greek mercenary help.

The Saite pharaohs, especially Amasis, presided over a prosperous Egypt that welcomed Greek merchants at the trading town of Naukratis. In 525 BC the Persian king Cambyses defeated the last Saite ruler at Pelusium and made Egypt a province of the Achaemenid Empire. Darius I later completed a canal linking the Nile to the Red Sea.

Egypt was a Persian satrapy, paying tribute to distant Achaemenid kings while temples and local life continued much as before. Egyptians revolted repeatedly, notably under Inaros c. 460 BC with Athenian help. The Greek historian Herodotus toured the country around this time, and in 404 BC Amyrtaeus won independence for native rule again.

Native pharaohs of the 30th dynasty, such as Nectanebo II, built temples until Persia reconquered Egypt in 343 BC. Alexander the Great took the country without a fight in 332 BC and founded Alexandria on the coast. After his death his general Ptolemy took control and declared himself king in 305 BC, founding the Ptolemaic dynasty.

The Greek-speaking Ptolemies ruled Egypt as pharaohs while running it as a royal estate taxed for grain. Alexandria, with its Great Library, Museum and Lighthouse, became the intellectual capital of the Hellenistic world, home to scholars like Eratosthenes. Wars with the Seleucids over Syria and a long revolt in Upper Egypt strained the kingdom.

Ptolemaic power weakened through dynastic feuds, rebellions and costly wars, and Rome increasingly arbitrated Egyptian affairs. The Rosetta Stone (196 BC) recorded a royal decree in hieroglyphic, Demotic and Greek, reflecting a mixed society. Alexandria remained a rich trading city, but the dynasty survived more by Roman favor than by its own strength.

Cleopatra VII, the last Ptolemaic ruler, allied with Julius Caesar and then Mark Antony to keep Egypt independent. Octavian defeated them at Actium in 31 BC, and after Cleopatra's death in 30 BC Rome annexed Egypt. It became a special province under the emperor's personal control, shipping huge quantities of grain to Rome.

As a Roman province governed by a prefect, Egypt was the empire's breadbasket, and Alexandria was its second city. Greek-speaking elites, Egyptian farmers and a large Jewish community lived side by side, sometimes violently, as in the Alexandrian riots of AD 38. According to tradition, Christianity was brought to Alexandria by Saint Mark.

Roman Egypt prospered from grain, papyrus and Red Sea trade with India. A Jewish revolt in 115 to 117 destroyed much of Alexandria's Jewish community. The scholar Claudius Ptolemy wrote his astronomy and geography in Alexandria, Emperor Hadrian toured the Nile, and a Christian school of learning grew in the city.

Under Rome, Egyptians became Roman citizens in 212, but heavy taxes and the empire's third-century crisis brought hardship. Christians faced persecutions while thinkers such as Origen shaped theology in Alexandria. Zenobia of Palmyra briefly seized Egypt c. 270, and around this time Saint Anthony retreated into the desert, launching Christian monasticism.

Diocletian reorganized Roman Egypt and fiercely persecuted Christians in 303, but Christianity soon became the favored, then official, faith. Alexandria's bishops Athanasius and Arius fought over doctrine, and Pachomius founded communal monasteries in Upper Egypt. In 391 Christians destroyed the Serapeum, and after 395 Egypt belonged to the Eastern Roman Empire.

Egypt was a wealthy province of the Eastern Roman (Byzantine) Empire, ruled from Constantinople. Religious conflict was intense: a Christian mob killed the philosopher Hypatia in 415, and after the Council of Chalcedon in 451 most Egyptian Christians rejected imperial doctrine, forming the Coptic Church and loosening loyalty to the emperors.

Byzantine emperors, especially Justinian, relied on Egyptian grain while trying to impose their version of Christianity on the Copts. The last temple of Isis at Philae was closed c. 537. The devastating Plague of Justinian reached the empire through Egypt's port of Pelusium in 541, killing large numbers across the Mediterranean.

Sasanian Persia occupied Egypt from 619 to 628 before the Byzantine emperor Heraclius won it back. Weakened and divided by religious quarrels, Egypt fell to Arab Muslim armies under Amr ibn al-As around 641. The conquerors founded a garrison city, Fustat, near the future Cairo, and Egypt became a province of the caliphate.

Egypt was governed by Umayyad and, after 750, Abbasid caliphs through appointed governors. Arabic replaced Greek in government records from 706, and heavy taxes on non-Muslims provoked several Coptic revolts. Most Egyptians were still Christians, but Arabic language and Islam were slowly spreading through cities and countryside.

Abbasid rule continued, but local tensions ran high; the Bashmurian revolt of Copts in the Delta was crushed in 831. In 868 the Turkish governor Ahmad ibn Tulun made Egypt effectively independent, building an army and the great Mosque of Ibn Tulun. The Tulunids extended their rule into Syria before the Abbasids reclaimed control in 905.

After a period of Abbasid and Ikhshidid governors, the Shia Fatimid Caliphate from North Africa conquered Egypt in 969. The Fatimids founded Cairo as their new capital and the al-Azhar mosque as a center of learning. Egypt became the seat of a rival caliphate challenging Baghdad, wealthy from Mediterranean and Red Sea trade.

The Fatimid caliphs ruled from Cairo over Egypt, Syria and the Hejaz. The erratic caliph al-Hakim destroyed Jerusalem's Church of the Holy Sepulchre in 1009. A severe famine and civil strife in the 1060s nearly toppled the state, until the general Badr al-Jamali restored order and rebuilt Cairo's walls and gates.

Weakened Fatimid caliphs faced Crusader states on their borders. A Kurdish commander, Saladin, became vizier and in 1171 ended the Fatimid line, restoring Sunni Islam and founding the Ayyubid dynasty. From Egypt he united Muslim Syria, built Cairo's Citadel, and recaptured Jerusalem from the Crusaders in 1187.

Ayyubid sultans repelled Crusades aimed at Egypt, including Louis IX's invasion in 1249 to 1250. Their slave-soldier regiments, the Mamluks, then seized power in 1250 and defeated the Mongols at Ain Jalut in 1260. Sultans such as Baybars hosted a figurehead Abbasid caliph in Cairo and expelled the last Crusaders from the Levant by 1291.

The Mamluk Sultanate reached its peak under al-Nasir Muhammad, ruling Egypt and Syria from Cairo, the largest city of the Islamic world. Mosques, madrasas and markets flourished on the profits of the spice trade. The Black Death struck in 1347 to 1349, killing a large share of the population, and Circassian Mamluks took power in 1382.

Mamluk Egypt struggled with recurring plague, falling farm output and costly factional fighting, while sultans taxed the lucrative spice trade between India and Europe. Timur sacked Mamluk Damascus in 1400. Sultan Qaitbay built fine monuments, but Portugal's sea route around Africa, opened in 1498, threatened Egypt's trade income.

In 1517 the Ottoman sultan Selim I defeated the Mamluks and conquered Egypt, ending Cairo's role as an imperial capital. Egypt became a wealthy Ottoman province ruled by a pasha sent from Istanbul. Mamluk households survived as local landholding elites, and Cairo grew rich on the new coffee trade from Yemen.

Egypt remained an Ottoman province, but real power shifted toward the Mamluk beys and rival military factions in Cairo. Governors from Istanbul came and went quickly while local grandees controlled tax farms and land. The coffee trade through Red Sea ports kept Cairo's merchants prosperous despite frequent political infighting.

Ottoman authority over Egypt was largely nominal as Mamluk beys and Janissary factions competed for control of revenue. The Qazdughli household gradually rose to dominate Cairo's politics. Egypt's farmers still produced grain for the empire, and coffee and textile trade connected Cairo to markets across the Ottoman world.

The Mamluk bey Ali Bey al-Kabir briefly broke from the Ottomans and invaded Syria c. 1770, before rivals Murad Bey and Ibrahim Bey took over. In 1798 Napoleon invaded, won the Battle of the Pyramids, and brought scholars who studied the country. The British destroyed his fleet at the Nile, and French troops found the Rosetta Stone in 1799.

After the French left in 1801, the Albanian officer Muhammad Ali took power in 1805 as Ottoman governor and ruled autonomously. He massacred the Mamluk leaders in 1811, built a modern army, monopolized trade and promoted cotton. He fought for the sultan in Arabia, conquered Sudan from 1820, and Champollion deciphered hieroglyphs in 1822.

Muhammad Ali's armies fought in the Greek War of Independence and, under his son Ibrahim, seized Syria in 1831. European powers forced Egypt to withdraw in 1840, but the Ottomans granted his family hereditary rule. His factories, schools and conscription remade Egyptian society, though at heavy cost to peasants. He died in 1849.

Muhammad Ali's successors Said and Ismail pursued grand modernization, aided by a cotton boom during the American Civil War. The Suez Canal, built with forced Egyptian labor, opened in 1869 and transformed world shipping. Ismail took the title Khedive in 1867 and rebuilt Cairo in European style, but borrowed heavily from European banks.

Facing bankruptcy, Ismail sold Egypt's Suez Canal shares to Britain in 1875 and accepted European financial control. Colonel Urabi's nationalist revolt led Britain to invade and occupy Egypt in 1882, ruling behind the khedive. Egypt lost Sudan to the Mahdist uprising, then shared it with Britain after the reconquest of 1898.

Britain's consul-general Lord Cromer effectively ran Egypt, balancing budgets and expanding irrigation, including the first Aswan Dam in 1902. Egyptians resented foreign control, especially after the Denshawai incident of 1906, when villagers were hanged after a clash with British officers. Nationalists like Mustafa Kamil built a growing independence movement.

When the Ottomans joined the Central Powers in 1914, Britain declared Egypt a protectorate and turned it into a major base for the war in the Middle East. Wartime requisitions and forced labor caused deep anger. In 1919, after Britain exiled the nationalist Saad Zaghlul, a nationwide revolution erupted across classes and religions.

Britain declared Egypt nominally independent in 1922 under King Fuad, while keeping control of defense, the Suez Canal and Sudan. A 1923 constitution created a parliament dominated by Zaghlul's Wafd party. Howard Carter found Tutankhamun's tomb in 1922, and in 1928 Hassan al-Banna founded the Muslim Brotherhood.

Egypt's constitutional monarchy struggled with royal interference, the Great Depression and falling cotton prices. Young King Farouk took the throne in 1936, the same year an Anglo-Egyptian treaty reduced but did not end the British military presence. Mass movements like the Muslim Brotherhood and nationalist youth groups grew rapidly.

Egypt was a key Allied base in the Second World War; British forces stopped the German advance at El Alamein in 1942 and forced a government on King Farouk. The Arab League was founded in Cairo in 1945. Defeat in the 1948 war against the new state of Israel discredited the monarchy and fueled unrest.

Gamal Abdel Nasser and the Free Officers overthrew King Farouk in 1952 and created a republic. Nasser became a hero of Arab nationalism by nationalizing the Suez Canal, surviving the 1956 British, French and Israeli invasion, and briefly uniting with Syria in 1958. Land reform and Soviet aid for the Aswan High Dam followed.

Nasser's Arab socialist state nationalized industry and expanded schools, while Egyptian troops fought a long war in Yemen. Israel's crushing victory in the 1967 Six-Day War cost Egypt the Sinai and shattered Nasser's prestige. The Aswan High Dam was completed in 1970, ending the Nile flood, and Nasser died that year.

Anwar Sadat succeeded Nasser, expelled Soviet advisers, and launched the 1973 October War, crossing the Suez Canal. He opened the economy to foreign investment and turned toward the United States. His Camp David accords led to a 1979 peace treaty with Israel, regaining Sinai but isolating Egypt in the Arab world.

Islamist officers assassinated Sadat in 1981, and Hosni Mubarak became president, ruling under emergency law. Israel completed its withdrawal from Sinai in 1982, and Egypt gradually returned to the Arab League. Large American aid supported the army, while rapid population growth strained Cairo, jobs and housing.

Mubarak joined the US-led coalition in the 1991 Gulf War, earning debt relief, and began market reforms. An Islamist insurgency targeted officials, Copts and tourists, culminating in the 1997 Luxor massacre before militants were crushed. The ruling party monopolized politics as Cairo's population swelled past ten million.

Mubarak's long rule continued amid economic growth that benefited a narrow elite, and speculation that his son Gamal would succeed him. The 2005 elections allowed limited competition, and the Kefaya movement and labor strikes, including in Mahalla in 2008, showed rising discontent over prices, corruption and police abuse.

Mass protests in Tahrir Square toppled Mubarak in 2011 during the Arab Spring. The Muslim Brotherhood's Mohamed Morsi won the 2012 election, but in 2013 the army under Abdel Fattah el-Sisi removed him and crushed his supporters. Sisi became president in 2014, expanded the Suez Canal, and ruled with tight control.

President Sisi's government pressed on with megaprojects such as a New Administrative Capital and the Grand Egyptian Museum near Giza. Debt, inflation and sharp currency devaluations brought repeated IMF loans and hardship. Wars in Gaza and Sudan and Houthi attacks on Red Sea shipping, which cut Suez Canal income, affected Egypt deeply.
North Africa: During the humid 'Green Sahara' period, hunters, fishers and later cattle herders lived across what is now desert, leaving rock art at sites like Tassili n'Ajjer. Along the Maghreb, the Iberomaurusian and Capsian cultures hunted and gathered snails and plants. Between c. 9000 and 4000 BC the Sahara dried, pushing people toward the coasts and oases.

With the Sahara now largely desert, people of the Maghreb lived as herders of sheep, goats and cattle, with some farming near the coast. These were ancestors of the Berbers (Amazigh). Egyptian records describe western neighbors called Tehenu and Tjemehu, and Neolithic communities in Morocco had contacts across the Strait of Gibraltar.

Libyan peoples such as the Libu and Meshwesh pressed on Egypt's western frontier, joining the Sea Peoples in an invasion repelled c. 1208 BC. Horses and chariots spread into the Sahara, appearing in rock art. Late in this era, Phoenician sailors from the Levant began setting up trading stops along the North African coast.

Phoenicians from Tyre founded Carthage, traditionally in 814 BC, in what is now Tunisia, along with posts such as Utica and Lixus. Greek colonists from Thera founded Cyrene in Libya c. 631 BC. Inland, Berber peoples herded and farmed, while the Garamantes of the Fezzan began building an oasis society in the Sahara.

Carthage became the leading Phoenician city of the west, building a trading empire across Sardinia, western Sicily, Spain and the African coast. It allied with the Etruscans against Greek rivals c. 540 BC and signed a treaty with Rome in 509 BC. Greek Cyrene grew rich exporting the medicinal plant silphium.

Carthage suffered defeat by the Greeks of Syracuse at Himera in 480 BC, then turned inland to farm the fertile Tunisian countryside. Carthaginian navigators such as Hanno reportedly sailed down Africa's Atlantic coast. Herodotus described Libyan tribes and the Garamantes, who traded across the Sahara using horses and chariots.

Carthage fought repeated wars with Syracuse for Sicily; the tyrant Agathocles even invaded Africa in 310 BC. The Punic city was a wealthy republic ruled by merchant aristocrats, with grand harbors. In the east, Cyrene fell under Ptolemaic Egypt c. 322 BC, while Numidian and Mauri Berber kingdoms took shape inland.

Carthage clashed with Rome in the First and Second Punic Wars between 264 and 201 BC. Hannibal crossed the Alps and ravaged Italy, but Rome invaded Africa and defeated him at Zama in 202 BC. The Numidian king Masinissa, Rome's ally, emerged as a powerful Berber ruler at Carthage's expense.

Masinissa's Numidia pressed Carthage until Rome destroyed the city in 146 BC and created the Province of Africa. Numidia's king Jugurtha fought Rome from 112 to 105 BC before being captured. Rome gained Cyrenaica by bequest in 96 BC, while Berber kingdoms ruled most of the interior.

Julius Caesar defeated Pompey's allies and King Juba I of Numidia at Thapsus in 46 BC, expanding Roman Africa. Augustus refounded Carthage as a Roman colony, and North African grain began feeding Rome. In Mauretania (Morocco and western Algeria), the learned client king Juba II ruled with his wife Cleopatra Selene.

Rome tightened its hold, crushing the long revolt of the Berber leader Tacfarinas in AD 17 to 24. Caligula executed King Ptolemy of Mauretania in 40, and his kingdom was annexed as two Roman provinces. Olive oil and grain estates expanded, and cities like Leptis Magna were adorned with Roman monuments.

Roman North Africa enjoyed peace and prosperity, exporting grain, olive oil and pottery across the empire. Trajan founded the planned city of Timgad c. 100, and a legion guarded the frontier from Lambaesis. Latin culture flourished, producing writers like Apuleius, while Christianity began spreading in Carthage and other cities.

Septimius Severus, born at Leptis Magna, became Roman emperor in 193 and lavished his hometown with buildings. African Christians such as Tertullian and Bishop Cyprian of Carthage, martyred in 258, shaped Latin theology. The great amphitheater at El Djem was built, but the empire's third-century crises brought revolts and strain.

Under Diocletian's reforms North Africa remained a rich Roman region, now largely Christian. The Donatist schism split African churches bitterly for generations. Augustine, born in 354, became bishop of Hippo in 395 and one of Christianity's most influential thinkers, while Berber chiefs such as Firmus and Gildo revolted against imperial authority.

The Germanic Vandals under Gaiseric crossed from Spain in 429 and took Carthage in 439, creating a kingdom that dominated the western Mediterranean. Augustine died in 430 as they besieged Hippo. The Arian Christian Vandals persecuted Catholics and sacked Rome in 455, while Berber kingdoms grew in the mountains and desert edges.

Byzantine general Belisarius destroyed the Vandal kingdom in 533 to 534, restoring imperial rule over the coastlands. The Byzantines built fortresses but faced constant warfare with independent Berber (Moorish) kingdoms. Roman culture and Christianity persisted in cities, though much of the interior was now ruled by Berber chiefs.

Arab Muslim armies invaded from Egypt from 647, defeating the Byzantines at Sufetula. Uqba ibn Nafi founded Kairouan in 670 as a base, but Berber leaders, including Kusaila and the warrior queen Dihya (al-Kahina), fought back hard. Carthage fell in 698, and by c. 709 Arab rule reached the Atlantic.

North Africa was a province of the Umayyad Caliphate, and many Berbers converted to Islam and joined its armies, invading Spain in 711. Resentment at Arab discrimination sparked the Berber Revolt of 740. Independent states followed, including the Rustamids at Tahert, the Midrarids of trading Sijilmasa, and the Idrisids in Morocco from 788.

The Aghlabid dynasty ruled Ifriqiya (Tunisia) for the Abbasids from 800, rebuilding Kairouan's Great Mosque and conquering Sicily from 827. In Morocco the Idrisids built Fez, where Fatima al-Fihri founded al-Qarawiyyin in 859. Trans-Saharan caravans carrying gold and salt enriched oasis towns like Sijilmasa.

The Ismaili Fatimids, backed by Kutama Berbers, overthrew the Aghlabids in 909 and founded a rival caliphate, building a capital at Mahdia. After conquering Egypt in 969 they moved east, leaving the Zirid family to govern Ifriqiya. In the west, Morocco's tribes swung between Fatimid and Umayyad Cordoban influence.

The Zirids broke with the Fatimids c. 1048, and in revenge Bedouin Banu Hilal tribes migrated west, weakening cities and spreading Arabic. In the western Sahara, Sanhaja Berber reformers founded the Almoravid movement, built Marrakesh c. 1070, and conquered Morocco. They crossed into Spain and defeated Castile at Zallaqa in 1086.

The Almohads, a reform movement founded by Ibn Tumart among Masmuda Berbers, overthrew the Almoravids, taking Marrakesh in 1147. Under Abd al-Mumin they united the whole Maghreb and al-Andalus, expelling Norman outposts in Tunisia. Their court sponsored philosophers like Averroes and grand mosques like the Koutoubia.

Defeat by Christian Spain at Las Navas de Tolosa in 1212 began the Almohad collapse, completed in 1269. Three Berber dynasties divided the Maghreb: the Marinids at Fez, the Zayyanids at Tlemcen, and the Hafsids at Tunis. France's Louis IX died during a crusade against Tunis in 1270.

Marinid, Zayyanid and Hafsid sultans competed over the Maghreb and its trans-Saharan trade, building elegant madrasas in Fez and Tlemcen. Ibn Battuta of Tangier traveled the known world, and Ibn Khaldun wrote his pioneering history, the Muqaddimah, in 1377. The Black Death struck the region from 1348.

Portugal captured Ceuta in 1415 and later Tangier, beginning European expansion in Africa. In Morocco the Wattasids replaced the Marinids, while the Hafsids still ruled Tunis. After 1492 Muslims and Jews expelled from Spain settled in Maghrebi cities, bringing skills and resentment, and Spain seized Melilla in 1497.

Ottoman corsairs led by the Barbarossa brothers took Algiers, then Tripoli in 1551 and Tunis in 1574, making them Ottoman regencies and corsair bases. Morocco stayed independent under the Saadi dynasty, which crushed a Portuguese invasion in 1578. Sultan Ahmad al-Mansur grew rich from sugar and sent an army across the Sahara in 1591.

The Barbary corsairs of Algiers, Tunis and Tripoli raided Mediterranean shipping and coasts, enslaving thousands of Europeans. These regencies became largely self-governing under local deys and beys. Moriscos expelled from Spain in 1609 settled in the region, and in Morocco the Alaouite dynasty took power in 1666, with Moulay Ismail ruling from Meknes.

Local dynasties consolidated power under loose Ottoman sovereignty: the Husainid beys in Tunis from 1705 and the Karamanli family in Tripoli from 1711, while Algiers was governed by elected deys. Morocco's strong ruler Moulay Ismail died in 1727, plunging the kingdom into decades of succession struggles.

Sultan Sidi Mohammed ben Abdallah restored order in Morocco, founded the port of Essaouira, and in 1777 became one of the first rulers to recognize the United States. Corsair states collected tribute from European and American shippers for safe passage. Plague hit hard in the 1790s, and Spain gave up Oran in 1792.

The United States fought the First Barbary War against Tripoli in 1801 to 1805 and the Second Barbary War in 1815 to end tribute payments. A British and Dutch fleet bombarded Algiers in 1816, freeing captives. The age of the Barbary corsairs ended, leaving the regencies weaker and more exposed to European pressure.

France invaded Algeria in 1830, taking Algiers and launching a brutal conquest. Emir Abd al-Qadir led resistance until 1847, while Morocco's support for him brought defeat at Isly in 1844. The Ottomans reimposed direct rule on Tripoli in 1835, and Tunisia's Ahmad Bey abolished slavery in 1846.

France conquered Kabylia in 1857 and encouraged European settlers to take Algerian land; the Mokrani revolt of 1871 was crushed. Tunisia adopted the Arab world's first constitution in 1861 but fell into debt to European creditors. Spain defeated Morocco in 1860, and the Sanusi Sufi order spread across Libya's desert.

France made Tunisia a protectorate in 1881, adding to its Algerian colony, where settlers now held the best land and political power. Morocco's Sultan Hassan I worked to modernize and play European powers against each other to stay independent. Libya remained an Ottoman province, with the Sanusi order influential inland.

Morocco became the focus of European rivalry: Germany's Kaiser visited Tangier in 1905, and the Algeciras Conference of 1906 gave France and Spain special roles. French troops occupied Oujda and bombarded Casablanca in 1907. Algeria and Tunisia lived under settler-dominated French rule, while Libya stayed Ottoman.

Italy seized Libya from the Ottomans in 1911 to 1912, facing fierce Arab and Sanusi resistance. In 1912 France made most of Morocco a protectorate under Resident-General Lyautey, with Spain taking the north. Hundreds of thousands of North Africans served or labored for France in the First World War.

In Spanish Morocco, Abd el-Krim crushed a Spanish army at Annual in 1921 and founded a Rif Republic until French and Spanish forces defeated him in 1926. Italy waged a brutal reconquest of Libya against Omar Mukhtar's guerrillas. Tunisian nationalists formed the Destour party in 1920.

Italy hanged Omar Mukhtar in 1931, confined Libyans in camps, and brought in Italian settlers. Bourguiba founded Tunisia's Neo-Destour party in 1934, and Messali Hadj led Algerian nationalism. France lavishly celebrated a century in Algeria in 1930, and in 1936 Franco launched the Spanish Civil War from Spanish Morocco.

The Second World War brought desert battles to Libya, including the long siege of Tobruk, and Allied landings in Morocco and Algeria in Operation Torch in 1942. Roosevelt and Churchill met at Casablanca in 1943. Nationalist hopes rose, but French forces massacred thousands of Algerians after the Sétif protests of 1945.

Libya became independent in 1951 as a kingdom under Idris al-Sanusi. Algeria's National Liberation Front began a war against France in 1954 that killed hundreds of thousands. Morocco under Mohammed V and Tunisia under Bourguiba won independence in 1956, while oil was discovered in Libya in 1959.

Algeria won independence in 1962, and about a million European settlers fled; Ben Bella led until Boumediene's coup in 1965. Hassan II ruled Morocco firmly from 1961, and Algeria and Morocco fought the brief Sand War in 1963. Oil enriched Libya, where Muammar Gaddafi overthrew the monarchy in 1969.

Gaddafi used oil wealth to fund his 'Green Book' revolution and foreign causes. Algeria nationalized its oil and gas in 1971 under a socialist one-party state. Morocco's 1975 Green March claimed Western Sahara from Spain, starting a long war with the Algerian-backed Polisario Front, while Bourguiba aged in power in Tunisia.

The United States bombed Libya in 1986, and the Lockerbie bombing of 1988 deepened Gaddafi's isolation. Ben Ali replaced Bourguiba in Tunisia in 1987. Falling oil prices sparked riots in Algeria in 1988, forcing multiparty reforms, and the five Maghreb states formed the Arab Maghreb Union in 1989.

Algeria's army cancelled 1992 elections that Islamists were winning, triggering a civil war that killed perhaps 150,000 people. Libya endured UN sanctions over Lockerbie. A 1991 ceasefire froze the Western Sahara conflict, and in Morocco Mohammed VI succeeded his father Hassan II in 1999 with promises of reform.

Algeria's President Bouteflika offered amnesties as the civil war wound down, though al-Qaeda in the Islamic Maghreb kept fighting in the Sahara. Gaddafi gave up weapons programs in 2003 and returned to international favor. Morocco expanded women's rights in 2004, and migration across the Mediterranean to Europe increased.

A Tunisian street vendor's self-immolation sparked the Arab Spring in 2010, ousting Ben Ali; Tunisia adopted a democratic constitution in 2014. NATO-backed rebels overthrew Gaddafi in 2011, but Libya split into rival governments. Morocco amended its constitution in 2011, and Algeria's Hirak protests ended Bouteflika's rule in 2019.

Tunisia's President Kais Saied suspended parliament in 2021 and concentrated power, reversing its democratic gains. Libya remained divided between rival eastern and western authorities, and floods in Derna killed thousands in 2023. Morocco normalized ties with Israel in 2020, gained US recognition over Western Sahara, and suffered a deadly earthquake in 2023.
West Africa: Hunter-gatherers lived across West Africa's forests and savannas for tens of thousands of years. During the humid 'Green Sahara' period, communities fished and hunted around lakes now gone, and some of the world's earliest pottery was made at Ounjougou in Mali c. 9400 BC. Later, cattle herders spread across the Sahara before it dried.

As the Sahara turned to desert, herders and their cattle moved south into the Sahel. Farmers of the savanna were domesticating pearl millet, while forest peoples relied on yams and oil palm. The Kintampo culture of Ghana combined farming, herding and stone tools, and stone villages began at Dhar Tichitt in Mauritania.

At Dhar Tichitt, herders and millet farmers built large walled stone villages, an early complex society in the Sahel. African rice was being cultivated along the Niger, and the Kintampo culture flourished in Ghana. Near the Nigeria and Cameroon borderlands, Bantu-speaking peoples began the long expansion that would spread their languages across Africa.

Bantu-speaking farmers spread farming and, increasingly, iron-working eastward and southward from West-Central Africa over many centuries. In the savanna and forest, village communities grew yams, millet and sorghum. Iron smelting appeared in parts of West Africa by the early first millennium BC, and the Nok culture was developing in central Nigeria.

The Nok culture of central Nigeria smelted iron and made striking terracotta sculptures of human heads and figures, among the oldest in sub-Saharan Africa. Iron tools helped farmers clear land and grow more food. Across the region, villages of farmers and herders lived under local chiefs and lineage elders rather than large states.

The Nok culture continued to flourish in central Nigeria, producing terracottas and iron at sites like Taruga. Iron-working spread among neighboring peoples, making hoes and weapons more widely available. To the north, the Garamantes of the Libyan Sahara traded with Sahel peoples, while Sahel villages grew millet and herded livestock.

Farming and iron-working villages spread through the savanna and forest, and settlements such as Dia on the inland Niger Delta grew. The Nok culture remained a major artistic and technological center in Nigeria. Societies were largely organized around kinship, with craft specialists such as smiths gaining special status.

Jenne-jeno was founded c. 250 BC on the inland Niger Delta in Mali, growing into one of sub-Saharan Africa's earliest known towns. Its people fished, farmed rice, worked iron and traded along the river, apparently without a single ruler. The Nok culture continued in Nigeria, and iron-using farmers expanded across the region.

Jenne-jeno and neighboring settlements grew as trading hubs where fishers, farmers and craftspeople exchanged rice, fish, iron and copper. Specialized groups lived in clusters of villages that formed a town without a palace or king. Across the forest and savanna, iron-working farming communities continued to expand.

Towns along the Niger, including Jenne-jeno, prospered from regional trade in food, iron and salt. The Nok culture was beginning to wane in Nigeria. Contact across the Sahara was limited but real, as Saharan peoples like the Garamantes linked the Sahel to the Roman Mediterranean world.

Iron-working farming societies now covered much of West Africa, from the Senegal River to the Lake Chad basin. The Nok terracotta tradition faded in this period. Jenne-jeno kept growing, and village communities were organized by kin groups, age sets and ritual leaders rather than kingdoms.

The camel, introduced to the Sahara from the east, gradually made long desert crossings more practical. Jenne-jeno expanded and traded in copper, salt and stone from distant sources. In Senegambia, people began raising stone circles over burials, and the Soninke peoples of the western Sahel were laying foundations for later states.

Camel herding spread through the Sahara, and desert Berber groups began to act as middlemen between the Sahel and North Africa. Jenne-jeno became a large town with satellite villages. Among the Soninke, chiefs gained power from controlling trade in gold, salt and slaves, setting the stage for the first great Sahel empire.

The Ghana Empire, called Wagadu by its Soninke founders, emerged in the region between the Senegal and Niger rivers. Its kings controlled trade routes linking the gold fields to the south with salt from the Sahara. Camel caravans opened regular trans-Saharan trade, linking West Africa to North Africa.

Ghana grew stronger by taxing gold and salt passing through its territory and by commanding cavalry and iron-armed soldiers. Jenne-jeno flourished as a river trading city, and settlements like Gao developed on the middle Niger. In Senegambia, the building of megalithic stone circles continued.

Ghana extended its influence over neighboring peoples of the Sahel. Gao on the Niger was growing as a trading center, and farther east, peoples near Lake Chad were forming the communities that would become Kanem. Saharan Berbers such as the Sanhaja controlled desert routes between the Sahel and the north.

Ghana's kings, ruling from towns in the western Sahel, prospered from gold and salt trade. After the Arab conquest of North Africa, Muslim merchants increasingly organized the trans-Saharan caravans. The Kanem kingdom was taking shape northeast of Lake Chad, and Gao grew as a Niger River market.

Arab writers first mentioned Ghana in the 700s, calling it a land of gold. Trading towns like Sijilmasa in Morocco, founded in 757, linked caravans to the Sahel. Kanem emerged as a state near Lake Chad, and Gao and Takrur on the Senegal River grew through trans-Saharan trade.

Ghana dominated the western Sahel's gold trade, and Muslim merchants settled in its towns. In southeastern Nigeria, the Igbo-Ukwu culture produced remarkably intricate bronze castings and imported glass beads, showing complex society and long-distance trade. Kanem expanded near Lake Chad, and Gao rose on the Niger.

Ghana stood at its height, its king famed in Arabic sources for vast gold and a large army. Its capital, probably Koumbi Saleh, had a royal town and a separate Muslim merchant quarter. Igbo-Ukwu bronze-making flourished in Nigeria, and Kanem and Gao grew as trading kingdoms.

The geographer al-Bakri described Ghana's wealth and court in 1068. The Almoravid movement from the western Sahara pressured Ghana, which began to weaken. Islam spread among Sahel rulers: Takrur's king converted, Gao's rulers were Muslim, and Kanem's king Hummay embraced Islam c. 1085. In the forest, Ife was rising.

Ghana declined as trade routes shifted and vassal states broke away, including the Sosso kingdom. In Yoruba country, the city of Ife became a sacred and political center, producing naturalistic bronze and terracotta heads. Hausa city-states such as Kano were forming in northern Nigeria, while Kanem remained powerful.

Sundiata Keita defeated the Sosso king Sumanguru and founded the Mali Empire in 1235, controlling the gold trade from the upper Niger. Mali's kings, the mansas, ruled a vast realm of many peoples. Kanem reached its height near Lake Chad, Ife flourished, and the Benin kingdom took shape in the forest.

Mali was at its peak; Mansa Musa's lavish pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324 made its gold famous across the Islamic world and Europe. Timbuktu became a center of trade and Islamic scholarship, with mosques like Djinguereber. Ibn Battuta visited in 1352, Ife and Benin flourished, and Kanem's rulers moved to Bornu.

Mali weakened as Tuareg took Timbuktu in 1433 and Songhai rose under Sunni Ali from 1464, building a vast empire based at Gao. Portuguese sailors reached the Gold Coast and built Elmina in 1482. Benin expanded under Oba Ewuare, and the Hausa cities and Bornu grew stronger.

Songhai reached its peak under Askia Muhammad, ruling a vast empire with Timbuktu a renowned center of learning. A Moroccan army with firearms destroyed Songhai at Tondibi in 1591. Bornu prospered under Idris Alooma, Benin traded with the Portuguese, and the Atlantic slave trade grew along the coast.

With Songhai gone, the Sahel fragmented, and Moroccan-descended rulers held Timbuktu. On the coast the Atlantic slave trade expanded rapidly as Dutch, English and French joined the Portuguese. New kingdoms built on firearms and trade rose, including Asante c. 1670 and Dahomey, while the Oyo Empire expanded with cavalry.

Asante, unified under Osei Tutu and the sacred Golden Stool, expanded under Opoku Ware. Dahomey conquered the slaving port of Ouidah in 1727 but paid tribute to Oyo. The Bambara kingdom of Segou rose on the Niger, and the Atlantic slave trade neared its peak, carrying tens of thousands of captives a year.

The Atlantic slave trade reached its height, deeply shaping coastal kingdoms such as Asante, Dahomey and Oyo. Islamic reform movements created new states in Futa Jallon and Futa Toro. Britain founded Freetown in Sierra Leone for freed slaves in 1787 to 1792, and the explorer Mungo Park traveled the Niger in 1795.

Usman dan Fodio's Fulani jihad from 1804 overthrew Hausa kings and created the Sokoto Caliphate, one of Africa's largest states. Britain abolished its slave trade in 1807 and patrolled the coast against slavers. Freetown became a British colony, and freed African Americans began settling Liberia in 1822.

The Oyo Empire collapsed c. 1835, unleashing Yoruba wars and the rise of new cities such as Ibadan and Abeokuta. Seku Amadu's Masina Caliphate ruled the inland Niger Delta. Trade shifted toward palm oil for Europe's factories, and Liberia declared independence in 1847, becoming Africa's first modern republic.

Al-Hajj Umar Tall's jihad built the Tukulor Empire across the western Sudan in the 1850s and 1860s. France expanded from Senegal under Governor Faidherbe, founding Dakar in 1857, while Britain annexed Lagos in 1861. British troops burned the Asante capital Kumasi in 1874 during the Anglo-Asante War.

Britain made the Gold Coast a colony in 1874, and after the Berlin Conference European powers raced to conquer the interior. Samori Touré resisted the French until his capture in 1898, Dahomey fell in 1894, and the British sacked Benin City in 1897, looting its bronzes. Only Liberia stayed independent.

Britain conquered the Sokoto Caliphate in 1903 and crushed Asante's last revolt, led by Yaa Asantewaa, in 1900. France ruled French West Africa as a federation from Dakar. Colonial rule brought forced labor, taxes and railways, and farmers turned to cash crops such as cocoa, making the Gold Coast a leading producer.

Britain merged its territories into Nigeria in 1914 under Lugard's indirect rule through local chiefs. During the First World War, Allied troops took German Togoland and Kamerun, and France recruited many tirailleurs sénégalais. Blaise Diagne became the first black African deputy in the French parliament in 1914.

Colonial governments ruled through chiefs while expanding cash crops like cocoa, peanuts and palm oil. Western-educated Africans formed the National Congress of British West Africa in 1920 to demand a voice, and Herbert Macaulay led early Nigerian politics. Liberia leased vast land to the Firestone rubber company in 1926.

The Great Depression slashed crop prices, and Gold Coast farmers staged cocoa hold-ups in 1937 to 1938. Nnamdi Azikiwe's newspapers spread nationalist ideas in Nigeria, while in Paris Léopold Senghor and others launched the Négritude movement celebrating African culture. Colonial rule still seemed firmly entrenched.

The Second World War drew West African soldiers to fight in Burma and Europe. After the war, the French granted limited political rights, and the RDA party formed in 1946; French troops killed returning soldiers at Thiaroye in 1944. Riots in Accra in 1948 led to Kwame Nkrumah's mass nationalist party in 1949.

Nationalist parties won elections under new constitutions as colonial rule loosened. Nkrumah led Ghana, formerly the Gold Coast, to independence in 1957, the first sub-Saharan colony to break free. Guinea, under Sékou Touré, voted to leave the French community in 1958 and became independent immediately.

Nigeria and most of French West Africa became independent in 1960, led by figures such as Senghor in Senegal. Military coups soon followed, including Nkrumah's overthrow in 1966. Nigeria's Civil War over Biafra's secession in 1967 to 1970 killed perhaps a million people, many from famine.

Oil wealth transformed Nigeria while its military governments ruled. West African states formed ECOWAS in 1975 to promote trade and cooperation.
