A severe Sahel drought in the early 1970s caused famine. Guinea-Bissau won independence from Portugal in 1974, and Jerry Rawlings first seized power in Ghana in 1979.

Falling commodity prices and debt forced many states into harsh structural adjustment programs. Samuel Doe seized power in Liberia in 1980, and Thomas Sankara led a revolutionary government in Burkina Faso until his murder in 1987. Military rule persisted in Nigeria, and Liberia's civil war began in 1989.

Brutal civil wars engulfed Liberia and Sierra Leone, fueled by diamonds and child soldiers, as a Nigerian-led ECOWAS force intervened. Nigeria's dictator Sani Abacha executed activist Ken Saro-Wiwa in 1995, then civilian rule returned in 1999. Elsewhere, countries like Benin and Mali held multiparty elections.

The wars in Sierra Leone and Liberia ended in 2002 and 2003, and Ellen Johnson Sirleaf became Africa's first elected female head of state in 2006. Côte d'Ivoire was split by civil war. Nigeria and Ghana held regular elections, while the Boko Haram insurgency erupted in northeastern Nigeria in 2009.

Islamist rebels seized northern Mali in 2012, prompting French intervention, and Boko Haram kidnapped the Chibok schoolgirls in 2014. The Ebola epidemic of 2014 to 2016 killed over 11,000 people in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone. Nigeria saw its first peaceful transfer to an opposition president in 2015.

Military juntas seized power in Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger from 2020 to 2023, expelled French troops, and turned to Russia, forming an Alliance of Sahel States outside ECOWAS. Jihadist violence spread across the Sahel. Coastal states such as Senegal and Ghana held competitive elections, while Nigeria faced inflation and insecurity.
East Africa: East Africa is the cradle of humankind: the hominin 'Lucy' lived in Ethiopia 3.2 million years ago, and some of the oldest known Homo sapiens fossils come from Omo, Ethiopia. Later hunter-gatherers fished the then-larger lakes of the Rift Valley and Nile, and cattle herding spread into Sudan before 5000 BC.

In Nubia, along the Nile south of Egypt, the A-Group culture traded with early Egypt, and the Kerma culture arose c. 2500 BC, becoming the first kingdom of Kush. Herders brought cattle, sheep and goats into the Kenyan Rift Valley, while Ethiopian highlanders began cultivating local crops such as teff and ensete.

The kingdom of Kush, centered at Kerma, became a wealthy rival to Egypt before New Kingdom pharaohs conquered Nubia c. 1500 BC and ruled it for centuries. Egypt traded for incense, ebony and exotic animals with the Land of Punt, probably on the southern Red Sea coast. Pastoralists spread through the highlands of Kenya and Tanzania.

After Egypt withdrew, a new kingdom of Kush arose at Napata, and its king Piye conquered Egypt c. 744 BC, ruling as pharaohs until expelled by Assyria. In northern Ethiopia and Eritrea, the kingdom of D'mt built temples at Yeha with South Arabian links. Iron-working farmers appeared around the Great Lakes.

Driven from Egypt, the Kushite kings ruled from Napata and increasingly from Meroë farther south, especially after an Egyptian raid on Napata in 593 BC. The D'mt kingdom continued in the Ethiopian highlands. Around Lake Victoria, Bantu-speaking farmers of the Urewe tradition were smelting iron and growing crops.

The Kushite kingdom flourished on the Nile, its royal tombs topped by steep pyramids. Herodotus wrote of these 'long-lived Ethiopians', and a Persian army had failed to conquer them. D'mt faded in the Ethiopian highlands, while iron-using Bantu-speaking communities expanded around the Great Lakes.

Meroë grew into Kush's capital and a major center of iron-working, surrounded by slag heaps and fields of sorghum. Its rulers traded ivory, gold and ebony with Ptolemaic Egypt. In the Great Lakes region, Bantu-speaking farmers continued spreading iron tools, cattle and crops among existing hunting and herding peoples.

Under rulers like Arkamani, Meroë developed its own culture, including the Meroitic script and temples to the lion god Apedemak at Musawwarat es-Sufra. Ptolemaic Egypt sent ships to the Red Sea coast to hunt war elephants. Bantu-speaking farmers moved toward the East African coast.

The Meroitic kingdom prospered, ruled at times by powerful queens called Kandakes, such as Shanakdakhete. Its pyramids and temples blended Egyptian and local traditions. Along the coast and in the interior, iron-working farming villages multiplied, and Red Sea trade linked the region to the Mediterranean and Arabia.

The Kushite queen Amanirenas fought Rome after it annexed Egypt, and a 21 BC treaty ended the war on favorable terms for Meroë. Communities in the Ethiopian highlands were forming the polity that would become Aksum. Iron-working Bantu-speaking farmers were spreading along the East African coast.

A Greek merchant's guide, the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, described the Red Sea port of Adulis and the trading town of Rhapta on the Swahili coast. Aksum was growing in the Ethiopian highlands, and Meroë remained powerful on the Nile. Nero sent explorers up the Nile to investigate Kush.

The Kingdom of Aksum rose in northern Ethiopia and Eritrea, growing rich on Red Sea trade in ivory and gold. Its rulers erected tall carved stone stelae. Meroë continued on the Nile, while coastal towns like Rhapta traded with Roman and Arabian merchants, and Bantu-speaking farmers settled ever more widely.

Aksum minted its own coins and was counted by the Persian prophet Mani among the four great kingdoms of the world. It controlled trade between the Roman world, Arabia and India. Meroë was declining as trade shifted to the Red Sea, and farming communities spread through the interior.

King Ezana of Aksum adopted Christianity c. 330, making it one of the first Christian states. Aksum campaigned against the declining Meroë c. 350, and the Kushite kingdom collapsed. In Nubia new states emerged: Nobadia, Makuria and Alodia. On the coast and around the Great Lakes, Bantu farming communities expanded.

Christianity deepened in Aksum as the Nine Saints, monks from the Roman world, founded monasteries, and the Bible was translated into Ge'ez. Aksum's stelae and palaces showed its wealth. In Nubia, successor kingdoms buried rulers in rich mound tombs, while farming villages grew along the East African coast.

Aksum's King Kaleb invaded Himyar in Yemen c. 525, briefly extending power across the Red Sea. Missionaries from Byzantium converted the Nubian kingdoms to Christianity from c. 543. On the coast, early farming and fishing villages with distinctive pottery were the ancestors of later Swahili towns.

Aksum's king sheltered early Muslim refugees from Mecca in 615, but Aksum declined as Arab expansion shifted Red Sea trade. In Nubia, Makuria defeated Arab invaders and in 652 signed the Baqt treaty with Muslim Egypt, a trade pact that lasted centuries. Makuria absorbed neighboring Nobadia.

Aksum faded and Ethiopian Christian power moved south into the highlands. Christian Makuria flourished, decorating churches like the cathedral at Faras with vivid paintings. On the coast, Swahili towns such as Shanga built early mosques as Islam arrived with Indian Ocean traders seeking ivory and other goods.

Swahili towns grew along the coast, trading ivory, gold and enslaved people across the Indian Ocean. Enslaved East Africans, called Zanj, rose in a massive revolt in Iraq from 869 to 883. Makuria and Alodia were thriving Christian Nubian kingdoms, while Ethiopia's history in this era is poorly recorded.

Arab traveler al-Masudi described the Swahili coast and its gold trade c. 916, and according to tradition Kilwa was founded around this time. Ethiopian tradition tells of a queen, Gudit, who sacked Aksum c. 960. Makuria was at its height in Nubia, and pastoral and farming peoples spread inland.

Swahili towns from Mogadishu to Kilwa adopted Islam and traded ivory, gold and timber with Arabia, Persia and India. Gold from Zimbabwe passed through Sofala to Kilwa. Christian Nubian kingdoms remained strong, and in the Ethiopian highlands, Christian rulers reorganized after Aksum's fall.

Swahili city-states such as Kilwa, Mombasa and Zanzibar thrived on Indian Ocean trade, building coral stone mosques and houses. The Zagwe dynasty took power in Ethiopia c. 1137. Mogadishu was a major port, and in the Great Lakes region, earthwork sites like Ntusi show growing cattle-based states.

King Lalibela of the Zagwe dynasty built churches carved from solid rock. In 1270 Yekuno Amlak founded the Solomonic dynasty, claiming descent from Solomon and Sheba. Kilwa grew rich controlling the gold trade from Sofala, while Mamluk Egypt weakened Christian Makuria and Muslim sultanates rose in Ethiopia's east.

Emperor Amda Seyon expanded Ethiopia against the Muslim sultanate of Ifat, and the Kebra Nagast legend glorified the dynasty. Ibn Battuta admired Kilwa and Mogadishu in 1331, where Kilwa built the palace of Husuni Kubwa. Makuria collapsed as Arab nomads moved into Sudan, and kingdoms formed in the Great Lakes.

Ethiopia's Emperor Zara Yaqob strengthened the church and the crown. Swahili towns traded with Asia, and Chinese admiral Zheng He's fleet visited in 1418 to 1419. Vasco da Gama reached Mombasa and Malindi in 1498. Inland, the kingdoms of Bunyoro and Buganda were taking shape.

The Portuguese sacked Kilwa and Mombasa in 1505 and built Fort Jesus at Mombasa in 1593 to control the coast. In Ethiopia, Ahmad Gragn of Adal invaded from 1529 until Ethiopians with Portuguese help defeated him in 1543. Oromo peoples migrated north, and the Funj Sultanate ruled Sudan from Sennar.

Emperor Fasilides founded Gondar as Ethiopia's capital in 1636 and expelled the Jesuits after a disastrous attempt to convert the country to Catholicism. Omani Arabs captured Fort Jesus in 1698, ending Portuguese power north of Mozambique. Buganda and Bunyoro competed in the Great Lakes, and the Funj ruled Sudan.

Omani Arabs dominated the Swahili coast, though local families like the Mazrui of Mombasa acted largely independently. Ethiopian emperors at Gondar built castles and churches but struggled with regional nobles. The Funj Sultanate ruled Sudan, and Buganda expanded its power around Lake Victoria.

Ethiopia entered the Zemene Mesafint, the Era of the Princes, from 1769, as regional warlords overshadowed powerless emperors. The Funj Sultanate weakened in Sudan. Buganda and Rwanda grew stronger, centralizing under powerful kings, while ivory and slave trades linked the interior to the coast.

Muhammad Ali's Egypt conquered Sudan from 1820, founding Khartoum as its capital and raiding for slaves and gold. Ethiopia remained divided among rival princes. On the coast, Sayyid Said of Oman strengthened his hold on the Swahili towns, while Buganda's kings expanded their power.

Sultan Said of Oman moved his capital to Zanzibar in 1840, building a commercial empire on clove plantations worked by enslaved people. Arab and Swahili caravans pushed deep inland for ivory and captives. European missionaries arrived, and Egyptian rule extended through Sudan, while Ethiopia stayed fragmented.

Tewodros II reunited Ethiopia from 1855 but died at Magdala during a British expedition in 1868. European explorers like Speke and Burton sought the Nile's source. Under British pressure, Zanzibar closed its slave market in 1873, while Buganda's Kabaka Mutesa I welcomed foreign traders and missionaries.

Britain, Germany and Italy partitioned the region, but Menelik II's Ethiopia crushed Italy at Adwa in 1896 and stayed independent. In Sudan, the Mahdist uprising took Khartoum in 1885 until Anglo-Egyptian forces won at Omdurman in 1898. A rinderpest epidemic devastated cattle-herding peoples.

Britain's Uganda Railway reached Lake Victoria in 1901, bringing white settlers to Kenya's highlands. In German East Africa, the Maji Maji rebellion of 1905 to 1907 was crushed, causing famine and many deaths. Menelik II modernized Ethiopia from Addis Ababa, and Sudan was ruled by an Anglo-Egyptian condominium.

The First World War brought a long campaign in East Africa as Germany's Lettow-Vorbeck evaded British forces, while many African porters died of disease and hunger. In Ethiopia, Lij Iyasu was deposed in 1916, and Ras Tafari became regent. British forces defeated the Somali Dervish leader Sayyid Muhammad in 1920.

Britain took over Tanganyika and Belgium Rwanda-Burundi as League of Nations mandates. Ethiopia joined the League in 1923 under regent Ras Tafari. In Kenya, early African protest leaders such as Harry Thuku challenged settler privileges, and Sudan's huge Gezira cotton scheme opened in 1925.

Ras Tafari was crowned Emperor Haile Selassie in 1930 and pursued modernization. Fascist Italy invaded Ethiopia in 1935 to 1936, using poison gas, and joined it with Eritrea and Somalia as Italian East Africa. Haile Selassie's appeal to the League of Nations went unanswered, while Jomo Kenyatta campaigned in Britain.

British and Commonwealth forces drove Italy out of Ethiopia in 1941, and Haile Selassie returned to his throne. Eritrea and Italian Somaliland came under British administration. In Kenya, land pressure and settler dominance fueled African political organization, while colonial development schemes expanded.

Kenya's Mau Mau uprising of 1952 to 1960 was brutally suppressed, with mass detentions. Eritrea was federated with Ethiopia in 1952. Sudan won independence in 1956, but civil war had begun in the south in 1955. In Rwanda, the Hutu revolution of 1959 overthrew the Tutsi monarchy.

Somalia, Tanganyika, Uganda, Kenya, Rwanda and Burundi won independence between 1960 and 1963. Tanganyika merged with Zanzibar as Tanzania in 1964, and Julius Nyerere pursued African socialism. Eritrean rebels began a war against Ethiopian rule in 1961, while Kenyatta led Kenya.

Idi Amin seized Uganda in 1971, expelled its Asian community, and killed many thousands before Tanzania ousted him in 1979. Ethiopia's monarchy was overthrown in 1974 by the Marxist Derg, which waged the Red Terror and fought Somalia over the Ogaden. Sudan's first civil war ended in 1972.

A catastrophic famine struck Ethiopia in 1983 to 1985, worsened by war and policy, prompting the Live Aid concerts. Sudan's second civil war began in 1983. Yoweri Museveni took power in Uganda in 1986, Kenya became a one-party state, and HIV/AIDS spread widely in the region.

Ethiopia's Derg fell in 1991, and Eritrea gained independence in 1993. Somalia's government collapsed in 1991, leading to famine and a failed UN mission. In Rwanda, extremists killed about 800,000 Tutsi and moderate Hutu in 1994. Ethiopia and Eritrea fought a bloody border war from 1998.

Sudan's Darfur conflict from 2003 killed hundreds of thousands, while a 2005 peace deal ended the north-south civil war. Kenya's disputed 2007 election sparked deadly violence. Ethiopian troops intervened in Somalia in 2006, fueling the al-Shabaab insurgency, and Rwanda rebuilt rapidly under Paul Kagame.

South Sudan won independence in 2011 but fell into civil war in 2013. Ethiopia's economy boomed as it built the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam, and Abiy Ahmed made peace with Eritrea in 2018, winning a Nobel Prize. Protests toppled Sudan's Omar al-Bashir in 2019, and al-Shabaab attacked Kenya.

Ethiopia's Tigray War from 2020 to 2022 killed hundreds of thousands. Sudan descended into civil war between its army and the RSF militia in 2023, creating one of the world's largest displacement and hunger crises. Kenya saw youth-led protests in 2024, and Ethiopia completed its great Nile dam.
South Africa: Southern Africa holds deep human history: early hominins left fossils at Sterkfontein and Taung, and c. 75,000 years ago people at Blombos Cave engraved ochre and made shell beads, some of the earliest symbolic art. In later millennia, ancestors of the San lived as hunter-gatherers across the region.

Southern Africa was home to hunter-gatherers, ancestors of today's San, who lived in small mobile bands. They hunted antelope with bows and poisoned arrows, gathered plants, and harvested shellfish on the coasts. Their rich rock paintings and engravings in places like the Drakensberg and Matobo Hills depict animals and spiritual rituals.

San hunter-gatherers continued to live across southern Africa, using small, finely made stone tools and ostrich-eggshell beads, which they also traded. Families moved seasonally across deserts, grasslands and coasts. No farming or herding had yet arrived, and there were no states, only bands bound by kinship and sharing.

Hunter-gatherer bands, ancestors of the San, occupied the region, from the Kalahari to the Cape. Far to the north, Bantu-speaking farmers were beginning to spread iron-working and agriculture through central Africa, but they had not yet reached the south. Rock art remained central to San religious life.

San hunter-gatherers continued their long-established way of life, painting eland and trance dances on rock shelters. Coastal groups fished and gathered shellfish, leaving large shell middens. Meanwhile, iron-working Bantu-speaking farmers were establishing themselves around the Great Lakes, far to the north.

Southern Africa remained the land of hunter-gatherers, whose deep knowledge of plants, water sources and animal behavior allowed them to thrive in harsh environments such as the Kalahari. Their societies were egalitarian, and sharing food and gifts bound bands together across wide territories.

Hunter-gatherer communities, ancestors of the San, occupied mountains, plains and shores across the region. Coastal peoples used stone fish traps and gathered abundant shellfish. Farming and herding peoples were still far to the north, and southern Africa's population remained small and widely scattered.

Domesticated sheep began reaching the far north of the region, appearing in Namibia c. 200 BC, probably through contact with herders farther north. Most people were still San hunter-gatherers. The arrival of livestock started changing how some groups lived, introducing ideas of property and wealth in animals.

Sheep herding and pottery spread south among some hunter-gatherer groups, giving rise to pastoralist ways of life. These herders were ancestors of the Khoekhoe. San bands continued hunting and gathering, while to the north, Bantu-speaking farmers advanced through the Zambezi region.

By about 2,000 years ago, sheep had reached the Cape, kept by pastoralists ancestral to the Khoekhoe, who moved with their flocks between seasonal pastures. San hunter-gatherers lived alongside them. North of the Limpopo, iron-using Bantu-speaking farmers were approaching the region.

Khoekhoe herders grazed sheep and soon cattle across western and southern parts of the region, while San bands hunted and gathered. Iron-working Bantu-speaking farmers spread through Zambia and Malawi, bringing crops like sorghum and millet. Contact between herders, hunters and farmers grew.

Bantu-speaking farmers began crossing the Zambezi into Zimbabwe and Mozambique, bringing iron tools, pottery, cattle and grain crops. Early farming villages appeared near the Mozambique coast. Khoekhoe herders and San hunter-gatherers still occupied most of the south and west.

Iron-using farmers reached the Limpopo valley and the coast of today's KwaZulu-Natal, building villages of round houses near fertile land. They grew sorghum and millet and herded cattle. These newcomers interacted, traded and sometimes intermarried with San and Khoekhoe peoples.

Bantu-speaking farmers settled widely across the eastern half of the region, from Zimbabwe to the Eastern Cape, establishing Early Iron Age villages. Cattle were becoming central to wealth and marriage. The drier west remained the domain of Khoekhoe herders and San hunter-gatherers.

Early Iron Age farming communities grew across the eastern grasslands and river valleys, smelting iron and making distinctive pottery. Villages were organized around cattle enclosures. San hunter-gatherers continued living in the mountains and drier lands, sometimes trading game and skins with farmers.

Farming villages flourished across the east; the Lydenburg Heads, terracotta sculptures from c. 500, show their rich ritual life. Sites like Ndondondwane in KwaZulu-Natal reveal cattle, iron-working and ivory craft. Khoekhoe herders and San hunter-gatherers held the Cape and Kalahari.

Iron Age farming communities continued to grow in what are now Zimbabwe, Botswana, Mozambique and South Africa. Trade on the Mozambique coast, at sites like Chibuene, began linking the interior to Indian Ocean merchants, who offered glass beads and cloth for ivory and other goods.

Farmers of the Zhizo culture in the Shashe-Limpopo region began trading ivory to the coast for glass beads, linking them to the Indian Ocean economy. Cattle herding and grain farming supported growing villages. Khoekhoe herders and San hunter-gatherers lived in the west and south.

Zhizo farming communities thrived in the Limpopo basin, and the trading town of Schroda grew as an ivory-trading center. In Botswana, the Toutswe culture built hilltop settlements with huge cattle herds. Long-distance trade began to concentrate wealth and power in the hands of chiefs.

Trade in ivory and other goods with the Swahili coast grew, and Leopard's Kopje farmers took over the Shashe-Limpopo region, founding K2. Cattle and trade wealth increased social inequality. Toutswe chiefdoms prospered in eastern Botswana, while Khoekhoe and San lived across the west.

K2 grew into a sizable town in the Limpopo valley, its rulers controlling trade in ivory and, increasingly, gold from Zimbabwe's goldfields. Society became more divided between elites and commoners. Elsewhere, farming communities spread south through the grasslands of today's South Africa.

The capital moved from K2 to Mapungubwe hill, where rulers lived above commoners in a new class-based society, the first state in southern Africa. Gold and ivory went to Kilwa via the coast. On the Zimbabwe plateau, the settlement at Great Zimbabwe was beginning to grow.

Mapungubwe reached its height, its elite buried with gold objects such as the famous golden rhinoceros, before it was abandoned c. 1290, possibly due to climate change. Power shifted north to Great Zimbabwe, whose rulers took control of the gold trade.

Great Zimbabwe reached its peak, a stone city of perhaps 10,000 or more people built with mortarless granite walls, including the Great Enclosure. Its Shona-speaking rulers grew rich from cattle and gold exported through Sofala to Kilwa. Chinese porcelain and Persian pottery found there show its global connections.

Great Zimbabwe declined after c. 1450, as its successor states rose: the Mutapa kingdom in the north and the Torwa state at Khami in the southwest. Bartolomeu Dias rounded the Cape of Good Hope in 1488, and Vasco da Gama sailed past in 1497. Khoekhoe herders held the Cape.

The Portuguese built forts at Sofala and Mozambique Island and traded with the Mutapa kingdom for gold, sometimes interfering in its politics. A Portuguese conquest attempt in 1569 to 1572 failed. Sotho-Tswana and Nguni-speaking communities expanded on the highveld and in the east.

The Dutch East India Company founded Cape Town in 1652 as a supply station, soon granting land to settlers and importing enslaved people from Asia and Africa. Khoekhoe herders lost land and cattle in wars. On the plateau, the Rozvi under Changamire drove out the Portuguese in the 1690s.

Dutch settlers, called trekboers, pushed inland from the Cape with their herds, displacing Khoekhoe and San. A smallpox epidemic in 1713 devastated Khoekhoe communities. The Rozvi state ruled the Zimbabwe plateau, while Sotho-Tswana towns and Nguni chiefdoms grew in the interior.

Trekboer expansion reached the Fish River, leading to the first of many frontier wars with the Xhosa in 1779. Britain seized the Cape from the Dutch in 1795. In the east, Nguni chiefdoms such as the Mthethwa and Ndwandwe grew more powerful as competition for land intensified.

Britain took permanent control of the Cape in 1806 and brought British settlers in 1820. Shaka built the Zulu Kingdom from 1816, and wars and migrations known as the Mfecane spread across the region. Mzilikazi's Ndebele moved north, and Moshoeshoe founded the Basotho nation at Thaba Bosiu.

Britain abolished slavery in the Cape in 1834, and many Boers, resenting British rule, set off on the Great Trek into the interior from 1835. They defeated the Zulu at Blood River in 1838. Britain annexed Natal in 1843, and Mzilikazi's Ndebele settled in western Zimbabwe.

Britain recognized the Boer republics of the Transvaal and the Orange Free State in 1852 and 1854. The Xhosa cattle-killing of 1856 to 1857 brought famine. Basutoland became a British protectorate in 1868, and the discovery of diamonds near Kimberley in 1867 began an industrial revolution.

The Zulu defeated the British at Isandlwana in 1879 but lost the Anglo-Zulu War. Gold was found on the Witwatersrand in 1886, creating Johannesburg. Cecil Rhodes' company colonized Rhodesia, crushing Ndebele and Shona risings in 1896 to 1897, and the Boer War began in 1899.

Britain won the Boer War in 1902 after burning farms and confining Boer and African civilians in deadly camps. In German South West Africa, Germany committed genocide against the Herero and Nama from 1904 to 1908. Gandhi led Indian resistance in South Africa, and the Bambatha rebellion was crushed in 1906.

The Union of South Africa was formed in 1910 under white minority rule, and the African National Congress was founded in 1912 to resist. The 1913 Natives Land Act limited African land ownership to small reserves. During the First World War, South African forces seized German South West Africa.

White miners' Rand Revolt of 1922 was crushed by force. South Africa ruled South West Africa as a League mandate, and Southern Rhodesia became a self-governing settler colony in 1923. Hertzog's government favored white workers, while the ICU union drew mass support from African workers.

The Great Depression hit hard, and Hertzog and Smuts merged their parties in 1934. In 1936 laws removed African voters from the Cape rolls and fixed African reserves at a fraction of the land. In Northern Rhodesia, the Copperbelt mining boom drew African workers, who struck in 1935.

South Africa fought with the Allies in the Second World War, and its industry boomed. Young activists including Mandela formed the ANC Youth League in 1944, and African mineworkers struck in 1946. In 1948 the National Party won power and began making apartheid the law.

Apartheid laws classified everyone by race, segregated cities and created separate ethnic 'homelands'. The ANC's Defiance Campaign of 1952 and the 1955 Freedom Charter mobilized resistance, met by the Treason Trial. Britain created the Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland in 1953.

Police killed 69 protesters at Sharpeville in 1960, and the ANC turned to armed struggle; Mandela was sentenced to life in 1964. South Africa became a republic in 1961. Zambia, Malawi, Botswana and Lesotho gained independence, while Rhodesia's white government declared independence in 1965.

Student protests in Soweto in 1976 were met with deadly force, and Black Consciousness leader Steve Biko died in police custody in 1977. Mozambique and Angola won independence in 1975, and guerrilla war intensified in Rhodesia, while South Africa declared some homelands 'independent'.

Zimbabwe became independent in 1980 under Robert Mugabe, whose forces later massacred thousands in Matabeleland. In South Africa, township uprisings and states of emergency met growing international sanctions. South Africa backed wars in Mozambique and Angola, and F. W. de Klerk became president in 1989.

De Klerk freed Mandela in 1990 and unbanned the ANC, and Namibia gained independence that year. After tense negotiations, South Africa's first multiracial elections in 1994 made Mandela president. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission examined apartheid's crimes, and Mozambique's civil war ended in 1992.

Thabo Mbeki led South Africa, but his denial of AIDS science worsened a devastating epidemic. In Zimbabwe, land seizures from 2000 and political repression led to economic collapse and hyperinflation by 2008. South Africa's economy grew, and Jacob Zuma became president in 2009.

South Africa hosted the 2010 World Cup, but police killed 34 striking miners at Marikana in 2012. Mandela died in 2013. Corruption scandals forced Zuma to resign in 2018, and power shortages hit the economy. In Zimbabwe, the army forced Mugabe out in 2017.

Southern Africa was hit by COVID-19 and deadly unrest in South Africa in 2021. In 2024 the ANC lost its majority for the first time and formed a coalition government, and Botswana's long-ruling party was voted out. An Islamist insurgency troubled northern Mozambique.
Central Asia / Steppe: The steppe and oases were home to hunter-gatherers and, increasingly, herders and farmers. Farming villages like Jeitun appeared in Turkmenistan c. 6000 BC, while the Botai people of northern Kazakhstan were herding, riding and milking horses by c. 3500 BC, a change that would transform steppe life for millennia.

Yamnaya herders on the Pontic-Caspian steppe, living in wagons and burying leaders under kurgan mounds, spread far east and west, probably carrying Indo-European languages. Related Afanasievo herders reached the Altai, and in the southern oases the Oxus civilization (BMAC) built fortified towns with bronze metalwork c. 2300 BC.

Around 2000 BC the Sintashta people of the southern Urals built fortified settlements and the first spoked-wheel chariots. The related Andronovo culture spread herding, bronze and horse warfare across the steppe, and Indo-Iranian speakers moved south toward Iran and India as the Oxus oasis towns declined.

True mounted nomadism took hold as riders with bows and mobile herds replaced wagon-based life. Scythians, Saka and Cimmerians dominated the grasslands, burying chiefs in rich kurgans such as Arzhan in Tuva and creating gold animal-style art, while some raided deep into the Near East in the 600s BC.

Persia's Achaemenid kings conquered the southern oases, turning Bactria, Sogdiana and Chorasmia into tribute-paying provinces. Cyrus the Great reportedly died fighting the nomadic Massagetae c. 530 BC, and beyond the Persian frontier Saka and Scythian horse peoples remained independent, trading and raiding across the grasslands.

The Achaemenid satrapies of Bactria and Sogdiana supplied Persia with soldiers, lapis lazuli and gold. On the steppe, Scythians north of the Black Sea traded with Greek colonies and were described by Herodotus, while the Pazyryk people of the Altai left frozen tombs preserving tattooed bodies, carpets and horses.

Alexander the Great fought a hard campaign in Bactria and Sogdiana in 329 to 327 BC, facing local resistance under Spitamenes and marrying the Bactrian noblewoman Roxana. After his death the Seleucids inherited the region, while on the western steppe the Sarmatians began displacing the Scythians.

Greek settlers in Bactria broke from the Seleucids c. 250 BC to form the Greco-Bactrian kingdom, and the Parthians rose to the west. In Mongolia Modu Chanyu forged the Xiongnu confederation in 209 BC, crushing rivals like the Yuezhi and forcing the new Han dynasty to pay tribute.

Driven west by the Xiongnu, the Yuezhi and Saka overran Greco-Bactria c. 130 BC. Han China fought back: Zhang Qian's missions of 138 to 126 BC mapped the western lands, Han armies pushed into the Tarim Basin and Ferghana for horses, and the trade routes later called the Silk Road began to take shape.

The Xiongnu weakened and split, and one faction under Huhanye submitted to Han China in 51 BC. Han established a Protectorate of the Western Regions over the Tarim oasis cities c. 60 BC, while the Yuezhi settled in Bactria in five clans and Parthia controlled the routes to the west.

One Yuezhi clan under Kujula Kadphises united the others c. AD 30 to found the Kushan Empire, which grew from Bactria into northern India. The Xiongnu split permanently in AD 48, and the Han general Ban Chao reasserted Chinese control over the Tarim oases, securing the Silk Road.

The Kushan Empire peaked under Kanishka (c. 127 to 150), a patron of Buddhism whose lands linked Rome, Parthia, India and China. Buddhist monks and Sogdian merchants carried ideas and goods along the Silk Road, while the Xianbei replaced the Xiongnu as masters of the Mongolian steppe.

Kushan power faded as Sasanian Persia seized its western lands c. 230s and set up Kushano-Sasanian rulers in Bactria. The Xianbei confederation fractured after its great leader's death, and Sogdian merchant families from Samarkand and Bukhara became the main middlemen of the Silk Road trade.

Peoples from the eastern steppe pressed in every direction. The Huns appeared north of the Caspian and in the 370s crossed the Volga, defeating the Alans and Goths and setting off migrations into the Roman world. Chionites and Kidarites took Bactria, and Xianbei and other nomads ruled much of northern China.

The Rouran Khaganate dominated Mongolia, while the Hephthalites, or White Huns, built an empire over Bactria and parts of the Tarim, defeating and killing the Sasanian king Peroz in 484. Far to the west, Attila's Huns terrorized Europe until his death in 453.

In 552 the Turks under Bumin overthrew their Rouran overlords and founded the Göktürk Khaganate, the first empire to carry the Turkic name, stretching from Manchuria to the Black Sea. Allied with Persia they destroyed the Hephthalites c. 560, though the empire soon split into eastern and western halves.

Tang China defeated the Eastern Turks in 630 and the Western Turks by 657, ruling the Tarim oases through protectorates. Meanwhile Arab armies conquered Persia and reached Khorasan by the 650s. The pilgrim Xuanzang crossed the region, and in 682 the Turks revived their khaganate in Mongolia.

Arab armies under Qutayba conquered Bukhara and Samarkand in 705 to 715, and in 751 the Abbasids defeated Tang forces at Talas, helping Islam spread through Central Asia. The Turks carved the Orkhon inscriptions, then were overthrown in 744 by the Uyghurs, who rescued the Tang during the An Lushan Rebellion.

The Kyrgyz destroyed the Uyghur Khaganate in 840, and Uyghurs resettled in the Turfan and Gansu oases, becoming farmers and traders. In Bukhara the Persian Samanid dynasty built a brilliant Islamic state, while the Khazars and Pechenegs dominated the western steppe north of the Caspian and Black Seas.

Samanid Bukhara flourished as a center of Persian poetry and Islamic learning, but the Turkic Kara-Khanids, who converted to Islam c. 934, took Bukhara in 999. Turkic Ghaznavids rose in Afghanistan, the Khitan built the Liao empire to the east, and the Rus' destroyed the Khazar state in the 960s.

Oghuz Turks led by the Seljuk family moved out of the Aral region, defeated the Ghaznavids at Dandanaqan in 1040 and conquered Persia. The Kara-Khanids ruled the oases, Kipchak and Cuman nomads dominated the western steppe, and scholars like Ibn Sina and al-Biruni made the region a center of science.

Khitan refugees founded the Qara Khitai state and crushed the Seljuks at Qatwan in 1141. Late in the century the Khwarezmian shahs built a large but brittle empire, while in Mongolia rival tribes such as the Tatars, Keraites, Naimans and Mongols fought each other. Temüjin was born c. 1162.

In 1206 Temüjin united the Mongol tribes as Genghis Khan, then destroyed the Khwarezmian Empire in 1219 to 1221 with enormous slaughter. His successors built the largest land empire in history, which split after 1260 into the Golden Horde, Chagatai Khanate, Ilkhanate and Yuan, while trade flowed under the Pax Mongolica.

The Golden Horde converted to Islam under Uzbeg Khan, the Chagatai Khanate broke apart, and plague probably spread along steppe routes. From 1370 to 1405 Timur, a Turkic-Mongol emir based in Samarkand, conquered Persia, crushed the Golden Horde and sacked Delhi and Damascus, building a short-lived empire.

Timur's heirs presided over a cultural flowering, with Shah Rukh at Herat and the astronomer-prince Ulugh Beg building his observatory at Samarkand in the 1420s. The Golden Horde broke into rival khanates, the Oirats captured a Ming emperor in 1449, and the Kazakh Khanate emerged c. 1465.

Shaybanid Uzbeks seized Samarkand in 1500, driving the Timurid Babur toward India, and founded the Khanate of Bukhara. Russia took Kazan in 1552 and Astrakhan in 1556 and began crossing into Siberia. As European sea routes grew, overland caravan trade became less central, and Tibetan Buddhism spread among Mongols.

The Oirat Mongols formed the powerful Dzungar Khanate in western Mongolia and Xinjiang, while one Oirat group, the Kalmyks, migrated to the Volga. Russian traders and Cossacks swept across Siberia to the Pacific, and the Manchu Qing absorbed the southern Mongols and fought the Dzungar leader Galdan, defeating him in 1696.

Dzungar attacks on the Kazakhs in 1723 began the 'Years of Great Disaster', and in 1731 the Kazakh Junior Horde sought Russian protection. Russia built fortress lines like Orenburg, while the khanates of Bukhara and Khiva weakened and were briefly overrun by the Persian conqueror Nader Shah in 1740.

Exploiting a Dzungar succession crisis, the Qing conquered Dzungaria in 1755 to 1758, and war, smallpox and massacre nearly wiped out the Dzungar people. The Qing then took the Tarim oases, forming Xinjiang. The Kalmyks' 1771 flight from Russia ended in disaster, and Bukhara and Kokand gained new dynasties.

Central Asia's oases were ruled by three Uzbek khanates, Bukhara, Khiva and the expanding Kokand, while the Qing held Xinjiang. Russia tightened its grip on the Kazakh steppe, abolishing the Middle Horde's khan in 1822, and Afghanistan's Durrani kingdom slid into civil war among rival princes.

Britain and Russia began the 'Great Game' for influence. Britain invaded Afghanistan in 1839 but its army was destroyed retreating from Kabul in 1842, while a Russian winter march on Khiva failed. Kenesary Kasymov led a Kazakh revolt against Russia, and Bukhara executed two British officers in 1842.

Russia conquered the heart of Central Asia, taking Tashkent in 1865, Samarkand in 1868 and Khiva in 1873, and made Bukhara a protectorate. The new province of Turkestan was turned toward cotton growing. In Xinjiang a great Muslim revolt allowed Yakub Beg to rule Kashgar from 1865.

Russia annexed Kokand in 1876 and crushed the Turkmen at Geok Tepe in 1881, then built the Trans-Caspian Railway. Britain fought a second Afghan war in 1878 to 1880, and the Durand Line and Pamir agreements fixed Afghan borders. The Qing reconquered Xinjiang, making it a province in 1884.

The Anglo-Russian Convention of 1907 eased the Great Game by fixing spheres of influence. The Orenburg to Tashkent railway opened in 1906, tying the region to Russia, and Russian peasant settlers took Kazakh pastures. Muslim reformers called Jadids pushed for modern schools and new ideas.

Mongolia broke from the collapsing Qing in 1911. In 1916 a revolt against Russian labor conscription was savagely crushed, sending many Kazakhs and Kyrgyz fleeing to China. After 1917 the Bolsheviks destroyed the Kokand autonomy and fought Basmachi rebels, and Afghanistan won full independence in 1919.

The Soviets abolished the old khanates and in 1924 drew new national republics such as the Uzbek and Turkmen SSRs. Mongolia became the world's second communist state. Soviet campaigns attacked Islam and the veil, and in Afghanistan King Amanullah's rapid reforms provoked a revolt that toppled him in 1929.

Stalin's collectivization forced Kazakh nomads onto collective farms, and the resulting famine of 1930 to 1933 killed about 1.5 million people, a huge share of the population. The purges of 1937 to 1938 destroyed local elites. In 1939 Soviet and Mongolian forces defeated Japan at Khalkhin Gol.

During World War II whole factories and deported peoples, including Chechens, Volga Germans and Crimean Tatars, were sent to Central Asia. A Soviet-backed East Turkestan Republic existed in northern Xinjiang until the Chinese Communists took the region in 1949, the year the Soviets tested their first atomic bomb at Semipalatinsk.

Khrushchev's Virgin Lands campaign ploughed up vast areas of the Kazakh steppe for wheat and brought in Slavic settlers. The Baikonur Cosmodrome opened, launching Sputnik in 1957. China created the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region in 1955 and sent Han settlers, while Afghanistan accepted Soviet aid.

Soviet planners diverted the Amu Darya and Syr Darya rivers to grow cotton, and the Aral Sea began to shrink. Yuri Gagarin launched from Baikonur in 1961, Tashkent was rebuilt after a 1966 earthquake, and the Sino-Soviet split brought armed border clashes in 1969, including along Xinjiang.

Under Brezhnev, Uzbekistan became a vast cotton monoculture run by entrenched local party bosses. In Afghanistan the monarchy fell in 1973, a communist coup followed in 1978, and in December 1979 the Soviet army invaded, beginning a war that would last ten years.

The Soviet-Afghan War killed perhaps a million or more Afghans and drove millions into exile, while mujahideen received US, Pakistani and Saudi support. Soviet troops withdrew in 1989. Gorbachev's reforms exposed the Uzbek cotton scandal and the Aral disaster, and protests erupted in Almaty in 1986.

When the USSR collapsed in 1991, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Turkmenistan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan became independent, mostly led by former Communist bosses. Tajikistan suffered a civil war from 1992 to 1997, Mongolia became a democracy, and in Afghanistan the Taliban seized Kabul in 1996 after years of civil war.

After 9/11 the US invaded Afghanistan in 2001, toppling the Taliban and opening bases in Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan. Oil and gas wealth transformed Kazakhstan and Turkmenistan, China and Russia formed the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, and protests brought violence in Andijan and a revolution in Kyrgyzstan in 2005.

China launched its Belt and Road Initiative in Kazakhstan in 2013, pouring money into railways and pipelines, and from c. 2017 detained large numbers of Uyghurs in Xinjiang camps. Uzbekistan opened up after Karimov's death in 2016, Nazarbayev stepped down in 2019, and NATO's Afghan combat mission ended in 2014.

The US withdrew from Afghanistan in 2021 and the Taliban returned, sharply restricting women's lives. Kazakhstan saw deadly unrest in 2022, and Russia's invasion of Ukraine pushed the region to diversify trade and routes. Rivalry among Russia, China, Turkey and the West for influence intensified.
India: South Asia had been home to hunter-gatherers for tens of thousands of years, who left paintings at sites like Bhimbetka. At Mehrgarh, c. 7000 BC, people began farming wheat and barley and herding cattle, and by the 4000s BC farming villages had spread across the Indus plains.

The Indus Valley civilization flourished c. 2600 to 1900 BC in planned cities like Harappa, Mohenjo-daro and Dholavira, with brick houses, drains and standard weights. Its people used a still-undeciphered script and traded with Mesopotamia, while farming villages spread elsewhere in the subcontinent.

The Indus cities declined c. 1900 BC as rivers shifted and the climate dried, and people moved into smaller villages. From c. 1500 BC Indo-Aryan speaking herders settled the Punjab, composing the Rigveda, and the Vedic age began, with cattle wealth, fire sacrifices and warrior chiefs.

Vedic peoples moved east into the Ganges plain, clearing forest with iron tools and growing rice. Kingdoms like the Kurus and Panchalas emerged, the varna social order hardened, and the early Upanishads explored ideas of soul and rebirth. By c. 600 BC sixteen large states had formed.

The sixteen states competed for power, and Magadha rose under King Bimbisara. Towns and coinage grew, and new teachers challenged Vedic ritual: Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha, and Mahavira of the Jains taught in Magadha. In c. 518 BC Persia's Darius took the Indus region as a province.

Magadha expanded under Ajatashatru, defeating the Vajji confederacy and Kosala and building a fort at Pataliputra that became its capital. Buddhist and Jain communities spread after their founders' deaths, and the grammarian Panini (c. 5th or 4th century BC) codified Sanskrit. Persia still ruled the northwest.

The Nanda kings made Magadha rich and feared. Alexander the Great reached the Indus in 326 BC and defeated King Porus, but his army refused to go farther. In 322 BC Chandragupta Maurya, advised by Chanakya, overthrew the Nandas and founded the Maurya Empire, later taking the northwest from Seleucus.

The Maurya Empire reached its peak under Ashoka. After his bloody Kalinga War c. 261 BC he embraced Buddhism and dhamma, carving edicts on rocks and pillars and sending missions to Sri Lanka and beyond. After his death c. 232 BC the empire weakened, while Tamil kingdoms ruled the far south.

The last Maurya was killed c. 185 BC by his general Pushyamitra, founder of the Shunga dynasty. Indo-Greek kings such as Menander ruled the northwest, the Satavahanas rose in the Deccan, and Buddhist sites like Sanchi and Bharhut were richly decorated. Saka nomads began arriving from Central Asia.

India was divided among many powers. Saka (Indo-Scythian) kings ruled the northwest, the Kanvas replaced the Shungas in Magadha, and the Satavahanas controlled the Deccan. In the Tamil south the Chera, Chola and Pandya kingdoms flourished, and sea trade with the Roman world began to grow.

Indo-Parthian kings such as Gondophares ruled the northwest, and Kushan rulers from Bactria expanded into northern India. Roman ships using the monsoon winds bought pepper, gems and textiles at ports like Muziris, paying in gold. Tamil Sangam poetry celebrated the kings and life of the south.

Under Kanishka the Kushans ruled from Peshawar and Mathura, sponsoring Buddhism as Mahayana ideas spread. Gandhara and Mathura artists made some of the first images of the Buddha. In the Deccan the Satavahanas revived, and around 150 the Saka ruler Rudradaman left an early long Sanskrit inscription.

The Kushan and Satavahana empires declined, and India broke into regional kingdoms. Sasanian Persia took the old Kushan northwest, Western Satraps ruled Gujarat, and the Vakatakas rose in the Deccan. Hindu traditions centered on Vishnu and Shiva developed further in texts like the Puranas.

In 320 Chandragupta I founded the Gupta Empire in the Ganges valley. His son Samudragupta won wide conquests, and Chandragupta II defeated the Western Satraps, controlling trade to the west. Gupta courts patronized Sanskrit literature, including the poet Kalidasa, and the Pallavas rose in the south.

The Gupta golden age continued, with Nalanda founded as a great center of learning and the Chinese pilgrim Faxian praising the realm. In 499 Aryabhata wrote on astronomy and place-value mathematics. In the late 400s Huna invaders from Central Asia attacked the northwest, straining Gupta power.

The Gupta Empire collapsed as Huna kings like Mihirakula ruled the northwest until they were pushed back c. 528. Northern India fragmented among regional dynasties, the Chalukyas rose at Badami in the Deccan, and the astronomer Varahamihira worked. In the Tamil south devotional bhakti poetry began to spread.

Harsha of Kanauj (606 to 647) united much of the north, and the Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang studied at Nalanda. The Chalukya king Pulakeshin II stopped Harsha in the Deccan and fought the Pallavas, who built the shore monuments at Mahabalipuram. Brahmagupta set out rules for zero in 628.

In 711 to 712 Arab forces under Muhammad bin Qasim conquered Sindh, bringing Islam to the subcontinent. Three powers, the Gurjara-Pratiharas, the Buddhist Palas of Bengal and the Rashtrakutas of the Deccan, fought over Kanauj. The Kailasa temple at Ellora was carved, and Adi Shankara taught Advaita philosophy.

The three-way struggle for Kanauj continued, with the Pratiharas dominant in the north under Mihira Bhoja. The Palas supported Buddhist universities at Nalanda and Vikramashila, the Rashtrakutas were among the strongest Deccan powers, and the Chola dynasty revived c. 850 around Thanjavur in the Tamil south.

The Pratiharas declined after Rashtrakuta raids, and the north splintered into Rajput kingdoms such as the Chandelas, who later built Khajuraho. The Rashtrakutas fell in 973, and the Cholas grew powerful under Rajaraja I from 985. Late in the century Turkic Ghaznavid raiders appeared in the northwest.

Mahmud of Ghazni raided northern India repeatedly from 1000 to 1027, looting temples like Somnath, and the Ghaznavids annexed the Punjab. In the south the Chola Empire peaked: Rajaraja built the great temple at Thanjavur and Rajendra I's navy raided Srivijaya in 1025. Al-Biruni wrote a famous study of India.

Rajput kingdoms, among them Prithviraj Chauhan's, dominated the north while the Cholas slowly weakened. Muhammad of Ghor invaded, losing at Tarain in 1191 but winning in 1192 and taking Delhi. Turkic forces swept into Bengal, and Nalanda was sacked c. 1193, a heavy blow to Buddhism in India.

In 1206 the Turkic general Qutb ud-Din Aibak founded the Delhi Sultanate, building the Qutb Minar. Sultans like Iltutmish, Razia, India's first Muslim woman ruler, and Balban held off Mongol raids, while Persian became the court language. The south was ruled by Pandyas, Hoysalas and Kakatiyas.

Alauddin Khalji repelled the Mongols and raided the far south, and Muhammad bin Tughluq experimented with token coins and moving his capital. Southern rebels founded the Vijayanagara Empire in 1336 and the Bahmani Sultanate in 1347. In 1398 Timur sacked Delhi, shattering the sultanate's power.

After Timur, Delhi's Sayyid and Lodi sultans ruled a shrunken realm, while Bengal, Gujarat and Malwa became independent sultanates. Vijayanagara grew rich in the south, and the Bahmani state split into Deccan sultanates. Kabir and Guru Nanak preached devotion beyond caste, and in 1498 Vasco da Gama reached Calicut.

The Portuguese seized Goa in 1510. In 1526 Babur, a Timurid prince from Central Asia, won at Panipat and founded the Mughal Empire. Akbar the Great (1556 to 1605) conquered most of the north, built an efficient administration and practiced religious tolerance, while Vijayanagara fell in 1565.

The Mughals were at their richest under Jahangir and Shah Jahan, who built the Taj Mahal, and largest under Aurangzeb. European trading companies set up posts, with the English East India Company founded in 1600. Indian cotton textiles were in demand worldwide, and Shivaji founded the Maratha kingdom in 1674.

After Aurangzeb died in 1707, Mughal power crumbled as governors in Hyderabad, Bengal and Awadh became virtually independent. The Marathas expanded across central India under their Peshwas, and in 1739 the Persian ruler Nader Shah sacked Delhi and carried off the Peacock Throne. British-French rivalry grew.

The East India Company's victory at Plassey in 1757 gave it Bengal, and by 1765 it collected the province's taxes. The Afghans defeated the Marathas at Panipat in 1761, a famine devastated Bengal in 1770, and the Company fought Mysore, killing Tipu Sultan in 1799.

The British defeated the Marathas in 1803 to 1818, making the Company the dominant power in India while many princes ruled under its protection. Ranjit Singh built a strong Sikh kingdom in the Punjab. Missionaries were allowed in from 1813, and reformers like Ram Mohan Roy debated Hindu custom.

Company rule brought reforms and intrusions: sati was banned in 1829 and English-language education promoted from 1835. British machine-made cloth undercut Indian weavers. After Ranjit Singh's death, the British fought two wars with the Sikhs and annexed the Punjab in 1849, and launched a disastrous war in Afghanistan.

Railways and telegraphs spread from 1853, while annexations of princely states fed resentment. The great Indian Rebellion of 1857 was crushed with heavy reprisals, and in 1858 the British Crown replaced the Company, beginning the British Raj. Universities opened, and a cotton boom followed the American Civil War.

Queen Victoria was proclaimed Empress of India in 1877 even as the Great Famine of 1876 to 1878 killed millions. Educated Indians founded the Indian National Congress in 1885, while reform movements like the Arya Samaj and Sayyid Ahmad Khan's Aligarh college reshaped Hindu and Muslim life.

Viceroy Curzon partitioned Bengal in 1905, sparking the Swadeshi movement to boycott British goods. The Muslim League was founded in 1906, Congress split between moderates and radicals like Tilak, and the 1909 reforms gave Indians limited seats with separate Muslim electorates.

The capital moved to Delhi in 1911 and over a million Indians served in World War I. Gandhi returned from South Africa in 1915 and began peaceful protests. In 1919 British troops killed hundreds at Amritsar, while the influenza pandemic killed millions, turning many against British rule.

Gandhi led the mass Non-Cooperation Movement of 1920 to 1922, joined with Muslim Khilafat activists, before calling it off after violence. Protests met the all-white Simon Commission in 1928, revolutionaries like Bhagat Singh emerged, and in 1929 Congress demanded full independence.

Gandhi's Salt March in 1930 launched civil disobedience, and talks in London followed. The 1935 Government of India Act widened self-rule, and Congress won provincial elections in 1937, while Jinnah's Muslim League grew. In 1939 Britain declared war for India without consulting Indian leaders.

The Muslim League called for Pakistan in 1940, Congress launched Quit India in 1942, and the Bengal famine of 1943 killed about 3 million. In 1947 India gained independence and was partitioned into India and Pakistan amid mass migration and killing. Gandhi was assassinated in 1948.

India became a republic under its new constitution in 1950, and its first general election in 1951 to 1952 was the largest democratic vote ever held. Prime Minister Nehru pursued state-led industry, non-alignment and secular democracy, and states were redrawn along language lines in 1956. Pakistan saw its first coup in 1958.

India took Goa from Portugal in 1961 but lost a border war with China in 1962. Nehru died in 1964, India and Pakistan fought in 1965, and Indira Gandhi became prime minister in 1966. New high-yield seeds launched the Green Revolution, ending fears of mass famine.

In 1971 India intervened in East Pakistan's war of independence, defeating Pakistan and helping create Bangladesh. India tested a nuclear device in 1974. Indira Gandhi's Emergency of 1975 to 1977 suspended civil liberties, and voters ousted her in 1977, though she returned in 1980.

Indira Gandhi ordered troops into the Golden Temple in 1984 and was assassinated by her Sikh bodyguards, followed by anti-Sikh massacres. The Bhopal gas leak killed thousands that year. Her son Rajiv promoted technology, and an insurgency broke out in Kashmir in 1989.

Rajiv Gandhi was assassinated in 1991, and that year's economic crisis led to liberalization that opened India to trade and investment. The Babri Masjid's destruction in 1992 brought deadly riots and the rise of Hindu nationalist politics. India and Pakistan both tested nuclear weapons in 1998.

India's economy grew rapidly, driven by IT services and outsourcing, and a new middle class expanded. Deadly riots struck Gujarat in 2002, the Indian Ocean tsunami hit in 2004, and Manmohan Singh led a Congress coalition. The 2008 Mumbai terror attacks killed 166 people.

Cheap smartphones and data connected hundreds of millions of Indians. Narendra Modi's BJP won a majority in 2014, introducing a national biometric ID, demonetization in 2016 and a national sales tax. In 2019 the government ended Kashmir's special status and a citizenship law sparked mass protests.

Covid-19 brought a harsh lockdown in 2020 and a deadly wave in 2021, and Indian and Chinese troops clashed in the Himalayas. In 2023 India became the world's most populous country and Chandrayaan-3 landed near the Moon's south pole. Modi won a third term in 2024.
China: Early humans lived in China for hundreds of thousands of years. From c. 7000 BC people farmed rice along the Yangtze and millet along the Yellow River, building Neolithic villages. Cultures such as Yangshao, with painted pottery, Hemudu and Hongshan, with carved jades, flourished by c. 5000 to 3000 BC.

Neolithic societies grew more complex, with walled towns, elite burials and fine jades. The Liangzhu culture near the Yangtze built large water works, and the Longshan culture made thin black pottery. Later Chinese tradition placed the legendary Yellow Emperor and Xia dynasty in this age, and bronze-working appeared at its end.

The Erlitou culture, possibly the Xia, built palaces c. 1900 BC. The Shang dynasty (c. 1600 to 1046 BC) ruled the Yellow River plain with bronze vessels, chariots, human sacrifice and oracle-bone writing, the ancestor of Chinese script. In 1046 BC the Zhou conquered the Shang, claiming the Mandate of Heaven.

Zhou kings granted lands to relatives and allies who ruled them as lords. In 771 BC invaders sacked the western capital, and the court moved east to Luoyang, beginning the Spring and Autumn period. The kings lost real power as states like Qi and Jin led coalitions, and iron began to appear.

The Zhou kings were figureheads while states like Jin, Chu, Qi, Wu and Yue fought for supremacy. Amid the turmoil Confucius (551 to 479 BC) taught that good government came from virtue and ritual, and tradition credits Laozi with founding Daoism. Iron tools and written law codes spread.

The Warring States period began c. 475 BC, and the great state of Jin split into Han, Zhao and Wei. Rulers built large infantry armies with crossbows and centralized bureaucracies. The 'Hundred Schools of Thought' flourished, including Mozi's ideas of universal love.

War grew larger and more ruthless. Shang Yang's Legalist reforms from 356 BC made Qin a disciplined military state, Zhao adopted nomad-style cavalry, and states built walls against rivals and steppe raiders. Thinkers such as Mencius and Zhuangzi debated human nature and the good life.

Qin conquered its rivals, and in 221 BC its king became Qin Shi Huang, the First Emperor. He standardized script, coins and weights, linked walls into a Great Wall and was buried with the Terracotta Army. Harsh rule sparked revolts after his death, and Liu Bang founded the Han dynasty in 206 to 202 BC.

The Han consolidated imperial rule after crushing a rebellion of princes in 154 BC. Emperor Wu (141 to 87 BC) made Confucianism the state ideology, set up salt and iron monopolies, fought the Xiongnu and expanded into Korea, Vietnam and Central Asia as the Silk Road opened. Sima Qian wrote his great history.

Han China was at its height, with a large bureaucracy and growing trade. The Xiongnu submitted in 51 BC, and a protectorate oversaw the western oases. But wealthy landed families grew powerful and court politics fell under the influence of empresses' clans, paving the way for the usurper Wang Mang.

A census in AD 2 counted nearly 60 million people. Wang Mang seized the throne in AD 9 and attempted radical reforms, but floods and the Red Eyebrows revolt destroyed him. The Han was restored in 25 with its capital at Luoyang, Buddhism arrived from Central Asia, and Ban Chao secured the Tarim Basin.

The Eastern Han produced inventions like improved paper, traditionally credited to Cai Lun in 105, and Zhang Heng's seismoscope. But eunuchs and consort clans fought over a weak court, landlords grew stronger, and the Yellow Turban Rebellion of 184 opened the way for warlords to tear the empire apart.

The Han dynasty ended in 220, and China split into the Three Kingdoms of Wei, Shu and Wu, an age later romanticized in literature. Decades of war cut the registered population sharply. In 280 the Jin dynasty briefly reunified China, and Buddhism continued to spread.

Civil war among Jin princes opened the north to non-Chinese peoples such as the Xiongnu and Xianbei, who sacked Luoyang in 311. The north fractured into the Sixteen Kingdoms, while the Eastern Jin ruled the south from Jiankang (Nanjing) and many northerners fled south. Buddhism grew strongly.

The Xianbei-led Northern Wei united north China in 439, carved Buddhist cave temples at Yungang, and adopted Chinese ways under Emperor Xiaowen, who moved the capital to Luoyang. In the south a series of short-lived dynasties ruled. This era is called the Northern and Southern Dynasties.

Northern Wei split in 534, and the south's Liang dynasty became a great patron of Buddhism before civil war wrecked it. In 581 Yang Jian founded the Sui dynasty, and in 589 he conquered the south, reunifying China after nearly three centuries of division.

The Sui built the Grand Canal (605 to 611) linking north and south but collapsed after costly wars in Korea. The Tang dynasty, founded in 618, made Chang'an a cosmopolitan capital, defeated the Turks and expanded into Central Asia. Wu Zetian ruled as China's only empress regnant from 690 to 705.

Under Emperor Xuanzong the Tang reached a cultural high point, with poets like Li Bai and Du Fu. Defeat at Talas in 751 and the An Lushan Rebellion of 755 to 763 devastated the empire, and afterward regional military governors grew powerful while the court survived in a weaker form.

The late Tang struggled with eunuch power and regional governors. In 845 the court persecuted Buddhism, closing thousands of monasteries. The Diamond Sutra of 868 is the oldest dated printed book, and the Huang Chao Rebellion of 874 to 884 sacked major cities and ruined the dynasty.

The Tang fell in 907, and China split into the Five Dynasties in the north and Ten Kingdoms in the south. The Khitan Liao empire took lands near Beijing. In 960 the general Zhao Kuangyin founded the Song dynasty, which reunified most of China and placed civilian officials above generals.

The Song saw an economic revolution: paper money, movable type, the magnetic compass and gunpowder weapons all appeared, rice farming expanded and cities boomed as population passed about 100 million. But the Song paid tribute to the Liao and Tangut Xi Xia, and Wang Anshi's reforms divided the court.

The Jurchen Jin destroyed the Liao and captured the Song capital Kaifeng in 1127. The Song survived in the south as the Southern Song, based at Hangzhou, prospering through trade and sea commerce. Zhu Xi shaped Neo-Confucianism, which would guide Chinese thought for centuries.

The Mongols destroyed Xi Xia, conquered the Jin in 1234 and finally the Southern Song in 1279. Kublai Khan founded the Yuan dynasty in 1271 with his capital at Dadu, today's Beijing. Mongols and Central Asians held top posts, while visitors like Marco Polo described the empire's wealth.

Yuan rule weakened amid epidemics, Yellow River floods and inflation, and the Red Turban rebellions began in 1351. Zhu Yuanzhang, a former peasant and monk, drove out the Mongols in 1368 and founded the Ming dynasty, ruling as an autocrat from Nanjing and rebuilding farming.

The Yongle Emperor moved the capital to Beijing and built the Forbidden City by 1420, and Zheng He led great fleets as far as East Africa from 1405 to 1433. After the Mongols captured an emperor in 1449, the Ming turned defensive, rebuilding the Great Wall and restricting overseas trade.

Ming China grew rich as American silver flowed in through Manila after 1571 and New World crops spread. Zhang Juzheng's reforms let taxes be paid in silver, the Portuguese settled Macau, and Jesuits like Matteo Ricci arrived. The Ming rebuilt the Great Wall in brick and aided Korea against Japan.

Famine, revolt and a weak court brought down the Ming when rebels took Beijing in 1644. The Manchus then seized the capital and founded the Qing dynasty, forcing men to wear the queue. The Kangxi Emperor crushed rebellions, took Taiwan in 1683 and fixed the Russian border in 1689.

Under the Kangxi, Yongzheng and Qianlong emperors the Qing were at peace and prosperous, and the population grew rapidly. Yongzheng reformed taxes and created the Grand Council, the Qing extended control over Tibet, and Europeans bought ever more tea and porcelain. Christianity was banned in 1724.

Qianlong conquered Dzungaria and the Tarim oases, doubling Qing territory. Foreign trade was confined to Canton from 1757, and Britain's Macartney mission of 1793 failed to win better terms. As the population neared 300 million, corruption spread and the White Lotus Rebellion broke out in 1796.

The Jiaqing Emperor suppressed the White Lotus rebels and executed the corrupt minister Heshen, but the state was strained. British merchants smuggled growing amounts of opium from India, reversing the flow of silver. Population pressure caused land shortages and environmental damage.

Opium imports soared. When commissioner Lin Zexu destroyed British opium in 1839, Britain launched the First Opium War. The 1842 Treaty of Nanjing opened five ports, ceded Hong Kong and began the 'unequal treaties' that gave foreigners special rights in China.

The Taiping Rebellion, led by a man claiming to be Jesus's brother, killed 20 to 30 million people. Britain and France won the Second Opium War, burning the Summer Palace in 1860, and Russia took the Amur lands. Empress Dowager Cixi took power, and officials began 'self-strengthening' reforms.

Cixi dominated the court as famine in north China killed millions in 1876 to 1879. China lost influence over Vietnam to France, then lost Korea and Taiwan to Japan in 1894 to 1895. Foreign powers grabbed ports in 1898, and Cixi crushed the emperor's Hundred Days' Reform.

The anti-foreign Boxer Rebellion of 1900 to 1901 was crushed by eight foreign powers, which imposed a huge indemnity. Russia and Japan fought a war on Chinese soil, the Qing abolished the ancient civil service exams in 1905, and Sun Yat-sen's revolutionaries organized. Cixi died in 1908.

The 1911 revolution ended over 2,000 years of imperial rule, and the Republic of China was founded in 1912. Yuan Shikai's attempt to become emperor failed, and warlords divided the country after his death. When Japan gained German rights in Shandong, students protested on May Fourth, 1919.

The Chinese Communist Party was founded in 1921 and joined the Nationalists to fight the warlords. In 1927 Chiang Kai-shek turned on the Communists in Shanghai, beginning civil war, and set up a Nationalist government at Nanjing. Mao Zedong organized peasants in the countryside.

Japan seized Manchuria in 1931. Chiang's forces drove the Communists on the Long March of 1934 to 1935 to Yan'an. In 1937 Japan launched full-scale invasion, committing the Nanjing Massacre, and the Nationalist government retreated to Chongqing while the Communists waged guerrilla war.

China fought Japan until 1945 at a cost of many millions of lives, including the 1942 Henan famine. Civil war resumed in 1946, and the Communists won. On 1 October 1949 Mao proclaimed the People's Republic of China, and Chiang's Nationalists fled to Taiwan.

China fought the US in the Korean War, carried out violent land reform and industrialized on the Soviet model. It took control of Tibet. After the brief Hundred Flowers openness came the Anti-Rightist purge, and Mao's Great Leap Forward from 1958 caused a famine that killed tens of millions.

China recovered slowly from the famine and broke with the Soviet Union, testing its own atomic bomb in 1964. In 1966 Mao launched the Cultural Revolution: Red Guards persecuted teachers, officials and 'class enemies', schools closed and millions were sent to the countryside.

China took the UN seat in 1971 and welcomed Nixon in 1972. In 1976 the Tangshan earthquake killed hundreds of thousands, Mao died, and the radical Gang of Four was arrested. From 1978 Deng Xiaoping launched market reforms, letting farmers sell their own crops and opening to the world.

The one-child policy began in 1980. Special economic zones like Shenzhen drew foreign investment, rural enterprises boomed and living standards rose rapidly, but inflation and corruption bred discontent. In 1989 the army crushed pro-democracy protests in Tiananmen Square.

Deng's 1992 southern tour relaunched market reforms, and coastal cities like Shanghai boomed while state firms laid off millions. Work began on the Three Gorges Dam. Britain returned Hong Kong in 1997 and Portugal returned Macau in 1999, while Taiwan held its first direct presidential election in 1996.

China joined the WTO in 2001 and became the 'workshop of the world', drawing hundreds of millions to factory cities. It sent its first astronaut into space in 2003 and hosted the Beijing Olympics in 2008, the same year an earthquake struck Sichuan and unrest flared in Tibet.

In 2010 China became the world's second-largest economy. Xi Jinping took power in 2012, launching an anti-corruption drive, the Belt and Road Initiative and island-building in the South China Sea. Controls tightened, with mass detentions in Xinjiang and, in 2019, huge protests in Hong Kong.

Covid-19 emerged in Wuhan, and China imposed strict 'zero-Covid' controls until late 2022. A 2020 security law curbed dissent in Hong Kong, and Xi won a third term in 2022. The population began to fall, a property slump slowed growth, and China led the world in electric vehicles and solar power.
Southeast Asia: Southeast Asia was home to Hoabinhian hunter-gatherers who foraged forests, rivers and coasts with stone tools. As the Ice Age ended, rising seas drowned the land bridge called Sundaland, creating today's islands and coastlines. Late in this era, the first farmers from southern China began edging toward the region.

Austronesian-speaking peoples began expanding from Taiwan c. 3000 BC, sailing outrigger canoes south toward the Philippines and carrying pottery, pigs and rice. On the mainland, Neolithic farmers from southern China settled river valleys, growing rice and millet in villages such as Ban Kao in Thailand and Phung Nguyen in Vietnam.

Austronesian seafarers spread through the Philippines, Borneo, Sulawesi and the Indonesian islands, mixing with older populations, and some pushed into the open Pacific. On the mainland, farming villages multiplied and bronze working appeared c. 1500 to 1000 BC at sites such as Ban Chiang in Thailand, slowly enriching local elites.

The Dong Son bronze culture flourished in the Red River valley of northern Vietnam, famous for great decorated bronze drums. Later Vietnamese tradition places the Van Lang kingdom of the Hung kings here. Across the region, wet-rice farming villages grew larger and chiefs gained power by controlling metal, land and trade.

Dong Son chiefdoms in northern Vietnam kept producing bronze drums that were traded far into the islands, while the Sa Huynh culture of central Vietnam buried its dead in large jars. Iron tools were beginning to spread, helping farmers clear land, and sea trade routes slowly linked the coasts together.

Iron working spread across mainland Southeast Asia, strengthening farming and warfare among chiefdoms. Sa Huynh traders exchanged distinctive jade and glass ornaments across the South China Sea with the Philippines, Borneo and Taiwan. Dong Son drums circulated across the archipelago as prized symbols of rank and wealth.

Iron Age chiefdoms ruled villages across the mainland and islands, and trade quickened. Ports on the Thai-Malay peninsula such as Khao Sam Kaeo began exchanging goods with merchants from India, an early sign of the Indian influence that would later shape religion, writing and kingship across the region.

In northern Vietnam, tradition credits An Duong Vuong with founding the kingdom of Au Lac c. 257 BC, centered on the spiral citadel of Co Loa. Late in the century, the Chinese general Zhao Tuo founded Nanyue in the south of China. In Burma, early Pyu walled towns were beginning to appear.

Nanyue absorbed Au Lac early in the century, and in 111 BC Han China conquered Nanyue and northern Vietnam, beginning about a thousand years of Chinese rule. Elsewhere, Pyu city-states grew in Burma, and maritime trade increasingly linked India, Southeast Asian ports and China.

Northern Vietnam was governed as the Han province of Jiaozhi, where Chinese officials, taxes and customs pressed on local Viet lords. Further south and west, Pyu towns, Mekong delta settlements and island chiefdoms grew rich on the sea trade carrying beads, spices and metals between India and China.

In AD 40 the Trung Sisters led a revolt against Han rule in northern Vietnam, but Chinese general Ma Yuan crushed it by 43, tightening Chinese control. In the Mekong delta, the kingdom later known as Funan began to emerge, trading with India and adopting Indian ideas about kingship.

Funan grew into the region's first great trading state, with its port of Oc Eo handling goods from India, China and even Rome. In 192 the Cham founded a kingdom on the central Vietnamese coast, later called Champa. Indian religions, Sanskrit and political ideas were steadily taking root.

Funan reached a peak under rulers such as Fan Shiman, controlling trade across the Gulf of Thailand, and Chinese envoys visited c. 245 and wrote the first detailed accounts. In northern Vietnam, Lady Trieu led a famous revolt against Chinese rule in 248. Champa and the Pyu cities continued to grow.

Funan, Champa and the Pyu cities flourished as Indian-influenced kingdoms whose rulers used Sanskrit titles and patronized Hindu and Buddhist cults. Northern Vietnam remained under Chinese dynasties. Late in the century, kings in eastern Borneo began carving Sanskrit inscriptions, the oldest known writing in the Indonesian islands.

Sanskrit inscriptions record kings at Kutai in Borneo and Tarumanagara in western Java, showing Indian-style kingship spreading through the islands. Funan and Champa remained major coastal powers, and Buddhism grew among merchants and courts. Northern Vietnam stayed a Chinese province ruled by southern Chinese dynasties.

Funan declined and the Khmer kingdom of Chenla rose in its place along the Mekong. The Mon people built the Buddhist Dvaravati culture in central Thailand. In northern Vietnam, Ly Bi briefly declared an independent state in 544, though Chinese rule returned by 602.

Srivijaya, based at Palembang in Sumatra, rose c. 670 to control the Strait of Malacca and the sea trade between India and China. It became a famous Buddhist center visited by the Chinese pilgrim Yijing. On the mainland, Khmer Chenla, Mon Dvaravati and Champa thrived, while Tang China ruled northern Vietnam as Annam.

The Buddhist Sailendra dynasty rose in central Java, rivaling Hindu kings and launching sea raids on Champa and Chenla. Chenla split into rival halves, while Srivijaya kept its grip on the straits. Late in the century, work began in Java on the vast Buddhist monument of Borobudur.

Borobudur was completed in Java c. 800, followed by the Hindu temples of Prambanan. In 802 Jayavarman II proclaimed himself universal king and founded the Khmer Empire in Cambodia. In Burma, raids from Nanzhao weakened the Pyu cities, and Bamar people settled the dry zone around Pagan.

In 938 Ngo Quyen defeated Chinese fleets at the Bach Dang River, winning Vietnam's independence after about a thousand years of Chinese rule; by 968 it was the kingdom of Dai Co Viet. The Khmer built grand temples around Angkor, and Javanese power shifted from central to eastern Java.

King Anawrahta unified Burma from Pagan and championed Theravada Buddhism. Vietnam's Ly dynasty moved the capital to Thang Long, today's Hanoi, in 1010. The Indian Chola empire raided Srivijaya in 1025, weakening it, while Airlangga rebuilt a strong kingdom in eastern Java and the Khmer expanded under Suryavarman I.

The Khmer Empire peaked as Suryavarman II built Angkor Wat c. 1113 to 1150, the world's largest religious monument. Pagan's kings filled the Burmese plain with thousands of temples. After a Cham army sacked Angkor in 1177, Jayavarman VII drove them out and began rebuilding his capital on a grand scale.

The Mongols invaded Vietnam, Burma and Java, but were largely repelled; Tran Hung Dao's victories in Vietnam became legendary, though Pagan's kingdom collapsed after 1287. Thai peoples founded Sukhothai c. 1238 as Khmer power waned. In northern Sumatra, Samudra Pasai became one of the first Muslim kingdoms in the region.

Majapahit, founded in Java in 1293, came to dominate much of the archipelago under its minister Gajah Mada. On the mainland, Thai kings founded Ayutthaya in 1351 and the Lao kingdom of Lan Xang arose in 1353, both pressing on a weakening Khmer Empire. Dai Viet fought long wars with Champa.

Malacca rose c. 1400 as the region's great port, and its rulers' conversion helped Islam spread along trade routes. Siam sacked Angkor in 1431, and the Khmer moved their capital south. Ming China briefly occupied Vietnam from 1407 to 1427 before the Le dynasty restored independence and later crushed Champa in 1471.

Portugal seized Malacca in 1511, and Magellan's fleet reached the Philippines in 1521; from 1565 Spain colonized the islands from Manila. Majapahit faded as Muslim sultanates such as Demak, Aceh and Johor rose. In Burma, the Toungoo king Bayinnaung built a huge empire and conquered Ayutthaya, which regained freedom under Naresuan.

The Dutch East India Company founded Batavia in 1619, took Malacca in 1641 and gradually seized control of the spice trade. Sultan Agung's Mataram dominated Java, while Spanish galleons linked Manila to Mexico. Vietnam was split between rival Trinh and Nguyen lords, and Ayutthaya traded and sparred with Europeans under King Narai.

The Dutch East India Company deepened its control of Java by meddling in Mataram's succession wars, and in 1740 its forces massacred Chinese residents of Batavia. The southern Nguyen lords pushed Vietnamese settlement into the Mekong delta. Ayutthaya enjoyed a prosperous last golden age, while Burma's Toungoo dynasty declined.

Burma revived under the Konbaung dynasty and sacked Ayutthaya in 1767. Taksin rallied the Siamese, and in 1782 Rama I founded the Chakri dynasty with a new capital at Bangkok. The Tay Son rebellion overturned Vietnam's ruling houses, Britain took Penang in 1786, and the bankrupt Dutch company dissolved in 1799.

In 1802 Gia Long founded the Nguyen dynasty and unified Vietnam. Britain briefly ruled Java under Raffles, then founded Singapore in 1819 as a free port. The Anglo-Dutch Treaty of 1824 divided the Malay world into British and Dutch spheres, and the First Anglo-Burmese War began that same year.

Burma lost coastal provinces to Britain in 1826, and Britain grouped Penang, Malacca and Singapore as the Straits Settlements. In Java, Prince Diponegoro's revolt of 1825 to 1830 was crushed, and the Dutch imposed the Cultivation System, forcing peasants to grow export crops. Siam and Vietnam vied for control of Cambodia.

France invaded Vietnam in 1858, took Cochinchina in 1862 and made Cambodia a protectorate in 1863. Britain annexed Lower Burma in 1852. Siam's King Mongkut signed trade treaties to keep Europeans at bay, and in 1873 the Dutch began a long, brutal war to conquer Aceh in Sumatra.

France formed French Indochina in 1887 and added Laos in 1893, while Britain conquered all of Burma by 1885. Siam stayed independent as a buffer under the reforming King Chulalongkorn.
