Filipinos rose against Spain in 1896, but in 1898 the United States took the Philippines and soon fought a bloody war there.

The Philippine-American War left the US firmly in control, and the Dutch completed their conquest of Aceh, shaping the borders of modern Indonesia. Siam ceded border lands to France and Britain to keep its independence. Rubber and tin booms reshaped colonies, and early nationalist groups such as Budi Utomo appeared in Java.

Colonial economies boomed on rubber, tin, oil and rice exports, drawing in Chinese and Indian migrants. In the Dutch East Indies, Sarekat Islam became the first mass nationalist movement. Siam joined the Allies in World War I in 1917, and Vietnamese patriots such as Phan Boi Chau sought ways to end French rule.

Nationalism and communism spread among educated young people. Communists in the Dutch East Indies rose in revolt in 1926 to 1927 and were crushed, while Sukarno founded the Indonesian Nationalist Party in 1927. Ho Chi Minh organized Vietnamese revolutionaries from abroad, and colonial powers met dissent with arrests and exile.

The Great Depression hit export economies hard, sparking unrest such as the Yen Bai mutiny and the founding of the Indochinese Communist Party in 1930. A 1932 revolution made Siam a constitutional monarchy, renamed Thailand in 1939. The Philippines became a self-governing commonwealth in 1935, and Burma was separated from British India.

Japan occupied nearly all of Southeast Asia from 1942 to 1945, toppling European colonial rule. After the war, Vietnam, Indonesia, the Philippines and Burma declared or won independence, though Indonesians fought the Dutch until 1949 and the Vietnamese began a war against France. In Malaya, a communist insurgency began in 1948.

France was defeated at Dien Bien Phu in 1954, and the Geneva conference split Vietnam into a communist north and a US-backed south; Laos and Cambodia were already independent. Malaya gained independence in 1957. Indonesia hosted the 1955 Bandung Conference of newly free nations, and Sukarno moved toward authoritarian 'Guided Democracy'.

The US fought in the Vietnam War from 1965 to 1973, bombing heavily across Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia. In Indonesia, an alleged coup attempt led to mass killings of suspected communists in 1965 to 1966 and Suharto's rise. Malaysia formed in 1963, Singapore separated in 1965, and ASEAN was founded in 1967.

Saigon fell in 1975 and Vietnam was unified under communist rule, while Laos also became communist. In Cambodia, the Khmer Rouge genocide of 1975 to 1979 killed about 1.5 to 2 million people until Vietnam invaded. Indonesia occupied East Timor, Marcos ruled the Philippines under martial law, and refugees fled by sea.

Vietnam's Doi Moi reforms of 1986 opened its economy, while its army occupied Cambodia. People Power protests toppled Marcos in the Philippines in 1986, and a 1988 uprising in Burma was crushed by the army. Singapore, Thailand and Malaysia grew rapidly, and Brunei became independent in 1984.

Cambodia's war ended with the 1991 Paris accords and UN-run elections in 1993. ASEAN expanded to include Vietnam, Laos, Myanmar and Cambodia. The 1997 Asian financial crisis devastated economies and helped topple Suharto in 1998, opening Indonesia to democracy, and East Timor voted for independence in 1999 amid violence.

Timor-Leste became independent in 2002, and Indonesia consolidated democracy, making peace in Aceh in 2005. The 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami killed about 230,000 people around the ocean, many in Aceh and Thailand. Terrorist bombings struck Bali, Thailand's army staged a coup in 2006, and Cyclone Nargis devastated Myanmar in 2008.

Myanmar's military loosened its grip, and Aung San Suu Kyi's party won elections in 2015, yet the army drove over 700,000 Rohingya into Bangladesh in 2017. Thailand's army seized power again in 2014. Disputes with China over the South China Sea sharpened, while Vietnam, Indonesia and the Philippines grew fast.

Myanmar's military seized power in a 2021 coup, sparking a widespread civil war. The region recovered from COVID-19 and courted trade shifting away from China, while South China Sea tensions persisted. Ferdinand Marcos Jr. won the Philippine presidency in 2022, Prabowo took office in Indonesia in 2024, and Timor-Leste joined ASEAN in 2025.
Japan: People reached the Japanese islands at least 38,000 years ago, and from c. 14,000 BC the Jōmon culture made some of the world's oldest pottery. Jōmon people hunted deer, fished and gathered nuts, and as the climate warmed and seas rose, they settled into lasting villages of pit houses.

The Middle Jōmon period was the high point of this hunter-gatherer culture, with the largest population and big villages such as Sannai-Maruyama in northern Honshu. People made dramatic flame-style pottery and clay dogū figurines, managed chestnut groves and traded obsidian and jade over long distances.

In the Late Jōmon period, a cooler climate reduced food supplies and populations fell, especially in the east. Communities built ritual stone circles such as those at Ōyu and made elaborate dogū figures. People still lived mainly by hunting, fishing and gathering, perhaps with some small-scale plant growing.

Migrants from the Korean peninsula brought wet-rice farming to northern Kyushu, starting the Yayoi culture c. 900 to 300 BC, though dates are debated. Elsewhere Jōmon life continued. Later Japanese chronicles placed the legendary founding by Emperor Jimmu in 660 BC, a date historians treat as myth.

Yayoi rice farming spread slowly eastward from Kyushu into western Honshu, carried by newcomers and adopted by Jōmon descendants. Farmers dug irrigated paddies and stored grain, which allowed larger villages. Most of eastern and northern Japan still lived the older Jōmon way.

The Yayoi farming way of life kept spreading across western Japan, bringing new tools, woven cloth and continental-style pottery. Villages began building moats and fences for defense, a sign of growing competition over land and harvests. Bronze and iron objects arrived from the continent through Korea.

Yayoi farming communities grew larger and more unequal, with leaders buried in richer graves. Iron tools and bronze bells, swords and mirrors, first imported and then made locally, became symbols of power. In Hokkaido, people continued a hunting and fishing culture descended from the Jōmon.

Yayoi villages formed small chiefdoms, some ringed with deep moats like the growing settlement at Yoshinogari in Kyushu. Warfare between communities appears in weapons and injured skeletons. Rice farming had reached much of Honshu, while the north kept older lifeways that later fed into Ainu culture.

Chinese records describe the people of Wa, or Japan, as divided into more than a hundred small countries, some sending envoys to Han China's new commanderies in Korea after 108 BC. Chiefs prized Chinese bronze mirrors and iron, and rivalry among Yayoi chiefdoms was intensifying.

Wa chiefdoms in Kyushu traded with the Han outpost of Lelang in Korea, gaining mirrors, iron and prestige goods. Rice farming supported growing populations, and local rulers used bronze ritual objects to display power. Japan remained a patchwork of competing Yayoi polities.

In AD 57 the king of Na, a small Wa state in Kyushu, sent envoys to Han China and received a gold seal from Emperor Guangwu, a seal later found in 1784. Yayoi chiefdoms were consolidating into larger regional powers, competing for iron and continental contacts.

A Wa king sent envoys to Han China in 107, but late in the century Chinese sources describe the Wa lands falling into prolonged warfare. Larger confederations were forming, and leaders built bigger burial mounds. These conflicts set the stage for a ruling queen who would unite many states.

Queen Himiko of Yamatai, a ruler said to use spiritual powers, led a league of some 30 Wa states and sent envoys to the Chinese state of Wei in 239. After her death c. 248, the first huge keyhole-shaped tombs appeared, marking the start of the Kofun period.

In the Kofun period, the Yamato kings in the Nara basin built massive keyhole-shaped tombs and extended alliances across western Japan. Iron from the Korean peninsula was vital to their power, and Yamato forces were involved in peninsular wars, as a Goguryeo stele records from 391 onward.

Yamato power peaked with gigantic tombs such as the Daisen Kofun near Osaka, attributed to Emperor Nintoku. The 'five kings of Wa' sent envoys to China's Southern dynasties seeking titles. Immigrants from Korea brought writing, crafts and administrative skills, and society was organized into hereditary clans called uji.

Buddhism arrived from the Korean kingdom of Baekje in 538 or 552, dividing the court. The pro-Buddhist Soga clan defeated the rival Mononobe in 587 and dominated the Yamato court. Empress Suiko took the throne in 593, opening the Asuka period with Prince Shōtoku as her regent.

Prince Shōtoku issued his Seventeen-Article Constitution in 604 and sent envoys to Sui China. The Taika reforms of 645 began building a Chinese-style centralized state. After defeat by Tang and Silla in Korea in 663, rulers strengthened defenses, and under Emperor Tenmu the names 'Nihon' and 'tennō' came into use.

The Taihō Code of 701 set up a Chinese-style legal state, and in 710 the court moved to a grand planned capital at Nara. The Kojiki and Nihon Shoki chronicles were written, and Emperor Shōmu built the Great Buddha at Tōdai-ji. In 794 the capital moved to Heian, today's Kyoto.

The Heian court flourished in Kyoto as the Fujiwara clan married daughters into the imperial family and ruled as regents. The monks Saichō and Kūkai founded the Tendai and Shingon schools of Buddhism. Japan ended embassies to Tang China in 894, and kana scripts began to develop.

The Fujiwara regents dominated an elegant court culture, celebrated in poetry collections such as the Kokinshū of 905. In the provinces, private estates grew and warrior bands formed, shown by Taira no Masakado's revolt in 939. Real power was slowly shifting from the court to armed landowners.

Fujiwara no Michinaga brought the regents' power to its height, and court ladies wrote classics such as The Tale of Genji c. 1010 and The Pillow Book. Warrior clans fought wars in the north for the court. From 1086, retired emperors began ruling from the cloister to counter the Fujiwara.

Warrior clans became kingmakers in court disputes, and Taira no Kiyomori briefly dominated the government. The Minamoto won the Genpei War in 1185, and in 1192 Minamoto no Yoritomo became the first shogun, ruling from Kamakura. Samurai rule had begun, and lasted nearly seven centuries.

After Yoritomo, the Hōjō family ruled as regents for the Kamakura shoguns and defeated the court in 1221. New popular Buddhist movements such as Pure Land, Zen and Nichiren spread. Mongol invasions in 1274 and 1281 were repelled, helped by storms later called kamikaze, though the defense strained the shogunate.

Emperor Go-Daigo overthrew the Kamakura shogunate in 1333, but Ashikaga Takauji soon set up a new shogunate in Kyoto. Rival Northern and Southern imperial courts fought until 1392. Under Ashikaga Yoshimitsu, culture blossomed with Noh theater and the Golden Pavilion.

The Ashikaga shoguns traded with Ming China and patronized Zen arts like the tea ceremony and ink painting. But the Ōnin War of 1467 to 1477 wrecked Kyoto and started the Sengoku, or warring states, era, as regional lords called daimyō fought for power. Ryukyu was unified in 1429.

The Portuguese brought guns in 1543 and Francis Xavier introduced Christianity in 1549. Oda Nobunaga began uniting the country with gunpowder armies, and Toyotomi Hideyoshi completed unification in 1590. Hideyoshi then invaded Korea in 1592 to 1598, a costly failure that ended with his death.

Tokugawa Ieyasu won at Sekigahara in 1600 and founded the Tokugawa shogunate in 1603, bringing over 250 years of peace. After the Christian-led Shimabara uprising, Japan closed itself to most foreigners in the 1630s, trading only with the Dutch and Chinese at Nagasaki. Cities like Edo and Osaka boomed.

Under the Tokugawa peace, Edo grew to about a million people, one of the largest cities in the world. Shogun Yoshimune's Kyōhō reforms tried to repair finances, and he eased the ban on Western books, encouraging 'Dutch learning'. Kabuki, puppet theater and woodblock prints thrived in the cities.

Merchants grew rich while many samurai fell into debt, and the official Tanuma Okitsugu promoted commerce. The Tenmei famine of the 1780s killed many and led to the strict Kansei reforms. Scholars translated Western anatomy books, while others revived study of ancient Japanese texts. Russian ships began appearing in the north.

The Tokugawa shogunate still ruled a stable, closed Japan, but foreign ships increasingly appeared, including Russian raids in the north and a British warship at Nagasaki in 1808. Ino Tadataka mapped the coastline. Urban culture flourished, with kabuki, popular novels and the early work of Hokusai.

The shogunate ordered foreign ships repelled in 1825. Famine in the 1830s sparked unrest, including Ōshio Heihachirō's 1837 uprising in Osaka, and the Tenpō reforms tried to restore order. Hokusai's Great Wave was printed c. 1831, and news of China's defeat in the Opium War alarmed Japan's leaders.

Commodore Perry forced Japan open in 1853, and unequal treaties followed. Anger at the weak shogunate led samurai from domains like Satsuma and Chōshū to topple it, and the 1868 Meiji Restoration returned power to the emperor. Japan abolished domains and samurai privileges and raced to modernize.

Meiji Japan built railways, factories, schools and a conscript army, crushing the samurai Satsuma Rebellion in 1877. It annexed Ryukyu as Okinawa in 1879 and adopted a constitution in 1889. In 1894 to 1895 Japan defeated China and took Taiwan, joining the imperial powers.

Japan allied with Britain in 1902 and defeated Russia in 1904 to 1905, the first modern Asian victory over a European power. It made Korea a protectorate and gained influence in Manchuria. Industry grew quickly, but heavy war costs and taxes caused unrest at home.

Japan annexed Korea in 1910. Emperor Meiji died in 1912, beginning the Taishō era. In World War I Japan seized German holdings in China and the Pacific and pressed its Twenty-One Demands on China. Wartime booms brought inflation, and rice riots erupted in 1918.

'Taishō democracy' brought party governments and mass politics, and men gained universal suffrage in 1925, alongside a harsh law against radicals. The Great Kantō Earthquake of 1923 devastated Tokyo and Yokohama. Emperor Hirohito's Shōwa era began in 1926, and a financial panic struck in 1927.

The army seized Manchuria in 1931, and Japan left the League of Nations. Military officers gained control at home through assassinations and pressure on governments. In 1937 full-scale war with China began, including the Nanjing massacre, as Japan mobilized its whole economy for war.

Japan joined the Axis, attacked Pearl Harbor in 1941 and conquered much of Asia before being pushed back. After atomic bombs fell on Hiroshima and Nagasaki in 1945, Japan surrendered and was occupied by the US, which oversaw land reform and a 1947 constitution renouncing war.

Japan regained sovereignty in 1952 under a security treaty with the US. Boosted by Korean War orders, its 'economic miracle' began, with fast-growing steel, shipbuilding and electronics. The Liberal Democratic Party formed in 1955 and would govern for most of the following decades.

Japan's economy grew around 10 percent a year, and by 1968 it was the world's second-largest. The 1964 Tokyo Olympics and the first bullet train showcased its recovery. Mass protests opposed the 1960 security treaty with the US, while pollution scandals revealed the costs of rapid growth.

Japan hosted the 1970 Osaka Expo, regained Okinawa from the US in 1972 and established relations with China. The 1973 oil shock ended the era of super-fast growth, but Japanese cars and electronics conquered world markets thanks to efficient manufacturing.

Japan's economy reached its peak, with booming exports and soaring land and stock prices after the 1985 Plaza Accord. Emperor Hirohito died in 1989, beginning the Heisei era. The asset bubble burst in 1989 to 1991, leaving banks with massive bad debts.

The 'Lost Decade' of stagnation followed the bubble, with falling prices and a banking crisis in 1997 to 1998. In 1995 the Kobe earthquake killed over 6,000 people, and the Aum Shinrikyō cult released sarin gas in the Tokyo subway. The LDP briefly lost power in 1993.

Prime Minister Koizumi pushed reforms and privatization from 2001 to 2006, but deflation persisted and the 2008 global crisis hit exports. Japan's population began to shrink and age rapidly. In 2009 voters ended the LDP's long rule by electing the Democratic Party of Japan.

The 2011 Tōhoku earthquake and tsunami killed about 18,000 people and caused the Fukushima nuclear disaster. Shinzō Abe returned as prime minister in 2012, pursuing 'Abenomics' and a stronger defense role. Emperor Akihito abdicated in 2019, and Naruhito's Reiwa era began.

Japan weathered COVID-19 and held the delayed Tokyo Olympics in 2021. Former prime minister Abe was assassinated in 2022. Facing China and North Korea, Japan sharply raised defense spending, and in 2025 Sanae Takaichi became its first female prime minister amid a weak yen and a shrinking population.
Korea: Humans lived on the Korean peninsula from the Old Stone Age, hunting and gathering. From c. 8000 BC people of the Jeulmun culture made some of the region's earliest pottery and lived by fishing, shellfish gathering and hunting along coasts and rivers, leaving behind large shell middens.

Jeulmun people, known for comb-patterned pottery, lived in small villages and had begun growing millet alongside fishing and gathering. Korean tradition holds that the mythical Dangun founded Gojoseon, the first Korean kingdom, in 2333 BC, though historians see this as legend rather than recorded history.

The Mumun pottery period began c. 1500 BC as new farming communities grew rice, millet and beans in larger villages. People built thousands of stone dolmen tombs, and Korea now holds a large share of the world's dolmens. Bronze objects began to appear late in this era.

Mumun farmers expanded rice paddies, and local elites displayed wealth through bronze daggers and dolmen burials, such as those at Gochang, Hwasun and Ganghwa. In the northwest and Liaodong, Gojoseon was emerging as a real chiefdom or early state linked to the bronze cultures of northeast China.

Rice-farming villages such as Songguk-ri in the southwest grew large and were fortified with palisades and ditches. Bronze daggers and mirrors marked chiefs' status. In the north, Gojoseon's rulers were gaining power and contact with Chinese states across the Liao River.

Iron working began to reach the peninsula from China's Warring States, transforming tools and weapons over the following centuries. Gojoseon grew as a regional power in the north, while the south was home to farming chiefdoms later grouped under the name Jin.

Gojoseon clashed with the Chinese state of Yan, which c. 300 BC pushed it back and seized territory. Korean craftsmen developed the slender bronze dagger style that spread across the peninsula. Iron tools became more common, and southern chiefdoms grew in size and wealth.

Gojoseon remained the leading power in the north while China was unified by the Qin and then the Han. Wars in China sent refugees into the peninsula, bringing iron technology and new ideas. In the south, farming chiefdoms of the Jin area continued to develop.

In 194 BC the refugee leader Wiman seized Gojoseon's throne, and the kingdom grew rich on trade. In 108 BC Han China conquered Gojoseon and set up commanderies, including Lelang near Pyongyang. In the south, the Samhan confederacies of Mahan, Jinhan and Byeonhan took shape.

Tradition dates the founding of Silla to 57 BC, Goguryeo to 37 BC and Baekje to 18 BC, beginning the Three Kingdoms era. In reality these were still small chiefdoms. Buyeo ruled the northern plains, while the Chinese commandery of Lelang spread Chinese culture in the northwest.

Goguryeo grew in the mountains along the Yalu River, raiding Chinese outposts and conquering neighbors. In the south, Samhan chiefdoms formed the seeds of Baekje and Silla, and tradition dates the Gaya confederacy to AD 42. Lelang remained a center of Chinese goods and writing.

Goguryeo became a strong centralized kingdom under King Taejo, expanding its territory. The Gaya states in the south grew wealthy by producing iron and trading it to Japan and Lelang. Baekje and Silla were still building up from local chiefdoms within the Mahan and Jinhan confederacies.

Goguryeo battled Chinese states, and in 244 the Wei general Guanqiu Jian sacked its capital, though the kingdom recovered. Baekje under King Goi consolidated power over the Mahan region. Gaya traded iron with the Wa of Japan, and Silla slowly grew in the southeast.

Goguryeo destroyed the last Chinese commandery, Lelang, in 313, ending Chinese rule in Korea. Buddhism arrived in Goguryeo in 372 and Baekje in 384. Baekje reached a peak under King Geunchogo, and late in the century Goguryeo's King Gwanggaeto began expanding in all directions.

Goguryeo was at its height, with King Gwanggaeto's victories recorded on a great stele in 414. His son Jangsu moved the capital to Pyongyang in 427 and in 475 captured Baekje's capital, forcing Baekje south. Silla was strengthening its monarchy in the southeast.

Silla adopted Buddhism in 527 and expanded under King Jinheung, absorbing the Gaya states by 562 and training elite Hwarang youths. Baekje moved its capital to Sabi in 538 and sent Buddhism to Japan. The three kingdoms fought constantly for control of the Han River valley.

Goguryeo defeated huge Sui Chinese invasions, including at the Salsu River in 612. Silla then allied with Tang China and conquered Baekje in 660 and Goguryeo in 668, unifying Korea. Silla drove out the Tang by 676, and Goguryeo survivors founded Balhae to the north in 698.

Unified Silla enjoyed a golden age of Buddhist art and learning, building Bulguksa temple and the Seokguram grotto at Gyeongju. Society was ruled by a strict 'bone rank' aristocracy. In the north, the kingdom of Balhae flourished, calling itself successor to Goguryeo.

Silla's power declined as aristocrats fought over the throne and provincial lords grew stronger. The merchant Jang Bogo built a maritime trading empire from his base at Cheonghaejin. By 889 peasant revolts spread, and rebels began carving out rival states.

Rebels founded rival kingdoms, and in 918 Wang Geon established the Goryeo dynasty, origin of the name 'Korea'. Silla surrendered in 935 and Goryeo reunited the peninsula in 936, absorbing refugees from Balhae, which fell to the Khitan in 926. Goryeo adopted civil service exams in 958.

Goryeo fought off Khitan invasions, winning a great victory at Gwiju in 1019, and built a long defensive wall in the north. Buddhism thrived, and the first Tripitaka Koreana woodblocks were carved to seek divine protection. An aristocratic civil elite dominated government.

Goryeo celadon pottery reached its peak of beauty, and Kim Busik compiled the Samguk Sagi history in 1145. Tensions between civil and military officials exploded in a military coup in 1170. From 1196 the Choe family ruled as military dictators behind the Goryeo kings.

Goryeo pioneered printing with metal movable type. Mongol invasions began in 1231, and the court fled to Ganghwa Island, carving the Tripitaka Koreana woodblocks for protection. In 1259 Goryeo became a Mongol vassal, and its kings married Mongol princesses and supplied ships for the invasions of Japan.

As the Yuan dynasty weakened, King Gongmin restored Goryeo's independence. Red Turban rebels and Japanese pirates ravaged the land. Jikji, printed in 1377, is the oldest surviving book printed with metal type. In 1392 General Yi Seong-gye founded the Joseon dynasty, which embraced Neo-Confucianism.

Joseon ruled from its new capital Hanyang, today's Seoul. King Sejong created the Hangul alphabet in 1443 to help ordinary people read, and sponsored inventions such as rain gauges and water clocks. A national law code organized the Confucian state and its yangban aristocracy.

Bitter factional purges divided Joseon's Confucian scholar-officials, while thinkers such as Yi Hwang and Yi I shaped Korean Neo-Confucianism. Japan's invasions of 1592 to 1598 devastated the country, but Admiral Yi Sun-sin's turtle ships and Ming Chinese aid helped drive the Japanese out.

Joseon was still recovering when the Manchus invaded in 1627 and again in 1636 to 1637, forcing it to become a tributary of the Qing. Korea then limited foreign contact, earning the name 'Hermit Kingdom'. Tax reforms eased burdens on farmers, and commerce slowly grew.

King Yeongjo, who ruled from 1724 to 1776, tried to calm factional fighting with a policy of balanced appointments. Agriculture recovered, markets expanded and the population grew. Scholars of the Silhak, or practical learning, movement began calling for reforms to land, trade and government.

Yeongjo had his own son, Crown Prince Sado, locked in a rice chest to die in 1762. Sado's son King Jeongjo became a reforming ruler who built the Hwaseong fortress at Suwon. Catholicism entered Korea through books from China in 1784, and Silhak scholarship flourished.

After Jeongjo's death, a 1801 persecution killed many Catholics, and powerful in-law families took over the government, ruling through child kings. Corruption and heavy taxes sparked the Hong Gyeong-nae rebellion of 1811 to 1812 in the northwest. Joseon remained closed to the West.

In-law clans kept dominating the Joseon court while peasants suffered from famine and corrupt officials. Catholic converts, along with French missionary priests, were executed in the persecution of 1839. Western ships began appearing off the coasts, seeking trade that Joseon refused.

Choe Je-u founded the Donghak, or Eastern Learning, religion in 1860. The regent Heungseon Daewongun strengthened royal power, persecuted Catholics in 1866 and fought off French and American expeditions in 1866 and 1871, keeping Korea isolated from the outside world.

Japan forced Korea open with the 1876 Ganghwa Treaty, and China, Japan and Russia competed for influence. The Donghak peasant uprising of 1894 triggered the Sino-Japanese War. Japanese agents murdered Queen Min in 1895, and King Gojong proclaimed the Korean Empire in 1897.

After defeating Russia, Japan made Korea a protectorate in 1905. Japan forced Emperor Gojong to abdicate in 1907, and 'righteous armies' fought the Japanese across the countryside. In 1909 Korean patriot An Jung-geun assassinated Itō Hirobumi, Japan's former resident-general in Korea.

Japan annexed Korea in 1910 and ruled through a military government, surveying land and taking much of it for Japanese owners. On March 1, 1919, Koreans rose in nationwide peaceful protests for independence, which were brutally suppressed, and exiles formed a provisional government in Shanghai.

After the March 1st movement, Japan switched to 'cultural rule', allowing some Korean newspapers and groups, though control remained tight. Much of Korea's rice was shipped to Japan while many farmers went hungry. Nationalists and socialists organized, and students protested in Gwangju in 1929.

Japan turned Korea into an industrial and military base for its wars in China. Colonial authorities pushed forced assimilation, requiring Shinto worship, suppressing the Korean language and later pressuring Koreans to take Japanese names. Korean guerrillas fought the Japanese from Manchuria.

During World War II Japan conscripted Koreans as laborers and soldiers and forced many women into military sexual slavery. Korea was liberated in 1945 but divided at the 38th parallel between Soviet and US forces. In 1948 separate states were founded, North Korea and South Korea.

North Korea invaded the South in 1950, and the Korean War drew in US-led UN forces and China, killing about 3 million people before a 1953 armistice with no peace treaty. Afterward, Syngman Rhee ruled the South while Kim Il-sung consolidated total power in the North.

Student protests ousted Syngman Rhee in 1960, but General Park Chung-hee seized power in a 1961 coup and began the South's export-driven 'Miracle on the Han'. South Korea normalized relations with Japan in 1965 and sent troops to Vietnam. North Korea promoted Kim Il-sung's self-reliant Juche ideology.

Park Chung-hee made himself near-dictator under the 1972 Yushin constitution, pushing heavy industries like steel, ships and chemicals. South Korea's economy surged while dissent was repressed. Park was assassinated in 1979. In the North, a personality cult surrounded Kim Il-sung.

General Chun Doo-hwan seized power, and his troops crushed the 1980 Gwangju uprising, killing hundreds. Mass protests won democracy in the South in 1987, and the 1988 Seoul Olympics showcased a modern nation. North Korea grew more isolated and bombed a South Korean airliner in 1987.

Both Koreas joined the UN in 1991. Kim Il-sung died in 1994, and his son Kim Jong-il led North Korea through a devastating famine from 1994 to 1998. South Korea was hit hard by the 1997 Asian financial crisis, and Kim Dae-jung began a 'Sunshine Policy' of engagement with the North.

In 2000 the two Koreas held their first summit, and Kim Dae-jung won the Nobel Peace Prize. South Korea co-hosted the 2002 World Cup and its pop culture spread abroad as the 'Korean Wave'. North Korea conducted its first nuclear test in 2006, deepening tensions.

Kim Jong-un succeeded his father in North Korea in 2011 and expanded its nuclear and missile programs. In the South, President Park Geun-hye was impeached and removed in 2017 over a corruption scandal. Summits in 2018 and 2019 raised hopes of peace, while K-pop and Korean films gained global fame.

North Korea deepened ties with Russia, sending troops to fight in Ukraine's war. In South Korea, President Yoon Suk Yeol's martial-law decree of December 2024 led to his impeachment and removal in 2025, and Lee Jae-myung won the snap election. Han Kang became the first Korean Nobel laureate in literature in 2024.
Oceania / Islanders: Humans reached Australia c. 65,000 to 50,000 years ago, crossing open water to the joined landmass of Australia and New Guinea. Aboriginal cultures, among the oldest continuous on Earth, spread across the continent. New Guineans developed some of the world's earliest farming, growing taro and bananas at Kuk swamp c. 7000 BC.

Aboriginal Australians lived in hundreds of distinct language groups, managing the land with fire, trading over long distances and painting rich rock art. In New Guinea's highlands, farmers tended gardens of taro and bananas. The islands beyond the Solomons were still uninhabited, awaiting seafaring settlers.

The dingo arrived in Australia c. 1500 BC, likely brought by seafarers from Southeast Asia. Austronesian voyagers reached the Mariana Islands, and in the Bismarck Archipelago north of New Guinea the Lapita culture appeared, known for finely stamped pottery and skilled ocean sailing.

Lapita voyagers sailed into the open Pacific, reaching Vanuatu and New Caledonia and settling Fiji, Tonga and Samoa c. 1100 to 800 BC, islands no human had touched before. Aboriginal Australians and Papuan-speaking New Guineans continued their long-established ways of life.

In Tonga and Samoa, descendants of the Lapita settlers developed a distinct Ancestral Polynesian culture, language and society. Eastward voyaging paused for many centuries. Across Australia, Aboriginal peoples maintained complex kinship systems, ceremonies and songlines that mapped the land and its stories.

Lapita pottery designs faded into simpler plainware as island communities adapted to local conditions, farming taro, yams and breadfruit and fishing the reefs. Polynesian chiefly society was taking shape in Tonga and Samoa. Aboriginal Australians shaped landscapes through fire-stick farming and seasonal movement.

Pacific islanders lived in chiefdoms based on kinship, gardening and fishing, linked by canoe voyages between neighboring islands. In New Guinea, hundreds of language communities traded shells, stone and pigs. Torres Strait Islanders connected New Guinea and Australia through trade and ceremony.

Micronesian voyagers were spreading through the scattered atolls and high islands of the western Pacific. In western Polynesia, Tonga and Samoa developed chiefdoms with sacred leaders. Aboriginal Australians continued to manage their country, with deep local knowledge of water, plants and seasons.

Seafarers moved into eastern Micronesia, settling islands such as Pohnpei, Kosrae, the Marshalls and Kiribati around this era. In Melanesia, coastal and island peoples developed trade networks in shell valuables, pottery and food. Aboriginal life across Australia remained diverse and resilient.

Across Oceania, peoples lived without states or writing but with rich oral traditions, navigation knowledge and art. Polynesians in Tonga and Samoa still had not sailed farther east. Aboriginal groups in southeastern Australia managed eels with stone channels and traps first built thousands of years earlier.

Western Polynesian societies in Tonga and Samoa grew more stratified, with chiefs claiming descent from the gods. Micronesian communities settled their islands and developed outrigger sailing skills. In Australia, hundreds of Aboriginal nations held their own laws, languages and ceremonies.

Pacific island societies remained centered on chiefs, extended families and gardens, with canoes linking neighboring archipelagos. New Guinea highlanders tended gardens of taro, yams and bananas, long before the sweet potato arrived. Aboriginal Australians traded ochre, stone axes and shells along routes crossing the continent.

Polynesians in the west remained settled for a long pause before further voyaging. In Fiji, populations grew and communities interacted with both Polynesian and Melanesian neighbors. Aboriginal peoples continued to live by hunting, gathering, fishing and careful burning of the land.

Polynesian chiefdoms in Tonga and Samoa held power through sacred status and control of land and food. Older estimates placed settlement of eastern islands like the Marquesas around this time, but newer radiocarbon dating suggests it came much later. Aboriginal Australia remained a mosaic of peoples.

Island communities across Melanesia, Micronesia and western Polynesia continued farming, fishing and voyaging between nearby islands. Navigators kept detailed knowledge of stars, swells and winds. In Australia and New Guinea, life followed deep traditions tied to ancestral lands.

Pacific peoples lived in kin-based communities ruled by chiefs and elders, with ceremonial exchange binding islands together. In Micronesia, communities on Yap, Palau and the Carolines built ties through voyaging. Aboriginal Australians maintained their law, art and land management across the continent.

Polynesian, Melanesian and Micronesian societies continued to grow and diversify, with chiefs organizing food production and feasting. In northern Australia and New Guinea, coastal peoples traded across the Torres Strait. Eastern Polynesia beyond Samoa still remained unsettled.

Western Polynesian societies were developing more powerful chiefdoms, and voyaging skills were preparing them for a great expansion east. Across Melanesia, communities built trade and marriage networks. Aboriginal Australians maintained their long-established ways of living with the land.

After many centuries in Tonga and Samoa, Polynesians had refined their double-hulled canoes and navigation, yet the vast eastern Pacific remained empty of people. In Fiji and across Melanesia, island communities traded and intermarried, and Aboriginal Australians continued to care for their country through ceremony, law and fire.

In the Mariana Islands, the Chamorro latte period began c. 900, when people raised houses on large stone pillars. Polynesians in Tonga and Samoa were preparing for a wave of long-distance voyages, and tradition dates the founding of the sacred Tu'i Tonga line to about this period.

Polynesian voyagers launched a remarkable eastward expansion, settling the Society Islands, Cook Islands and Marquesas, then Hawaii and Rapa Nui (Easter Island) c. 1000 to 1200. They carried crops, pigs, chickens and dogs in large double-hulled canoes, navigating by stars and swells.

On Pohnpei, the Saudeleur dynasty built the stone city of Nan Madol on artificial islets, ruling the island. Polynesian settlement of Rapa Nui and other far islands continued, and Tonga's Tu'i Tonga chiefs extended their influence. Aboriginal peoples continued their ancient ways across Australia.

Māori ancestors settled New Zealand c. 1250 to 1300, the last major landmass reached by humans, and hunted the giant flightless moa. Rapa Nui islanders began carving their famous moai statues. Tonga's chiefs built a maritime network across the region, and Hawaiian chiefdoms grew.

In New Zealand, Māori hunting drove the moa toward extinction by c. 1400, and communities shifted to gardening and fishing. Long-distance voyaging across Polynesia gradually declined, leaving island groups more isolated. Rapa Nui islanders continued raising moai, and Hawaiian chiefdoms grew larger.

Māori society shifted toward tribal groups (iwi) living in fortified hilltop villages called pā, as conflicts over land grew. Hawaiian chiefs ruled larger territories with complex irrigation and fishponds. Moriori settled the Chatham Islands, and Rapa Nui islanders still carved moai.

Magellan crossed the Pacific in 1521 and reached Guam, the first European contact with Pacific islanders. Spanish voyages later reached the Solomon Islands. Otherwise, Polynesian, Melanesian and Micronesian societies continued under their own chiefs, and Aboriginal Australia remained unknown to Europeans.

Dutch sailors reached northern Australia in 1606, and Abel Tasman reached Tasmania and New Zealand in 1642, clashing with Māori. Spain colonized Guam and the Marianas from 1668, and war and disease devastated the Chamorro people. On Pohnpei, the Saudeleur dynasty was overthrown.

Dutch explorer Jacob Roggeveen reached Rapa Nui in 1722 and passed Samoa. Makassan fishermen from Sulawesi began visiting northern Australia to gather sea cucumbers, trading with Yolngu people. Elsewhere, Pacific islanders and Aboriginal Australians lived largely untouched by Europeans.

Europeans arrived in force. Captain Cook's voyages of 1768 to 1779 charted New Zealand, eastern Australia and Hawaii. In 1788 the British First Fleet founded a penal colony at Sydney, and smallpox and violence soon devastated local Aboriginal people. Kamehameha was rising to power in Hawaii.

Kamehameha unified the Hawaiian Islands by 1810. In New Zealand, Māori tribes armed with muskets fought devastating intertribal wars. British settlement spread to Tasmania and across the Blue Mountains, and missionaries converted rulers in Tahiti and, after 1820, in Hawaii.

Britain expanded its colonies in Australia, founding Perth, Melbourne and Adelaide, and frontier wars nearly destroyed Tasmania's Aboriginal people. In 1840 Māori chiefs and the British signed the Treaty of Waitangi in New Zealand, though its meaning was disputed. France took control of Tahiti in 1842.

Australian gold rushes from 1851 drew huge immigration and made colonies rich and self-governing. Wars between Māori and colonial forces raged in New Zealand in the 1860s, leading to land confiscations. Labor recruiters known as blackbirders took Pacific islanders to Queensland, and Fiji became a British colony in 1874.

New Zealand in 1893 became the first nation to give women the vote. In Hawaii, American businessmen overthrew the monarchy in 1893 and the US annexed the islands in 1898. Germany and Britain split eastern New Guinea, Chile annexed Rapa Nui in 1888, and Indian laborers arrived in Fiji.

Australia federated in 1901 as a dominion and quickly adopted the 'White Australia' immigration policy. New Zealand became a dominion in 1907. Europeans and Americans now controlled nearly every Pacific island, while Aboriginal Australians faced restrictive laws and removal of children.

In World War I, Australian and New Zealand troops fought at Gallipoli in 1915, forging the ANZAC identity. Australia seized German New Guinea, New Zealand took Samoa and Japan took Micronesia. The 1918 influenza pandemic killed about a fifth of Western Samoa's people.

Former German islands became League of Nations mandates run by Australia, New Zealand and Japan. In Samoa, the Mau movement campaigned peacefully for self-rule. Australia's parliament moved to Canberra in 1927, while the 1928 Coniston massacre showed continuing frontier violence against Aboriginal people.

The Great Depression hit export-dependent Australia and New Zealand hard. New Zealand police killed Mau leader Tupua Tamasese Lealofi III in 1929, but the movement continued. Aboriginal activists held a Day of Mourning in 1938, and Japan fortified its Micronesian islands.

The Pacific War of 1941 to 1945 brought battles at Midway, Guadalcanal, Kokoda and across the islands, and Japan bombed Darwin in 1942. In 1946 US nuclear tests began at Bikini Atoll in the Marshall Islands. Postwar Australia launched mass immigration from Europe.

Australia, New Zealand and the US signed the ANZUS alliance in 1951. US hydrogen bomb tests contaminated Marshall Islanders, and Britain tested atomic weapons in Australia at Maralinga. Melbourne hosted the 1956 Olympics as Australia's economy and population grew.

Western Samoa became the first independent Pacific island nation in 1962, followed by Nauru in 1968. In 1967 Australians voted overwhelmingly to count Aboriginal people in the census and allow federal laws for them. France began nuclear tests in French Polynesia, and both ANZAC nations sent troops to Vietnam.

Pacific island nations won independence, including Fiji and Tonga in 1970, Papua New Guinea in 1975 and the Solomons, Tuvalu and Kiribati by 1979. Australia ended the White Australia policy, Aboriginal activists set up a Tent Embassy, and New Zealand created the Waitangi Tribunal in 1975.

Vanuatu gained independence in 1980, and the Marshall Islands and Micronesia entered free association with the US. Fiji suffered two military coups in 1987. French agents sank the Greenpeace ship Rainbow Warrior in Auckland in 1985, and New Zealand declared itself nuclear-free.

Australia's High Court recognized Aboriginal native title in the 1992 Mabo decision. New Zealand began major treaty settlements with Māori iwi. France ended Pacific nuclear tests in 1996, Bougainville's civil war ended with a 1998 truce, and Australia led peacekeepers into East Timor in 1999.

Sydney hosted the 2000 Olympics. Fiji saw further coups in 2000 and 2006, and an Australian-led mission restored order in the Solomon Islands from 2003. In 2008 Australia formally apologized to the Stolen Generations of Aboriginal children taken from their families.

Earthquakes devastated Christchurch in 2010 to 2011, and a terrorist killed 51 worshippers at two Christchurch mosques in 2019. Bougainville voted overwhelmingly for independence from Papua New Guinea in 2019. Pacific nations warned of climate change as China competed with Australia for regional influence.

Rising seas threaten atoll nations like Tuvalu and Kiribati, and Australia offered Tuvaluans a migration pathway in 2023. Tonga's 2022 volcanic eruption was the largest in decades. Australians rejected an Indigenous Voice to Parliament in 2023, and a Vanuatu-led campaign won a 2025 world court opinion on climate duties.
United States: The first people crossed from Asia via Beringia by at least c. 15,000 years ago. Clovis hunters later stalked mammoths and bison, but after the Ice Age the big game vanished, and Archaic hunter-gatherers adapted to local forests, plains, deserts and coasts, moving north into Canada as the glaciers retreated.

Archaic hunter-gatherers lived across North America in small bands, fishing, gathering nuts and hunting deer. In the Southeast, people piled up shell rings and mounds, and eastern groups began tending local seed plants like sunflower and squash. Paleo-Eskimo peoples spread across the Arctic from Alaska to Canada and Greenland.

Around c. 1700 BC, people at Poverty Point in Louisiana built huge earthen ridges and mounds and traded for stone and copper from far away, all without farming. Maize had reached the Southwest by c. 2000 BC, while eastern foragers were domesticating native seed crops such as goosefoot and sumpweed.

The Early Woodland era began in the East, bringing pottery, more settled villages and the first burial mounds of the Adena culture in the Ohio Valley. In the Southwest, early farmers dug irrigation canals for maize. In the Arctic, the Dorset culture took shape among hunters of seal and caribou.

No states existed; hundreds of independent peoples lived by hunting, fishing, gathering and some gardening. The Adena of the Ohio Valley buried honored dead in earthen mounds with copper and mica ornaments. Pacific Northwest peoples relied on salmon, and Southwest farmers combined maize with wild foods.

Adena communities kept building burial mounds and trading goods such as Great Lakes copper and Gulf Coast shells. On the Plains, bison hunters moved with the herds, while in California dense populations lived on acorns and seafood without needing to farm. Life remained village-based and kin-centered.

Across the continent, regional ways of life grew more distinct. Late Adena peoples in the Ohio Valley built ever larger mounds, Basketmaker farmers on the Colorado Plateau grew maize and squash and wove fine baskets, and Northwest Coast villagers built plank houses and stored dried salmon for winter.

The Hopewell tradition began to emerge in Ohio and Illinois around c. 200 BC. Its people built large geometric earthworks and joined a vast exchange network carrying obsidian, copper, shells and mica. Elsewhere, foragers and small-scale farmers continued long-established ways of life.

Hopewell culture grew in the Midwest, with ceremonial centers where people gathered for feasts, burials and trade. Its craftsmen made copper ornaments, mica cutouts and carved stone pipes. Related mound traditions such as Marksville appeared in the lower Mississippi Valley.

The Hopewell Interaction Sphere linked communities from the Rockies to the Atlantic coast through shared rituals and long-distance trade. In the Southwest, farming villages were growing, and in the far north Dorset peoples hunted sea mammals across Arctic Canada.

Hopewell societies flourished, building giant earthworks such as those at Newark, Ohio, aligned with the movements of the Moon. In the deserts of southern Arizona, the ancestors of the Hohokam were beginning to farm with irrigation. Most people still lived in small villages or mobile bands.

Hopewell ceremonial life was at its height in the Ohio and Illinois valleys. In the Southwest, early Mogollon and Basketmaker communities lived in pithouse villages and farmed maize. Northwest Coast societies grew richer and more ranked, with chiefs, nobles and commoners.

Hopewell centers continued to draw people for rituals and trade. Mogollon villages took shape in the mountains of New Mexico and Arizona, making some of the region's earliest pottery. Across the Plains and Great Basin, mobile foragers followed the seasons.

Hopewell mound-building and long-distance trade began to fade, for reasons that are still debated. Hohokam farmers in Arizona extended irrigation canals along the Salt and Gila rivers. Across the East, people relied more on gardens of native seed crops alongside hunting and gathering.

The Hopewell era ended and the Late Woodland period began, with smaller, more scattered communities. The bow and arrow spread across much of the continent, changing hunting and warfare. In the Southwest, Basketmaker peoples adopted pottery and beans.

Late Woodland peoples lived in villages across the East, increasingly using the bow and arrow. Basketmaker communities on the Colorado Plateau built pithouse villages and stored maize in pots. Hohokam towns in Arizona grew around expanding canal networks.

In the Upper Midwest, Effigy Mound peoples began shaping earthen mounds into birds, bears and other animals. In Arkansas, the Plum Bayou culture built the Toltec Mounds center. Southwestern farmers were becoming more dependent on maize.

Ancestral Puebloans in the Four Corners began building above-ground, multi-room pueblos, while the Hohokam built ball courts and miles of canals. In the East, maize farming started to spread, supporting larger villages. Effigy mounds still rose in Wisconsin and Iowa.

In Chaco Canyon, New Mexico, Ancestral Puebloans started building multi-story great houses such as Pueblo Bonito. In the Mississippi Valley, maize-farming communities were laying the foundations of the Mississippian culture. Hohokam society thrived in the Arizona desert.

Chaco Canyon grew into a regional center linked by long straight roads and trade in turquoise and macaws. Along the Mississippi and its tributaries, maize-based chiefdoms took shape. In the 980s, Norse settlers from Iceland reached Greenland, on the eastern edge of the Arctic world.

Around c. 1050, Cahokia near modern St. Louis burst into a planned city of perhaps 10,000 to 20,000 people, the largest north of Mexico. Chaco Canyon reached its peak. The Norse briefly camped at L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland, and Thule Inuit began moving east from Alaska.

Cahokia was at its height, with the giant Monks Mound and a powerful elite. Mississippian chiefdoms spread across the Southeast, including Moundville in Alabama and Etowah in Georgia. Drought brought Chaco's decline, and Puebloans built new cliff dwellings at Mesa Verde.

Mesa Verde's cliff dwellings flourished until a great drought late in the century drove Puebloans out of the Four Corners. Cahokia began to shrink, while Moundville, Spiro and Etowah thrived. Thule Inuit, ancestors of today's Inuit, spread across Arctic Canada to Greenland.

Cahokia was largely abandoned by c. 1350, and Puebloans resettled along the Rio Grande and at Hopi and Zuni. Mississippian chiefdoms shared a striking religious art style across the Southeast. In the Northeast, Iroquoian peoples lived in fortified villages of longhouses, farming maize, beans and squash.

Millions of people lived in what is now the US and Canada, in hundreds of nations. Mississippian chiefdoms such as Coosa ruled the Southeast, the Hohokam system collapsed, and the Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) Confederacy may have formed in this era. In 1497, John Cabot reached Newfoundland.

Europeans arrived: Ponce de León reached Florida in 1513, de Soto and Coronado marched through the Southeast and Southwest, and Spain founded St. Augustine in 1565. In Canada, Cartier explored the St. Lawrence. Above all, European diseases devastated Native nations, often ahead of the Europeans themselves.

England planted colonies at Jamestown (1607) and Plymouth (1620), and enslaved Africans arrived in Virginia in 1619. France founded Quebec, the Dutch New Amsterdam. Native nations fought back in wars such as King Philip's War and the 1680 Pueblo Revolt as settlers took their land.

British colonies grew fast along the Atlantic coast, with Georgia founded in 1732, and enslaved Africans worked tobacco and rice plantations in the South. The Great Awakening stirred colonial religion. France held Canada and Louisiana, Spain held Florida and Texas, and the Comanche rose to power on the southern Plains.

Britain won the French and Indian War (1754 to 1763), taking Canada, but its new taxes sparked revolution. The colonies declared independence in 1776, won it by the 1783 Treaty of Paris, and wrote the Constitution in 1787. Native nations lost land as settlers pushed west.

The young republic doubled its size with the 1803 Louisiana Purchase, sent Lewis and Clark west, and fought Britain in the War of 1812, when invasions of Canada failed. The 1823 Monroe Doctrine warned Europe off the Americas. Cotton and slavery spread across the Deep South.

Under the 1830 Indian Removal Act, the Cherokee and other nations were forced west on the Trail of Tears. The US annexed Texas and took the Southwest in the Mexican-American War, and the 1849 Gold Rush drew crowds to California. Arguments over slavery's expansion intensified.

The fight over slavery led to the Civil War (1861 to 1865), which killed about 620,000 to 750,000 people. The Union won, slavery ended with the 13th Amendment, and Reconstruction began. The transcontinental railroad opened in 1869, and Canada became a self-governing confederation in 1867.

Reconstruction ended in 1877 and Jim Crow segregation took hold in the South. In the Gilded Age, railroads, steel and oil made the US an industrial giant, and millions of immigrants arrived. Plains nations were confined to reservations, and the 1898 Spanish-American War brought an overseas empire.

In the Progressive Era, reformers under presidents like Theodore Roosevelt tackled monopolies, corruption and unsafe food. Immigration peaked through Ellis Island, cities grew, and the Wright brothers flew in 1903. The US began building the Panama Canal and acted as a regional police power.

Henry Ford's assembly line made cars affordable, and new laws created the Federal Reserve and the income tax. The US entered World War I in 1917, emerging as a creditor nation. The Great Migration took Black Southerners north, and the 1918 flu killed hundreds of thousands.

Women won the vote with the 19th Amendment in 1920. The Roaring Twenties brought jazz, radio, movies and booming stock prices, alongside Prohibition, the Harlem Renaissance and strict new limits on immigration. The decade ended with the stock market crash of 1929.

The Great Depression left a quarter of workers jobless, and the Dust Bowl drove farm families off the Plains. Franklin D. Roosevelt's New Deal from 1933 created Social Security, public works jobs and banking regulations, greatly expanding the federal government.

Japan's attack on Pearl Harbor in 1941 brought the US into World War II, and its factories armed the Allies. The war ended with atomic bombs on Japan in 1945, leaving the US a superpower. The 1948 Marshall Plan and NATO opened the Cold War with the Soviet Union.

Postwar prosperity built suburbs, interstate highways and a baby boom, while the Korean War and McCarthyism reflected Cold War fears. The 1954 Brown v. Board of Education ruling struck down school segregation, and the Montgomery bus boycott launched the Civil Rights Movement.

President Kennedy was assassinated in 1963. The Civil Rights Act and Voting Rights Act of 1964 and 1965 ended legal segregation, but Martin Luther King Jr. was killed in 1968 amid war protests and urban unrest over Vietnam. In 1969, Apollo 11 landed astronauts on the Moon.

The US left Vietnam in 1973, and President Nixon resigned in 1974 over the Watergate scandal. Oil shocks brought inflation and slow growth, shaking confidence. The decade also saw the Roe v. Wade abortion ruling, the rise of environmentalism and new women's rights laws.

Ronald Reagan cut taxes, deregulated business and built up the military, taking a hard line against the Soviet Union. The economy recovered from inflation, and personal computers spread. By 1989, the Berlin Wall fell and the Cold War was ending.

With the Soviet collapse in 1991, the US became the world's sole superpower and led the Gulf War. NAFTA linked it to Canada and Mexico, and the internet fueled a dot-com boom and budget surpluses under President Clinton.

The 9/11 attacks in 2001 led to wars in Afghanistan and, from 2003, Iraq. A housing bubble burst into the 2008 financial crisis, the worst downturn since the Depression. That same year, Barack Obama was elected the first Black president.

The economy slowly recovered, the Affordable Care Act expanded health insurance, and the Supreme Court legalized same-sex marriage nationwide in 2015. Smartphones and social media reshaped daily life. Political polarization deepened, and Donald Trump won the presidency in 2016.

COVID-19 killed more than 1 million Americans. After Joe Biden won the 2020 election, a mob stormed the Capitol on January 6, 2021, and the US withdrew from Afghanistan that year. Inflation surged, and Donald Trump returned to the presidency in 2025.
Mexico: Hunter-gatherers lived in Mexico by the end of the Ice Age. In the highlands of Oaxaca and the Balsas Valley, Archaic foragers began domesticating squash and then maize, bred from the wild grass teosinte by c. 7000 BC. Beans and chili peppers followed, laying the foundation of Mesoamerican life.

Archaic peoples still moved seasonally, but maize cobs were slowly growing larger and gardens mattered more. Toward the end of this era, the first pottery and more permanent settlements appeared along the Pacific and Gulf coasts, setting the stage for village life.

Farming villages spread across Mesoamerica. From c. 1500 BC, the Olmecs of the Gulf Coast built San Lorenzo, carved colossal stone heads and shaped Mesoamerica's 'mother culture,' with its rulers, jade, ballgame and jaguar imagery. Villages like Tlatilco and San José Mogote grew in the highlands.

The Olmec center of La Venta in Tabasco rose to prominence with an earthen pyramid, colossal heads and buried offerings of jade. In Oaxaca, San José Mogote grew into a ranked chiefdom. Olmec styles spread widely through trade, showing a world of growing chiefs and ceremonial centers.

Around c. 500 BC, the Zapotecs founded Monte Albán on a hilltop in Oaxaca, which became one of Mesoamerica's first true cities and an early center of writing and calendars. Olmec La Venta was in its late phase, and Maya villages were growing in Chiapas and Yucatán.

La Venta declined around c. 400 BC, and the classic Olmec era came to an end. Monte Albán grew as the capital of a Zapotec state, carving stone monuments of conquered captives. In the Valley of Mexico, Cuicuilco built a round pyramid and became the region's leading town.

After the Olmecs, Epi-Olmec communities such as Tres Zapotes carried their traditions on along the Gulf Coast. The Zapotec state of Monte Albán expanded across Oaxaca, and Izapa in Chiapas carved story-telling stone monuments. Populations rose as farming intensified.

Rival towns competed in the Valley of Mexico, led by Cuicuilco. In the north of the valley, settlement began at Teotihuacan. Monte Albán dominated Oaxaca, and in West Mexico people buried their dead in deep shaft tombs filled with lively clay figures.

Teotihuacan grew rapidly as people moved there from across the Valley of Mexico. Monte Albán ruled much of Oaxaca, and Maya cities were growing in the Yucatán. Writing and the calendar were spreading through Mesoamerica.

At Tres Zapotes on the Gulf Coast, Stela C bears a date equivalent to 32 BC, one of the earliest known Long Count dates. Teotihuacan was becoming the Valley of Mexico's dominant city, while Cuicuilco faded. Monte Albán continued to rule Oaxaca.

Teotihuacan began its great construction projects, laying out a grid aligned on the Avenue of the Dead. Its people farmed the valley, worked obsidian and drew migrants from afar. Monte Albán ruled Oaxaca, and West Mexico's shaft-tomb cultures flourished.

Teotihuacan became one of the world's largest cities, peaking at perhaps 100,000 people between c. 100 and 550. Its builders raised the Pyramids of the Sun and Moon. The city's influence spread through trade in obsidian and fine goods across Mesoamerica.

Teotihuacan completed the Temple of the Feathered Serpent, burying sacrificial victims beneath it. Residents lived in large apartment compounds, including neighborhoods of Zapotec and Gulf Coast migrants. In the Maya lowlands of southern Mexico, Calakmul and other cities entered the Classic era.

Teotihuacan's reach extended deep into the Maya world; in 378 its agents helped install a new dynasty at Tikal. At home, the city's rulers stayed strikingly anonymous in its art. Monte Albán remained Oaxaca's capital, and Maya kingdoms grew in Campeche and Chiapas.

Teotihuacan was at the height of its power, a cosmopolitan city of artisans, traders and priests. Monte Albán thrived as Teotihuacan's partner in Oaxaca. In the Maya lowlands of southern Mexico, Calakmul's Snake dynasty and Palenque were rising.

Around c. 550, Teotihuacan's center was burned and the great city collapsed, perhaps through internal revolt. Its fall broke central Mexico into smaller rival states. In the south, the Maya kingdoms of Calakmul and Palenque flourished.

In the Epiclassic era after Teotihuacan, new centers rose: Cholula, Xochicalco, Cacaxtla and El Tajín on the Gulf Coast. At Palenque, King Pakal the Great (ruled 615 to 683) built splendid temples, and Calakmul fought Tikal for supremacy in the Maya world.

Fortified hilltop cities like Xochicalco competed for trade in central Mexico, and El Tajín's ballcourts flourished in Veracruz. Monte Albán gradually lost its power over Oaxaca. Late in the century, the Classic Maya cities of the south began to falter.

The Classic Maya kingdoms of Chiapas and Campeche collapsed, but in the northern Yucatán Puuc cities like Uxmal flourished and Chichén Itzá rose. In central Mexico, the Toltecs began building their capital at Tula. Power was shifting north.

The Toltecs, ruling from Tula in Hidalgo, became central Mexico's dominant power, remembered later as master craftsmen and warriors. In the Yucatán, Chichén Itzá rose to dominate the north, with art that shares striking Toltec-style features. Trade routes stretched to the American Southwest.

Tula was at its peak, with warrior columns and a far-reaching trade network. Chichén Itzá ruled much of Yucatán. In Oaxaca, Mixtec kingdoms flourished; the famous lord Eight Deer Jaguar Claw (1063 to 1115) united many of them through conquest and marriage.

Tula fell around c. 1150 and was burned, ending Toltec power. Waves of northern peoples, called Chichimecs, migrated into central Mexico, among them the Mexica, later known as the Aztecs. Chichén Itzá declined, and the Mixtecs produced fine codices and goldwork.

Central Mexico was divided among rival city-states such as Azcapotzalco and Culhuacan. The wandering Mexica arrived in the Valley of Mexico, serving as mercenaries. In Yucatán, Mayapán became the leading city, and in Michoacán the Purépecha (Tarascans) began to build their state.

In 1325, the Mexica founded Tenochtitlan on an island in Lake Texcoco, building chinampa farm plots in the lake. They served the powerful Tepanecs of Azcapotzalco while growing stronger. The Tarascans built a rival kingdom at Tzintzuntzan, and Mayapán ruled Yucatán.

In 1428, the Aztec Triple Alliance of Tenochtitlan, Texcoco and Tlacopan overthrew the Tepanecs and built a tribute empire across central and southern Mexico. Tenochtitlan grew to perhaps 200,000 people. The Tarascans defeated the Aztecs c. 1478, and Mayapán fell in the mid-1400s.

Hernán Cortés and Indigenous allies such as Tlaxcala conquered the Aztecs in 1519 to 1521, aided by smallpox. Spain built Mexico City on the ruins and created New Spain. Epidemics killed most of the Native population, while silver mines at Zacatecas began to enrich the empire.

New Spain was a prosperous Spanish colony whose silver, shipped via the Manila galleons, linked Europe and Asia. Haciendas and mines relied on Indigenous and African labor, and a mixed society of castas grew. The Native population hit its low point early in the century and slowly recovered.

Under the new Bourbon kings of Spain, New Spain's silver output rose and lavish Baroque churches were built. Mestizos became a growing share of the population. Spain founded missions and presidios in Texas to block French expansion from Louisiana.

The Bourbon Reforms tightened Spanish control and taxes, expelled the Jesuits in 1767, and favored Spanish-born officials over Mexican-born Creoles. Missions spread into California from 1769. Guanajuato's silver mines became the world's richest, but resentment of Spain grew.

In 1810, the priest Miguel Hidalgo launched a revolt against Spanish rule, followed by José María Morelos. Both were executed, but in 1821 Agustín de Iturbide won independence and briefly made himself emperor. In 1824, Mexico became a federal republic.

Mexico struggled with coups and debts, led on and off by Antonio López de Santa Anna. Texas broke away in 1836. In the Mexican-American War (1846 to 1848), Mexico lost about half its territory to the US, and the Caste War erupted among the Maya of Yucatán.

Liberals led by Benito Juárez passed reforms limiting the Church's power, sparking the Reform War (1858 to 1861). France then invaded and installed Emperor Maximilian (1864 to 1867), but Juárez's forces defeated and executed him, restoring the republic.

Porfirio Díaz ruled as a dictator from 1876 to 1911, bringing order, railroads and foreign investment. Mexico modernized, but land became concentrated in a few hands, and peasants and Indigenous peoples such as the Yaqui lost their lands. Dissent was suppressed.

Díaz's regime looked stable but grew brittle as he aged. Foreign companies owned mines, railways and newly discovered oil fields, and strikes at Cananea (1906) and Río Blanco (1907) were crushed. In 1910, Francisco Madero challenged Díaz's re-election.

The Mexican Revolution (1910 to 1920) toppled Díaz and became a bloody civil war among leaders like Madero, Huerta, Villa, Zapata and Carranza, killing perhaps a million or more people. The US intervened twice. The 1917 Constitution promised land reform and workers' rights.

Revolutionary generals Obregón and Calles rebuilt the state, while muralists like Diego Rivera celebrated Mexico's Indigenous past. Anticlerical laws sparked the Cristero War (1926 to 1929). In 1929, Calles founded the party that would later become the PRI.

President Lázaro Cárdenas (1934 to 1940) redistributed millions of acres of land to peasants, backed labor unions and in 1938 nationalized the oil industry, creating Pemex. These reforms made him a national hero and cemented the ruling party's grip.

Mexico joined the Allies in World War II, and the Bracero Program sent Mexican workers to US farms. The ruling party took the name PRI in 1946. Industrial growth began the 'Mexican Miracle,' and cities expanded rapidly.

The 'Mexican Miracle' brought steady growth, new factories and a booming middle class, all under the PRI's one-party rule. Women gained the right to vote in federal elections in 1953. Mexico City grew into a sprawling metropolis.

Growth continued, but resentment of PRI authoritarianism rose. Days before Mexico City hosted the 1968 Olympics, troops killed protesting students at Tlatelolco. The massacre shattered the image of a stable, democratic Mexico.

Presidents Echeverría and López Portillo spent heavily and borrowed abroad, especially after huge offshore oil fields were found in the late 1970s. Security forces fought a 'dirty war' against leftist guerrillas. Oil wealth hid deep economic problems.

Falling oil prices brought the 1982 debt crisis, and the peso collapsed. The 1985 Mexico City earthquake killed thousands and exposed government failings. The PRI's disputed 1988 election victory sparked protests, and Mexico began opening its economy.

NAFTA took effect in 1994, the same day the Zapatistas rose up in Chiapas for Indigenous rights. A peso crisis followed. Political reforms loosened the PRI's grip, and it lost control of Congress in 1997.

In 2000, Vicente Fox's victory ended the PRI's 71-year rule. In 2006, President Felipe Calderón sent the army against drug cartels, launching a drug war that brought soaring violence. Mexico's economy grew more tightly tied to the US through manufacturing.

Cartel violence continued, and the disappearance of 43 students from Ayotzinapa in 2014 provoked outrage. Enrique Peña Nieto brought back the PRI and opened the oil sector. In 2018, the leftist Andrés Manuel López Obrador won a landslide.

López Obrador expanded social programs and the army's role, while COVID-19 killed hundreds of thousands. In 2024, Claudia Sheinbaum was elected Mexico's first woman president. Mexico became the United States' largest trading partner, though tariffs and migration strained ties.
Caribbean: For most of this era the islands were empty of people. Foragers reached Trinidad, then close to South America, by c. 6000 BC, and canoe voyagers, perhaps from Central America, reached Cuba and Hispaniola by c. 4000 BC. These Archaic peoples fished, gathered shellfish and hunted with stone tools.

Small Archaic bands lived on Cuba, Hispaniola and Puerto Rico, while others island-hopped north from Trinidad into the Lesser Antilles. They had no pottery or farming to speak of, living from the sea, mangroves and forests, and some islands remained unsettled.

Archaic foragers continued to live along island coasts, leaving shell middens and ground stone tools. Some may have tended wild plants and fruit trees, moving useful species between islands. Population stayed small, scattered in kin-based groups without chiefs or towns.

Island life remained largely unchanged: Archaic peoples fished from canoes, collected shellfish and hunted small animals such as hutias. Several islands, including Jamaica and the Bahamas, still had no human settlers. On the South American mainland, farming peoples were preparing to move into the islands.

Around c. 500 BC, the Saladoid people, farmers and potters from the Orinoco region of Venezuela, began paddling up the Lesser Antilles into Puerto Rico. They brought cassava (manioc) farming and beautiful white-on-red pottery, settling in permanent villages near the older Archaic foragers.

Saladoid villagers spread through the Lesser Antilles and Puerto Rico, clearing gardens for cassava and sweet potatoes. A related group, the Huecoid, also lived in Puerto Rico and the Virgin Islands. Archaic foragers continued to occupy Cuba and Hispaniola.

Saladoid communities lived in circular villages arranged around central plazas, where they buried their dead. They made fine pottery and carved amulets from imported stones. Islands were linked by canoe trade to each other and to the South American mainland.

Saladoid farmers and Archaic foragers shared the islands, sometimes trading. Villages were organized around extended families and spiritual leaders, and early zemí-like carved objects suggest shared religious beliefs. Cassava bread baked on clay griddles became a staple.

Saladoid culture thrived from Trinidad to eastern Hispaniola. Villages grew larger, and long-distance exchange brought stones such as jadeite and carnelian into the islands. Most people lived from gardens, fishing and collecting shellfish.

The Saladoid way of life remained stable for centuries, with farming villages throughout the Lesser Antilles and Puerto Rico. Pottery decorated with modeled animals and painted patterns reflected a rich mythology. Archaic peoples still held much of Cuba.

Saladoid societies were at their height, with large villages in Puerto Rico and the Virgin Islands. Communities shared rituals and burial customs, and canoe routes connected many islands. Life remained village-based, without kingdoms or cities.

Saladoid villagers continued farming cassava, fishing and trading by canoe. Their art showed animals such as frogs, bats and turtles that held religious meaning. Archaic foragers continued older ways in the western islands.

Caribbean societies changed slowly. Saladoid villages dotted the eastern islands, while Archaic foragers lived in Cuba and parts of Hispaniola. Shell, stone and pottery crafts flourished, and village plazas served as ceremonial spaces.

The Saladoid world remained stable, with dozens of farming villages across the Lesser Antilles and Puerto Rico. Some communities began to show signs of ranking, with certain families gaining status. Canoe trade continued to knit islands together.

Late Saladoid pottery became simpler as local styles diverged from island to island. Populations grew in Puerto Rico and eastern Hispaniola. These changes set the stage for new cultures that would take shape over the next centuries.

The Saladoid era was drawing to a close as local traditions developed in Puerto Rico and Hispaniola. Farming communities expanded inland, and some villages grew larger and more permanent. Archaic peoples still lived in Cuba.

Around c. 600, the Ostionoid culture emerged from Saladoid roots in Puerto Rico and Hispaniola. Ostionoid farmers soon spread west to settle Jamaica for the first time and moved into eastern Cuba. Their villages were larger, and farming more intensive.

Ostionoid farmers settled the Bahamas, where their descendants became the Lucayans, and expanded across Hispaniola and Cuba. They built mounded fields for cassava. Chiefs were gaining power as populations grew.

Ostionoid societies grew denser, and the first stone-lined ball courts and plazas appeared in Puerto Rico. These spaces were used for ballgames, dances and ceremonies. Village chiefs began to form larger alliances.

Chiefdoms grew larger and more organized in Hispaniola and Puerto Rico. Ballgames, ancestor worship and carved stone collars and zemís became important parts of religious and political life. The islands were becoming one of the most densely populated areas in the Americas.

The Taíno culture took shape in Hispaniola, Puerto Rico, Cuba and Jamaica. Chiefs called caciques ruled villages and districts, and communities farmed cassava in mounds called conucos. In the Lesser Antilles, distinct island cultures developed.

Taíno chiefdoms expanded, with powerful caciques controlling multiple villages and receiving tribute. Religious life centered on zemís, spirit images carved in stone and wood. In the Lesser Antilles, ancestors of the Kalinago (Island Caribs) were living, though their origins are debated.

Taíno society reached a high level of complexity, with large ceremonial centers like Caguana in Puerto Rico, featuring stone-lined plazas and petroglyphs. Hispaniola was divided among several major chiefdoms. The Kalinago lived in the Lesser Antilles.

Taíno chiefdoms dominated the Greater Antilles, with a population that may have reached several hundred thousand or more. Large canoes carried trade and warriors between islands. The Lucayans of the Bahamas and the Kalinago of the Lesser Antilles had their own distinct cultures.

The Taíno lived in prosperous chiefdoms across the Greater Antilles. In 1492, Columbus landed in the Bahamas and Hispaniola, beginning European contact. Spain built its first settlement, La Isabela, in 1493, and soon began demanding gold and labor from the Taíno.

Under Spanish rule, the Taíno population collapsed from war, forced labor and disease. Spain founded Santo Domingo, Havana and San Juan, then turned to sugar plantations worked by enslaved Africans. Pirates and privateers from rival nations began raiding Spanish ports.

English, French and Dutch forces seized islands, including Barbados and Jamaica (1655), while France took western Hispaniola. A sugar boom built on African slavery transformed the islands into plantation colonies. Buccaneers based at Port Royal and Tortuga ushered in the golden age of piracy.

Sugar made the Caribbean the most valuable part of the colonial world, with Saint-Domingue becoming the richest colony on earth. Enslaved Africans made up the vast majority of people, enduring brutal conditions. Jamaica's Maroons won a treaty from Britain in 1739, and piracy was suppressed.

Britain briefly captured Havana in 1762 during the Seven Years' War. In 1791, enslaved people in Saint-Domingue rose up, beginning the Haitian Revolution under leaders like Toussaint Louverture. They abolished slavery and defeated French, Spanish and British forces.

In 1804, Haiti became the first independent Black republic, born of a successful slave revolt. Britain abolished its slave trade in 1807, while Cuba's sugar plantations expanded with enslaved labor. Haiti took control of Spanish Santo Domingo in 1822.

Britain freed the enslaved people in its Caribbean colonies between 1834 and 1838, and France followed in 1848. The Dominican Republic broke from Haiti in 1844, while Haiti struggled under a crushing indemnity demanded by France in 1825. Indentured laborers from India began arriving in Trinidad.

Cuba's sugar wealth still depended on slavery, and its Ten Years' War for independence began in 1868. Spain reoccupied the Dominican Republic from 1861 to 1865. Jamaica's Morant Bay Rebellion in 1865 was brutally crushed, and Puerto Rico abolished slavery in 1873.

Cuba abolished slavery in 1886, and José Martí launched a new independence war in 1895. In 1898, the US intervened in the Spanish-American War and took Cuba and Puerto Rico. The British colonies remained poor, dependent on falling sugar prices.

Cuba became independent in 1902 but under US control through the Platt Amendment, which granted the US Guantánamo Bay. Puerto Rico was governed directly as a US territory. In 1902, Mount Pelée's eruption on Martinique killed about 28,000 people.

The US occupied Haiti (1915 to 1934) and the Dominican Republic (1916 to 1924), and bought the Danish Virgin Islands in 1917. Puerto Ricans became US citizens in 1917. A World War I sugar boom briefly brought great wealth to Cuba.

The 1920 collapse of sugar prices ruined many Cuban planters, and US companies bought up land. Gerardo Machado became Cuba's strongman in 1925. Jamaican-born Marcus Garvey led a mass movement for Black pride and African unity.

Rafael Trujillo seized power in the Dominican Republic in 1930 and ordered the 1937 massacre of thousands of Haitians. In Cuba, Fulgencio Batista rose to power. Labor riots swept the British Caribbean, sparking trade unions and new political parties.

German U-boats attacked shipping in the Caribbean during World War II. France's islands became overseas departments in 1946, and Puerto Rico's Operation Bootstrap began rapid industrialization. In 1948, the Windrush brought Caribbean migrants to Britain.

Batista seized power in Cuba in 1952, and Fidel Castro's revolution toppled him in 1959. Puerto Rico became a US commonwealth in 1952, and François 'Papa Doc' Duvalier took power in Haiti in 1957. The British islands formed the short-lived West Indies Federation.

The US-backed Bay of Pigs invasion of Cuba failed in 1961, and the 1962 Cuban Missile Crisis brought the world close to nuclear war. Jamaica and Trinidad became independent in 1962, followed by Barbados. Trujillo was assassinated, and US troops intervened in the Dominican Republic in 1965.

More British islands became independent, including the Bahamas and Grenada. Reggae carried Jamaican culture worldwide, and Cuba sent troops to Angola. Jean-Claude 'Baby Doc' Duvalier ruled Haiti, and a leftist revolution took power in Grenada in 1979.

The 1980 Mariel boatlift brought about 125,000 Cubans to the US. The US invaded Grenada in 1983, and Haiti's Duvalier dictatorship fell in 1986. Tourism and offshore banking became key industries for many islands.
