The Soviet Union's collapse plunged Cuba into a severe economic crisis known as the Special Period. Haiti elected Jean-Bertrand Aristide, who was overthrown in 1991 and restored by US troops in 1994. Tourism boomed in the Dominican Republic and elsewhere.

Raúl Castro succeeded his brother Fidel in Cuba. Haiti's Aristide was ousted again in 2004, and UN peacekeepers arrived. Venezuela's PetroCaribe program provided cheap oil to many islands, while tourism grew across the region.

The 2010 Haiti earthquake killed over 100,000 people, and a cholera outbreak followed. The US and Cuba restored diplomatic relations in 2015. Puerto Rico faced a debt crisis, then devastating Hurricane Maria in 2017.

COVID-19 shut down tourism across the islands. Haiti's president was assassinated in 2021 and gangs took over much of Port-au-Prince. Cuba faced protests, blackouts and mass emigration, while Barbados became a republic in 2021.
Central America: Paleo-Indian hunters passed through the isthmus on their way into South America by the end of the Ice Age. Afterwards, Archaic foragers lived in its forests and coasts, and in Panama people were already cultivating plants such as squash and arrowroot by c. 7000 BC. Maize arrived from Mexico later.

Archaic peoples lived by foraging, fishing and small-scale gardening. In Panama, Monagrillo pottery, made c. 2500 BC, is among the earliest in the Americas. Communities were small, mobile and organized by kinship, with farming slowly becoming more important.

Farming villages appeared along the Pacific coast of Guatemala, and maize-growing settlers moved into the Maya lowlands toward the end of this era. Pottery and settled life spread through the region. In lower Central America, villages grew around root crops and maize.

Early Maya villages and ceremonial centers took shape in Guatemala and Belize, at sites like Ceibal and Nakbé, where people built the first platforms and plazas. Olmec styles from Mexico influenced local art. Communities were growing more organized and unequal.

Maya communities in the Mirador Basin of northern Guatemala built raised causeways and larger temples. In the highlands, Kaminaljuyu, on the site of today's Guatemala City, grew into a major center. Long-distance trade carried jade and obsidian.

Maya centers like Nakbé and El Mirador grew rapidly, with large stone platforms and plazas. In El Salvador, Chalchuapa thrived on trade. Society was becoming more hierarchical, with chiefs and specialists in crafts and rituals.

The Late Preclassic Maya began building on a monumental scale, especially at El Mirador. Early forms of Maya writing were emerging. Highland centers like Kaminaljuyu controlled trade in obsidian and jade.

El Mirador grew into a huge city with massive pyramids, while other centers spread across the Petén lowlands. Kings began to appear in art, holding religious and political power. The Maya were developing calendars and hieroglyphic writing.

The Preclassic Maya megacity El Mirador reached its peak, with the La Danta pyramid among the largest in the world. At nearby San Bartolo, murals painted c. 100 BC depict Maya myths and kingship. The highland and Pacific coast centers flourished.

El Mirador still dominated the Petén lowlands, linked to other cities by raised causeways. Kaminaljuyu and Takalik Abaj thrived in the highlands and Pacific slope, carving monuments with early writing and dates. Maya kingship was becoming firmly established.

El Mirador began to decline, possibly due to environmental damage and political change. Tikal and other cities were growing. In lower Central America, chiefdoms in Costa Rica and Panama traded jade, pottery and food.

Many Preclassic Maya cities, including El Mirador, were abandoned in a crisis whose causes are still debated, perhaps drought or deforestation. Tikal survived and grew stronger, laying foundations for the Classic era. In the highlands, Kaminaljuyu remained powerful.

The Classic Maya golden age began around c. 250, with dynasties ruling cities such as Tikal. The Maya refined their hieroglyphic writing, calendars, astronomy and use of zero, carving dated stone stelae such as Tikal's Stela 29 in 292.

In 378, warriors linked to Teotihuacan arrived at Tikal and installed a new dynasty, spreading central Mexican influence. Maya city-states grew in number and size. Lower Central American societies were organized as chiefdoms rather than kingdoms.

In 426, K'inich Yax K'uk' Mo' founded the royal dynasty of Copán in Honduras. Tikal dominated the central lowlands. The Ilopango volcano in El Salvador erupted massively c. 431, devastating the surrounding region.

Tikal was defeated in 562 by Caracol, in Belize, which was allied with the powerful Calakmul. A long hiatus followed at Tikal. Around c. 600, a volcanic eruption buried the village of Joya de Cerén in El Salvador, preserving everyday Maya life.
Calakmul dominated the Maya world through a network of allied cities, until Tikal's king Jasaw Chan K'awiil defeated it in 695. Copán grew wealthy and powerful. Maya art and architecture flourished.

Classic Maya population peaked, possibly in the millions. In 738, Copán's king Waxaklajuun Ub'aah K'awiil was captured and executed by Quiriguá. Copán built its great Hieroglyphic Stairway, while Tikal raised new temples.

The Classic Maya collapse swept through the southern lowlands between c. 800 and 900, caused by drought, warfare and overpopulation. Kings stopped erecting monuments and cities like Tikal and Copán were gradually abandoned.

The southern Maya lowlands emptied, and the last Long Count dates were carved. Maya communities survived in smaller villages, around lakes in the Petén and in the Guatemalan highlands. In Costa Rica and Panama, chiefdoms made gold ornaments and stone spheres.

In the Postclassic period, Nahua-speaking Pipil migrants from Mexico settled in El Salvador. Highland Maya peoples like the K'iche' and Kaqchikel formed new kingdoms. Lower Central America saw powerful chiefdoms, with centers like Guayabo in Costa Rica.

Small Maya kingdoms competed in the Guatemalan highlands, building fortified hilltop towns. Pipil communities grew in El Salvador, while chiefdoms flourished in Nicaragua and Costa Rica. Trade linked the region to Mexico and South America.

The K'iche' Maya were emerging as the main power of the Guatemalan highlands. Nahua-speaking Nicarao and Chorotega peoples lived around Nicaragua's lakes. Panama and Costa Rica were home to chiefdoms known for goldwork.

The K'iche' kingdom, ruling from Q'umarkaj (Utatlán), expanded its control over neighboring highland groups. In the Petén, the Itzá Maya ruled from their island capital Nojpetén. Chiefdoms traded gold, cacao and textiles.

The K'iche' kingdom reached its height under K'iq'ab, but the Kaqchikel broke away and founded Iximche c. 1470. Highland Maya kingdoms fought among themselves. Lower Central America's chiefdoms remained independent and prosperous.

Columbus reached the coast in 1502, Balboa crossed Panama to the Pacific in 1513, and Pedro de Alvarado conquered Guatemala in 1524. Disease and enslavement devastated Native peoples. Spain ruled the region from Guatemala, while Panama became a route for Peruvian silver.

The Kingdom of Guatemala exported indigo and cacao, and Spanish landowners relied on Indigenous labor. Pirate Henry Morgan sacked Panama in 1671. The last independent Maya kingdom, the Itzá at Nojpetén, fell to Spain in 1697.

Indigo from El Salvador became the region's main export. British logwood cutters settled in Belize, and the Miskito people allied with Britain on the Caribbean coast. Spanish control of the Caribbean side remained weak.

Earthquakes destroyed Antigua in 1773, and the capital moved to Guatemala City. Bourbon reforms tightened Spanish control. In Belize, British settlers defeated a Spanish attack at St. George's Caye in 1798.

Central America declared independence from Spain in 1821, briefly joined Mexico's empire, and then formed the Federal Republic of Central America (1823 to 1841), uniting Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras, Nicaragua and Costa Rica. Panama joined Gran Colombia instead.

The Federal Republic was torn by civil war between liberals led by Francisco Morazán and conservatives led by Rafael Carrera. It broke up into separate states between 1838 and 1841. Coffee cultivation began in Costa Rica.

American adventurer William Walker seized Nicaragua in 1856 but was defeated by Central American armies. The Panama Railroad opened in 1855. Liberal reforms began in Guatemala, and Belize became the colony of British Honduras.

Liberal regimes promoted coffee exports, taking land from Indigenous communities and forcing their labor. Railroads helped US companies start banana plantations. France's attempt to build a Panama canal failed in the 1880s.

Panama split from Colombia in 1903 with US backing, and the US began building the Panama Canal. United Fruit Company gained huge influence, and dictators like Guatemala's Manuel Estrada Cabrera ruled.

The Panama Canal opened in 1914, transforming world shipping and cementing US power in the region. The US occupied Nicaragua from 1912, and banana companies dominated Honduras. The term 'banana republic' captured how foreign firms controlled local politics.

Augusto Sandino led a guerrilla war against US Marines occupying Nicaragua until they withdrew in 1933. United Fruit controlled land, railways and ports in several countries. Coffee and banana prices shaped politics, and a small landowning elite held power.

The Depression brought dictators to power, including Ubico in Guatemala and Anastasio Somoza in Nicaragua, who had Sandino killed. In El Salvador, the army killed thousands of peasants in the 1932 Matanza.

In 1944, a revolution in Guatemala overthrew Ubico and began a decade of democracy. Costa Rica's brief 1948 civil war led to the abolition of its army. Somoza strengthened his family's grip on Nicaragua.

Guatemala's President Árbenz launched land reform that angered United Fruit. In 1954, a CIA-backed coup in Guatemala toppled him. Somoza was assassinated in 1956, but his sons continued ruling Nicaragua.

Guatemala's long civil war began in 1960, pitting leftist guerrillas against the army. The Sandinista guerrilla movement formed in Nicaragua, and a common market boosted regional trade. El Salvador and Honduras fought the brief 'Football War' in 1969.

A 1972 earthquake devastated Managua, and the Somozas' theft of aid fueled anger. The Sandinista revolution of 1979 toppled the dictatorship. The 1977 Torrijos-Carter treaties promised Panama control of its canal.

Brutal civil wars raged in El Salvador and Guatemala, where the army massacred Maya villagers, and in Nicaragua, where US-backed Contras fought the Sandinistas. Archbishop Romero was murdered in 1980. Belize became independent in 1981, and the US invaded Panama in 1989.

Peace accords ended the wars in El Salvador (1992) and Guatemala (1996), and Nicaraguans voted the Sandinistas out in 1990. Hurricane Mitch devastated Honduras and Nicaragua in 1998. In 1999, Panama took full control of the canal.

Street gangs like MS-13 spread violence, especially in El Salvador, Honduras and Guatemala. A free trade deal, CAFTA-DR, linked the region to the US. Daniel Ortega returned to power in Nicaragua in 2007, and a coup ousted Honduras's president in 2009.

Violence and poverty drove large migrations north from Guatemala, El Salvador and Honduras. Nicaragua's Ortega crushed protests in 2018. Panama's expanded canal opened in 2016, and protests against corruption toppled Guatemala's president in 2015.

El Salvador's President Bukele imprisoned tens of thousands in a crackdown on gangs and made bitcoin legal tender. Ortega ruled Nicaragua with increasing repression. Guatemala elected reformist Bernardo Arévalo, and drought disrupted the Panama Canal in 2023.
Brazil: Hunter-gatherers lived in Brazil by at least c. 12,000 years ago, painting caves in the Amazon and the eastern highlands, where the ancient 'Luzia' skeleton was found. Amazonian peoples later began domesticating manioc, coastal groups piled up shell mounds called sambaquis, and pottery at Taperinha is among the Americas' oldest.

Brazil's peoples lived by foraging, fishing and early gardening. Along the Atlantic coast, sambaqui builders raised huge shell mounds that served as cemeteries and landmarks. In the Amazon, communities tended manioc, peach palm and other useful plants, slowly shaping the forest itself.

Sambaqui communities along the southern coast built some of their largest shell mounds, a few as tall as 30 meters. In the southwestern Amazon, the ancestors of the Tupi-speaking peoples were living in their homeland. Farming of manioc and other crops spread through the forest.

Pottery-making and farming villages became more common in the Amazon basin. Sambaqui builders still thrived on the coast, living on fish and shellfish. Brazil was home to many separate peoples speaking languages of the Tupi, Arawak, Carib and Macro-Jê families.

Amazonian farmers began creating rich, fertile soils called terra preta (dark earth) by mixing charcoal, pottery and waste into the ground. Early pottery cultures appeared on Marajó Island at the mouth of the Amazon. Coastal shell-mound societies continued.

Villages grew along Amazonian rivers, supported by fishing, turtle farming and gardens on terra preta. Groups speaking Tupi-Guarani languages began gradually expanding outward from the southern Amazon. Life was organized around villages and kinship rather than states.

Amazonian societies were diverse, ranging from small mobile bands to large riverside villages that lasted for generations. Terra preta deposits grew around these long-lived settlements. On the coast, sambaqui builders continued their traditions of fishing and mound-building.

In western Amazonia, in today's Acre, people began building large geometric earthworks, ditched circles and squares now called geoglyphs, around this era. They were likely ceremonial spaces. Farming and managed forests supported growing populations.

Geoglyph-building continued in Acre, and riverside villages expanded along the Amazon and its tributaries. Tupi-Guarani peoples continued slowly migrating, carrying farming and pottery traditions. The coast remained home to shell-mound societies.

Brazil's many peoples had no single state but lived in a patchwork of villages. Amazonian communities built terra preta soils, cultivated forest orchards and fished the rivers. Pottery styles became more varied and elaborate.

Large villages flourished along the Amazon, and the Acre geoglyph tradition continued. Tupi-Guarani-speaking groups spread south and east toward the Paraná River and the coast. Life was village-based, with farming, fishing and hunting.

In the southern highlands, ancestors of today's southern Jê peoples began living in clustered pit houses in araucaria pine forests, eating pine nuts. Amazonian river societies grew larger. Tupi-Guarani migrations continued.

Amazonian peoples continued to manage the forest, planting useful trees like Brazil nuts and palms. On the coast, sambaqui societies slowly changed as farmers and potters moved in. Large chiefdoms were beginning to emerge in parts of the Amazon.

Riverside societies in the Amazon grew more complex, with larger villages and wider trade networks. In the south, pit-house villages spread across the highlands. Tupi-Guarani-speaking farmers expanded toward the Atlantic coast.

The Marajoara mound-builder culture (c. 400 to 1400) emerged on Marajó Island at the Amazon's mouth. Its people built large earthen mounds for homes and burials and made elaborately painted funerary urns. They may have been organized into chiefdoms.

Marajoara society thrived, with mound villages, fish ponds and polychrome pottery. Elsewhere, Tupi-Guarani peoples continued their migration, and Amazonian river societies grew. Brazil was home to millions of people spread across diverse cultures.

Marajoara chiefdoms ruled at the mouth of the Amazon, while villages and chiefdoms lined the main river. Terra preta soils supported intensive farming. Shell-mound building was fading on the coast as Tupi farmers arrived.

Amazonian societies continued to expand, with large settlements on bluffs above the rivers and causeways linking fields and villages. Marajoara culture remained strong at the river's mouth. In the south, Guarani farmers moved along the river valleys, clearing forest gardens.

In the Upper Xingu region, ancestors of today's Kuikuro people began building villages that would grow into networks of towns. Marajoara and other Amazonian chiefdoms thrived. Tupi-Guarani peoples spread along the coast.

The Santarém (Tapajós) culture began to rise near the mouth of the Tapajós River, known for intricate pottery. Amazonian chiefdoms controlled stretches of river. Sambaqui building had largely ended on the coast.

The Santarém culture grew into a powerful chiefdom with a large central town. Marajoara society continued. Tupinambá and other Tupi peoples occupied much of the Atlantic coast, farming manioc and fighting rival groups.

Amazonian chiefdoms flourished along the main rivers, with dense populations living on terra preta soils. The Santarém culture produced elaborate ceramics and green stone amulets called muiraquitãs. Tupi peoples dominated the coast.

In the Upper Xingu, villages surrounded by ditches and linked by roads formed 'garden cities' with plazas and bridges. Santarém and other chiefdoms thrived. Brazil's population may have been in the millions.

Marajoara culture declined by c. 1400. Xingu settlements and Santarém continued to flourish. Tupinambá and Guarani peoples lived in villages of large communal houses along the coast and southern rivers.

Brazil was home to millions of Native people in hundreds of societies. The 1494 Treaty of Tordesillas, drawn up by Spain and Portugal, gave Portugal the eastern part of South America, even before Europeans had seen it.

In 1500, Pedro Álvares Cabral claimed Brazil for Portugal. The Portuguese first traded for brazilwood, then built sugar plantations in the northeast worked by enslaved Africans. Salvador became the capital in 1549, while Jesuit missions and epidemics transformed and devastated Native societies.

The Dutch held the sugar-rich northeast from 1630 to 1654. Palmares, the largest runaway-slave community, resisted for decades until destroyed in the 1690s. Brazil became the largest destination of the slave trade, and bandeirante raiders pushed inland.

The discovery of gold in Minas Gerais sparked a gold rush, drawing settlers and enslaved Africans inland. Ouro Preto grew rich, building ornate Baroque churches. Diamonds were also found, making Brazil Portugal's most valuable colony.

Portugal's minister Pombal centralized control, expelled the Jesuits in 1759 and moved the capital to Rio de Janeiro in 1763. Gold output declined. In 1789, a plot for independence in Minas Gerais was crushed, and its leader Tiradentes was executed.
In 1808, the Portuguese court fled Napoleon to Rio, making Brazil the center of the empire. In 1822, Prince Pedro declared independence, founding the Empire of Brazil with himself as Emperor Pedro I.

Brazil lost Uruguay in 1828, and Pedro I abdicated in 1831. During the regency, revolts erupted in several provinces, including the Malê uprising of enslaved Muslims in Bahia. Pedro II took the throne in 1840, and coffee became a key export.

Brazil ended the Atlantic slave trade in 1850, but slavery continued. Coffee plantations expanded in São Paulo and Rio. Brazil joined Argentina and Uruguay in the brutal Paraguayan War (1864 to 1870), and the 1871 Free Womb Law freed the children of enslaved mothers.

In 1888, Brazil became the last country in the Americas to abolish slavery. The army overthrew Pedro II in 1889, creating a republic. Millions of European immigrants arrived, and the Amazon rubber boom made Manaus rich.

The republic was dominated by coffee planters of São Paulo and Minas Gerais. The Amazon rubber boom peaked, and Brazil acquired Acre from Bolivia in 1903. Rio de Janeiro was rebuilt with grand boulevards.
The rubber boom collapsed as plantations in Asia took over. Brazil joined World War I in 1917. Industry grew in São Paulo, and the Contestado War pitted peasants against the government in the south.

Young army officers known as tenentes rebelled against the coffee oligarchy, and the Prestes Column marched across the interior. São Paulo's 1922 Modern Art Week launched a new Brazilian culture. The 1929 crash devastated coffee prices and the old republic's finances.

In 1930, Getúlio Vargas took power in a revolution. In 1937, he imposed the Estado Novo dictatorship, centralizing power and promoting industry and nationalism. He introduced labor laws that won him support among workers.

Brazil joined the Allies in World War II and sent troops to fight in Italy. Vargas was overthrown in 1945, and a new democratic constitution was adopted in 1946. Industrialization continued, with state-backed steel mills.

Vargas returned to power by election in 1951 and created the oil company Petrobras, but took his own life in 1954. President Kubitschek promised 'fifty years of progress in five.' Brazil won its first World Cup in 1958.

In 1960, Brasília became the capital, built from scratch in the interior. Political turmoil led to a military coup in 1964, which began military rule lasting until 1985. The regime increasingly repressed opponents.

The military regime presided over an 'economic miracle' of rapid growth, while censoring the press and torturing opponents. The Trans-Amazonian Highway opened the rainforest to settlement. Late in the decade, the regime began a slow political opening.

The debt crisis brought soaring inflation and economic stagnation. Millions joined the Diretas Já campaign demanding direct elections, and democracy was restored in 1985. A new constitution was adopted in 1988, and activist Chico Mendes was killed defending the Amazon.

President Collor was impeached for corruption in 1992. The 1994 Real Plan ended hyperinflation, and Fernando Henrique Cardoso stabilized the economy and privatized state firms. Brazil hosted the 1992 Earth Summit in Rio, as global attention turned to the Amazon.

President Lula, a former metalworker, expanded social programs like Bolsa Família that cut poverty. A commodity boom fueled growth, and Brazil joined the BRICS group of emerging powers. Huge offshore oil reserves were discovered.

Dilma Rousseff faced mass protests, a deep recession and the Car Wash corruption scandal, and was impeached in 2016. Brazil hosted the 2014 World Cup and 2016 Olympics. Jair Bolsonaro won the presidency in 2018.

COVID-19 killed over 700,000 Brazilians. Lula won the 2022 election, and Bolsonaro supporters stormed government buildings in January 2023. Bolsonaro was later convicted of plotting a coup, and Brazil hosted the COP30 climate summit in 2025.
Andes: Hunter-gatherers spread through the Andes by c. 12,000 years ago, adapting to coasts, valleys and high grasslands. Over millennia, Andean peoples domesticated potatoes, squash and beans, and herders tamed llamas and alpacas from wild camelids. In Ecuador, the Valdivia culture made some of the Americas' earliest pottery.

Around c. 2600 BC, Caral in Peru's Norte Chico region became the oldest city in the Americas, with stone pyramids and sunken plazas, sustained by fishing and cotton farming. Valdivia potters in Ecuador and Puerto Hormiga in Colombia made early ceramics. Highland temples like Kotosh appeared.

Norte Chico declined, but large U-shaped temple centers rose on the Peruvian coast, such as Sechín Alto, with carved stones showing warriors and victims. Irrigation farming, pottery and weaving spread. Early metalworkers hammered gold into thin sheets.

The Chavín culture (c. 900 to 200 BC) centered on the temple of Chavín de Huántar in Peru's highlands, a pilgrimage site with stone carvings of jaguars and snakes. Its religious style spread widely. On the south coast, the Paracas culture emerged.

Chavín de Huántar was at its height, drawing pilgrims from far away and spreading a shared religious art. Around Lake Titicaca, villages like Chiripa built sunken temples, and Pukara was emerging. Llama caravans carried goods between coast and highlands.

Chavín influence remained strong across Peru, while the Paracas culture produced fine textiles on the south coast. On the coast of Ecuador and Colombia, the Tumaco-La Tolita culture made remarkable gold and even platinum objects. Societies were increasingly hierarchical.

Paracas weavers produced dazzling embroidered mantles, buried with the dead in large desert cemeteries. Chavín's religious influence started to fade. In the Titicaca basin, Pukara grew into a major ceremonial center with sunken courts and carved stone sculpture.

Chavín's religious influence ended around c. 200 BC, and regional cultures took its place. On the north coast, Salinar and Gallinazo peoples built irrigation canals. Paracas culture flourished on the south coast.

The Nazca culture emerged on Peru's south coast, growing out of Paracas. In Colombia, San Agustín carved large stone statues, and goldworkers in several regions made fine ornaments. The Andes were a patchwork of regional chiefdoms.

Nazca society grew, building the ceremonial center of Cahuachi, a place of pilgrimage. On the north coast, Gallinazo peoples farmed river valleys with canals, and Pukara dominated the Titicaca basin. In Colombia, Calima goldworkers made elaborate ornaments.

Moche society was emerging on Peru's north coast, while Nazca thrived in the south. Both cultures relied on irrigation to farm desert valleys. In Colombia and Ecuador, local chiefdoms produced fine goldwork and pottery.

The Moche of the north coast built huge adobe pyramids, the Huacas del Sol y de la Luna, and made realistic portrait pottery. In the south, the Nazca culture made the famous Nazca Lines in the desert. Each culture had its own powerful lords.

Moche lords were buried with rich treasures, such as the Lord of Sipán c. 250. Nazca society continued, with underground aqueducts. In the highlands, the Recuay culture flourished, and Tiwanaku grew on the shores of Lake Titicaca.

The Moche ruled the north coast valleys through powerful warrior-priests who staged ritual combat and sacrifice. Nazca potters made colorful vessels and people kept creating desert lines. Tiwanaku grew into an important city near Lake Titicaca.

Tiwanaku expanded its influence around Lake Titicaca, building monumental stone temples and raised fields that produced large harvests at high altitude. The Moche and Nazca flourished on the coast. In Colombia, many peoples lived in chiefdoms.

Severe floods and droughts, possibly linked to El Niño, disrupted Moche society. Tiwanaku built the Akapana pyramid and expanded its trade networks. In the highlands of Ayacucho, the Wari state was beginning to rise.

The Wari and Tiwanaku empires dominated the central Andes. Wari, based near Ayacucho, built administrative centers and roads that foreshadowed the Inca. Tiwanaku controlled the Titicaca basin and colonies in lower valleys, held together by religion and llama caravans.

Wari expanded its control, building centers like Pikillacta near Cusco. Moche society came to an end, and the Lambayeque (Sicán) culture rose on the north coast. In Colombia, the Muisca and Tairona were forming chiefdoms.
Wari and Tiwanaku remained powerful in the Andes. The Sicán culture flourished on the north coast, known for gold masks and metalwork. In Colombia, the Tairona began building Ciudad Perdida.
Sicán lords built pyramids and buried rulers with vast amounts of gold. Wari began to decline. The Chimú culture was emerging on the north coast, with its capital at Chan Chan.

Wari and Tiwanaku collapsed around c. 1000, possibly due to drought. The Chimú began building Chan Chan, the largest adobe city in the Americas. Muisca and Tairona chiefdoms flourished in Colombia, and the Chachapoya built fortresses like Kuélap.
The Chimú expanded along the north coast. Around Lake Titicaca, Aymara kingdoms like the Lupaca and Colla filled the gap left by Tiwanaku. Legend says the Inca founded Cusco around this time.

The Inca were a small kingdom in the Cusco valley, competing with neighbors. The Chimú grew stronger, and the Chincha traders thrived on the south coast. In Colombia, the Muisca formed confederations under rulers called the Zipa and Zaque.

The Chimú conquered the Lambayeque region around c. 1375, building the largest coastal kingdom. In the highlands, the Inca fought rivals like the Chanka. Muisca chiefdoms in Colombia traded gold, salt and emeralds.

In 1438, Pachacuti founded the Inca Empire after defeating the Chanka. The Inca conquered the Chimú and built Machu Picchu c. 1450. Their empire, called Tawantinsuyu, stretched from Ecuador to Chile. In 1498, Columbus reached Venezuela.

An Inca civil war and smallpox (1527 to 1532) weakened the empire. In 1532, Francisco Pizarro captured Atahualpa and conquered the Inca. Spain founded Lima and Bogotá, and silver from Potosí (from 1545) funded Spain's empire.

The Viceroyalty of Peru ruled from Lima, and Potosí became one of the world's largest cities. Spanish laws forced Indigenous people to labor in mines under the mita system. Cartagena became a major slave port.

Spain created the Viceroyalty of New Granada, centered on Bogotá. Potosí's silver production declined, and Venezuela grew rich from cacao. Indigenous and mixed-race communities resisted heavy taxes and forced labor.

In 1780 to 1781, Túpac Amaru II, claiming Inca descent, led a massive Indigenous rebellion against Spanish abuses that Spain crushed brutally. Túpac Katari besieged La Paz. In New Granada, the Comuneros revolted against taxes, and Creole discontent slowly grew.

Simón Bolívar and José de San Martín led the independence wars. Between 1819 and 1824, they liberated Colombia, Venezuela, Ecuador, Peru and Bolivia, culminating in the Battle of Ayacucho in 1824. Gran Colombia was formed.

Bolivia became independent in 1825, and Gran Colombia broke into Venezuela, Ecuador and New Granada (Colombia) by 1831. Military strongmen called caudillos ruled. A Peru-Bolivian Confederation failed in 1839, and Peru's guano exports began to boom.

Peru grew rich from guano fertilizer exports, importing Chinese laborers to dig it. Slavery was abolished across the region in the 1850s. Venezuela fought the bloody Federal War, and Colombia adopted a loose federal constitution in 1863.
In the War of the Pacific (1879 to 1884), Chile defeated Peru and Bolivia, and Bolivia lost its coast. Colombia's Regeneration created a centralized state, and its Thousand Days' War began in 1899.
Colombia's Thousand Days' War ended in 1902, and Panama broke away in 1903. In Venezuela, Juan Vicente Gómez seized power in 1908. Rubber barons brutalized Indigenous workers in the Amazon.
Oil was discovered in Venezuela in 1914, beginning its transformation. Hiram Bingham brought Machu Picchu to world attention in 1911. Augusto Leguía began an eleven-year rule in Peru in 1919.

Venezuela became one of the world's top oil exporters under the dictator Gómez, as foreign companies poured in. Peru's Víctor Raúl Haya de la Torre founded the APRA movement. In Colombia, troops killed striking banana workers in 1928.

Bolivia lost the Chaco War (1932 to 1935) against Paraguay, discrediting its old elite. Colombia and Peru fought over Leticia in the Amazon. The Depression hit export economies hard, and new nationalist and reformist movements grew.

Peru defeated Ecuador in a 1941 border war. In Colombia, the 1948 assassination of populist leader Jorge Eliécer Gaitán sparked riots in Bogotá and a decade of civil violence known as La Violencia. Venezuela's brief democracy ended in a 1948 coup.

Bolivia's 1952 revolution nationalized tin mines, gave land to peasants and granted universal suffrage. Venezuela's dictator Pérez Jiménez fell in 1958, beginning democracy. In Colombia, the National Front ended La Violencia.
Guerrilla movements like the FARC formed in Colombia. Che Guevara was killed in Bolivia in 1967. Venezuela helped found OPEC in 1960, and a military government took power in Peru in 1968.

Peru's military regime carried out sweeping land reform and nationalizations. Venezuela nationalized its oil industry in 1976 and enjoyed a boom. Bolivia was ruled by a military dictatorship under Hugo Banzer, and Peru returned to civilian rule in 1980.

Peru's Shining Path insurgency killed tens of thousands, and Colombian cocaine cartels like Pablo Escobar's spread terror. Hyperinflation struck Bolivia and Peru, and riots shook Caracas in 1989. In Colombia, a volcanic mudflow buried the town of Armero in 1985.

Peru's Alberto Fujimori captured Shining Path's leader in 1992 but ruled autocratically. Escobar was killed in 1993. In 1999, Hugo Chávez took power in Venezuela and launched his 'Bolivarian revolution.'

Chávez used oil wealth for social programs while concentrating power. Evo Morales became Bolivia's first Indigenous president in 2006, and Rafael Correa rose in Ecuador. Colombia's army, backed by the US, pushed back the FARC.

After Chávez's death in 2013, Venezuela collapsed under Nicolás Maduro, with hyperinflation and shortages, and some 7 million or more people emigrated. The 2016 Colombia-FARC peace deal ended a 52-year war. Bolivia's Evo Morales was ousted in 2019.

COVID-19 hit Peru with one of the world's highest death rates, and Peru cycled through presidents. Maduro claimed victory in Venezuela's disputed 2024 election. Gustavo Petro became Colombia's first leftist president, and gang violence surged in Ecuador.
Southern Tip: Around c. 14,500 years ago, people camped at Monte Verde in southern Chile, an early human site in the Americas. Hunters later pursued horses and giant sloths in Patagonia and stenciled hands at Cueva de las Manos, and by c. 5000 BC the Chinchorro of the Atacama coast made the world's oldest artificial mummies.

Chinchorro fishing communities on the Atacama coast continued their elaborate mummification. Guanaco hunters roamed Patagonia and the Pampas, while canoe peoples fished and hunted seals in the channels of Tierra del Fuego. In Uruguay's wetlands, people began building earthen mounds called cerritos.

Mound-building communities in Uruguay grew plants such as squash and maize alongside fishing and hunting. The Chinchorro tradition faded around c. 1500 BC. In the Atacama and northwest Argentina, people began herding llamas and farming in oases.

Formative farming villages appeared in the Atacama Desert and northwest Argentina, with sites like Tulor near San Pedro de Atacama. Llama caravans linked oases and highlands. Further south, hunter-gatherers still lived in Patagonia and Tierra del Fuego.

Northern farmers grew maize, beans and quinoa, irrigating desert valleys. Mound-builders lived in Uruguay's wetlands, while hunter-gatherer bands roamed the Pampas and Patagonia. No states existed; people lived in villages or mobile groups.

Villages in northwest Argentina produced fine pottery and carved stone objects. Canoe peoples in Tierra del Fuego developed a culture well suited to the cold seas. Patagonian hunters followed guanaco herds across the steppes.

Farming communities expanded in northwest Argentina, and pottery styles became more elaborate. In central Chile, foragers and early farmers lived along the rivers. The south remained the land of hunter-gatherers.

In northwest Argentina, the Tafí culture raised standing stones and terraced fields in mountain valleys. Atacama villages traded with the highlands. Mound-builders and hunter-gatherers lived in the east and south.

Agricultural villages in northwest Argentina grew in size and complexity, including the Ciénaga culture. Herders in the Atacama exchanged goods across the Andes. Elsewhere, people lived as hunters, fishers and foragers.

Village life deepened in the north, with metal objects starting to appear. In Uruguay and southern Brazil, mound-builders continued their traditions. Patagonia and the Pampas were home to mobile hunting peoples.

Northern farmers continued irrigating fields, and copper and gold were being worked in the Andean foothills. In south-central Chile, the ancestors of the Mapuche were beginning to farm and make pottery. Hunter-gatherers lived throughout the south.

The Ciénaga culture flourished in northwest Argentina, producing fine engraved pottery and early metalwork. Mapuche ancestors lived in the forests of south-central Chile. During the first millennium AD, Guarani-speaking farmers spread into the Paraná and Paraguay river basins.

Pitrén pottery appeared in south-central Chile among early Mapuche communities, who combined gardening with gathering and hunting. The Atacama oases grew more populous. Patagonian and Fuegian peoples continued their hunting and fishing ways, adapted to cold steppes and seas.

Farming and herding villages flourished in the north, linked by caravan routes across deserts and mountains. Guarani farmers settled in the forests of Paraguay, growing manioc and maize. The Pampas and Patagonia remained hunting lands for mobile bands.

The rising power of Tiwanaku, near Lake Titicaca, influenced San Pedro de Atacama through trade and religion. Villages in northwest Argentina grew larger. The region had no large states, and most people lived in villages or mobile bands.

Tiwanaku trade brought fine textiles, pottery and carved snuff trays to the Atacama oases, where local leaders gained status. Guarani villages spread along the Paraná River. Hunter-gatherers continued their ancient ways across the Pampas and Patagonia.

The Aguada culture emerged in northwest Argentina, with powerful leaders and art featuring jaguars, warriors and sacrifice. Tiwanaku's influence remained strong in the Atacama. Mapuche ancestors farmed and foraged in the forests of south-central Chile.

Aguada flourished, building ceremonial centers and producing fine bronze metalwork and painted pottery. Tiwanaku trade connected the region to the central Andes. Guarani farmers continued expanding through the river forests of Paraguay and beyond.

Aguada remained powerful in northwest Argentina, its society divided between elites and farmers. In south-central Chile, Mapuche communities farmed and gathered pine nuts. Patagonian peoples continued to hunt guanaco and rhea across the open steppe.

Aguada declined around c. 900, and new regional chiefdoms emerged in northwest Argentina. The Atacama oases faced change as Tiwanaku weakened. Guarani communities thrived in Paraguay, while Charrúa and other hunters roamed Uruguay's grasslands.

With Tiwanaku's collapse, fortified villages called pucaras appeared in the Atacama and northwest Argentina, reflecting increased conflict among local groups. The Diaguita culture flourished in north-central Chile, known for its painted pottery. Mapuche groups lived in the south.

Regional chiefdoms competed in northwest Argentina, building walled settlements on hillsides with terraced fields. The Diaguita prospered in Chile's transverse valleys. Mapuche communities lived in villages scattered across the forests and rivers of the south.

Settlements like Quilmes in northwest Argentina grew into large stone towns with thousands of people. Pucaras dominated the Atacama landscape. Charrúa hunters lived in Uruguay, Guarani farmers in Paraguay, and nomadic bands across the Pampas and Patagonia.

The Diaguita, Atacameño and Calchaquí peoples ruled their own valleys and oases. Guarani villages were densely populated along the rivers. Mapuche society was organized into kin-based groups without a central ruler, a structure that later made them hard to conquer.
The Inca expanded into northern Chile and Argentina in the late 1400s, building roads and forts. The Mapuche resisted, stopping the Inca at the Maule River. Patagonia remained beyond Inca reach.

In 1520, Magellan passed the strait that bears his name. Spain founded Asunción (1537), Santiago (1541) and Buenos Aires (refounded in 1580). The Mapuche resisted Spain in the Arauco War, killing the conqueror Pedro de Valdivia in 1553.

Spain ruled from Santiago, Buenos Aires and Asunción, but the Mapuche held the land south of the Bío-Bío River. Jesuits organized Guarani missions in Paraguay, and Buenos Aires grew through smuggling. Wild cattle multiplied on the Pampas.

Spain founded Montevideo in the 1720s to counter Portuguese expansion. Jesuit missions thrived, and cattle hides became key exports. In Paraguay, settlers revolted against colonial authorities in the Comuneros revolt.

Spain created the Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata in 1776, centered on Buenos Aires. The Jesuits were expelled in 1767, and Guarani communities fought the Guarani War (1754 to 1756). Trade reforms boosted Buenos Aires.
British invasions of Buenos Aires were defeated in 1806 and 1807. Paraguay won independence in 1811, Argentina declared it in 1816, and San Martín crossed the Andes in 1817 to liberate Chile by 1818.

Uruguay became independent in 1828 as a buffer between Argentina and Brazil. Juan Manuel de Rosas ruled Argentina as a strongman, while Chile's Diego Portales built a stable conservative state. Britain seized the Falkland Islands in 1833.

Rosas fell in 1852, and Argentina adopted a constitution in 1853. The Paraguayan War (1864 to 1870) devastated Paraguay, which lost much of its male population. Chile grew wealthy through copper and wheat.

Argentina's 'Conquest of the Desert' seized Patagonia from Indigenous peoples, and Chile occupied Mapuche lands. Mass European immigration transformed Argentina and Uruguay, while Chile won nitrate-rich lands in the War of the Pacific.

Argentina became one of the world's richest countries, exporting beef and grain. Uruguay's José Batlle y Ordóñez began building a welfare state. Chile's nitrate wealth was shaken by strikes, including the 1907 Iquique massacre.

Argentina's 1912 Sáenz Peña Law introduced secret, compulsory male suffrage, bringing Hipólito Yrigoyen's Radicals to power in 1916. Uruguay expanded social reforms. Chile's nitrate exports suffered from new synthetic fertilizers, and Argentina's 1919 Tragic Week saw workers killed.

Argentina prospered on beef and grain exports, but striking ranch workers in Patagonia were massacred by the army. Chile's nitrate industry declined, and Carlos Ibáñez ruled as a strongman from 1927. Uruguay remained a stable democracy.
A 1930 coup in Argentina began the 'Infamous Decade' of military-backed rule. Uruguay hosted and won the first World Cup in 1930. Paraguay defeated Bolivia in the Chaco War (1932 to 1935).

In 1946, Juan Perón was elected president of Argentina, and with his wife Eva he built a powerful movement based on workers and nationalism. Chile's Gabriela Mistral won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1945, and Chilean women gained the vote in 1949.

Perón was overthrown in 1955, and Argentina alternated between weak civilian governments and military rule. Alfredo Stroessner seized power in Paraguay in 1954, beginning a 35-year dictatorship. Chile and Uruguay remained democracies, though Uruguay's economy stagnated.

The 1960 Valdivia earthquake in Chile was the strongest ever recorded. Argentina suffered repeated military coups, and the 1969 Cordobazo uprising shook its regime. Uruguay's Tupamaro guerrillas grew active, and Chile's Eduardo Frei began land reform.

Socialist Salvador Allende was elected in Chile in 1970, but the 1973 Pinochet coup began a brutal dictatorship. Uruguay also fell to military rule, and Argentina's 'Dirty War' (1976 to 1983) disappeared thousands.

Argentina's defeat in the 1982 Falklands War brought down its junta, and Argentine democracy returned in 1983. Uruguay's democracy returned in 1985, Stroessner fell in 1989, and Chilean democracy was restored in 1990.

Under Carlos Menem, Argentina pegged its peso to the dollar and privatized industries, taming inflation. The Mercosur trade bloc formed in 1991. Chile's economy grew fast under restored democracy, and Pinochet was arrested in London in 1998.

Argentina's economy collapsed in 2001, leading to default and political chaos, before recovering under the Kirchners. Michelle Bachelet became Chile's first female president in 2006. Left-leaning governments rose in Uruguay and Paraguay.

Uruguay legalized marijuana in 2013 under José Mujica. Argentine Jorge Bergoglio became Pope Francis in 2013. Chile rescued 33 trapped miners in 2010, but in 2019 mass protests erupted against inequality.

Chile's voters rejected two proposed new constitutions in 2022 and 2023. Argentina won the 2022 World Cup and elected libertarian Javier Milei in 2023, who imposed sweeping austerity. Pope Francis died in 2025.
